articles.title: Ayuda to roads: Where the House wants to add billions in the 2027 budget
articles.summary: Rappler tracks which lawmakers proposed a bigger budget for certain agencies and programs

blocks.text: The House of Representatives’ Budget Amendments Review Subcommittee (BARSC) on Thursday, October 1, recommended P116.32 billion in budget realignments, with social assistance programs and infrastructure projects among the biggest proposed beneficiaries.
The recommendations are not yet final. They still have to undergo deliberation and approval by the House plenary before they are included in the 2027 General Appropriations Bill.

Among the biggest proposed increases are allocations for government assistance programs, including the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situation (AICS) and the Medical Assistance for Indigent Patients (MAIFIP).
BARSC recommended an additional P25.81 billion for AICS and P24.97 billion for MAIFIP.

These programs have drawn scrutiny from watchdogs, including the People’s Budget Coalition, over concerns about their use in distributing government assistance through lawmakers and local officials, including through guarantee letters. The proposed increases also come ahead of the 2028 elections.

BARSC also recommended P10 billion for the Presidential Assistance to Farmers and Fisherfolk (PAFF), another social assistance program that was not included in the original 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP).
See the chart below to see how much funding was recommended by lawmakers:
BARSC also recommended additional funding for infrastructure projects under the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH):

items: P6.9 billion for national roads
P175.87 million for national bridges
P307.5 million for national buildings
P4.09 billion for convergence and special support programs

blocks.text: The total proposed increase for DPWH is P11.49 billion. Surigao del Sur 1st District Representative Romeo Momo was the proponent of the DPWH realignments.
The Department of Agriculture’s (DA) farm-to-market roads program may also receive an additional P4.96 billion.
BARSC likewise recommended an additional P1.55 billion for the DA’s Health Facilities Enhancement Program.

For education, an additional P952 million was proposed for the Department of Education’s Basic Education Facilities Fund, which covers the construction, repair, and improvement of public school infrastructure.
BARSC also recommended additional funding for confidential funds for several agencies:

items: P10 million for the National Police Commission
P30 million for the Department of Justice
P50 million for the National Bureau of Investigation
P50 million for the Office of the Ombudsman

blocks.text: The proposed 2027 NEP contains P4.368 billion in confidential funds and P6.405 billion in intelligence funds
Among government agencies, the Department of Health received the largest proposed increase from the BARSC, at P28.36 billion.
It was followed by DSWD with P26.86 billion, DA P16.44 billion, and DPWH P11.49 billion.
BARSC also recommended an additional P5 billion funding for the House of Representatives.
See the breakdown of additional funding recommended for other agencies below.

blocks.caption: hierarchy visualization

blocks.text: Rappler also tracked which lawmakers proposed the budget realignments during the BARSC deliberations.
South Cotabato 2nd District Representative Ferdinand Hernandez proposed the largest total realignment, at P29.23 billion.
His recommendations included P24.97 billion for MAIFIP, P2.1 billion for the Tertiary Education Subsidy, and P1.77 billion for the Tulong Dunong Program.
He was followed by Guimaras Representative JC Nava, who proposed P28.86 billion in additional funding for DSWD. A large portion, P25.86 billion, was for AICS.
House Appropriations Committee chair Mikaela Suansing proposed P11.95 billion in realignments, including the P10 billion allocation for the Presidential Assistance to Farmers and Fisherfolk.
Meanwhile, Momo proposed P11.49 billion in additional funding for DPWH, including the allocations for roads, bridges, buildings, and convergence programs.
See the full breakdown below.

blocks.caption: hierarchy visualization

blocks.text: The BARSC’s hearing on Thursday was criticized by budget watchdogs over its lack of transparency.
The hearing, which was supposed to start at 1 pm, only started at 5:07 pm.
Unlike regular budget hearings, members of the media are not allowed to cover BARSC meetings in person.

blocks.caption: Executive session? House’s budget amendment review panel livestream delayed for hours

blocks.text: People’s Budget Coalition co-convener and technical adviser AJ Montesa said the coalition had asked the House to allow media and civil society organizations to observe the proceedings in person. But, he said, their request was ignored.
During the hearing, Sunasing apologized to the public over the delay.
Civil society organizations also expressed dismay over the House leadership, saying they were sidelined in the budget process. – with research from Zara Pineda/Rappler.com

Zara Pineda is a Rappler volunteer and third-year AB Literature student majoring in Creative Writing and minoring in Commercial Regulations at De La Salle University. She also serves as editor of The LaSallian.

articles.title: Senator-judges must learn to contradict presiding officer in impeachment trial - lawyer
articles.summary: The senator-judges should not always agree with whatever the ruling made by the presiding officer amid the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, a lawyer said on Sunday.

blocks.text: Published October 4, 2026 8:18am
The senator-judges should not always agree with whatever the ruling made by the presiding officer amid the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, a lawyer said on Sunday.

“Ang presiding officer is presiding officer only. Kung ang iba mga senator-judges ay may contrary opinion sa sinasabi ng presiding officer, pwede naman nila ilagay 'yan sa boto. Unfortunately, mukhang pinababayan ng ibang senator-judges ang presiding officer, hindi nila sinasalungat,” said Rico Domingo, chairperson of Movement Against Disinformation, in an interview with Super Radyo dzBB.

(The presiding officer is a presiding officer only. If the other senator-judges have a contrary opinion to what the presiding officer is saying, they can put that to a vote. Unfortunately, it seems the other senator-judges are just leaving everything up to the presiding officer and not contradicting him.)

Domingo, a former president of the Philippine Bar Association, made the statement after former senator Antonio Trillanes IV held a press conference following the withdrawal of his name as witness in the impeachment trial of the Vice President.

Trillanes also urged Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero to prioritize the presentation of evidence over technicalities. The former senator also said that he felt unwelcome after the presiding officer refused to issue a subpoena for him to appear.
“Kung hindi abogado siguro ang presiding officer, eh papasukin nila ang sasabihin ni [former] Senator Trillanes,” said Domingo.
(If the presiding officer were perhaps not a lawyer, they would allow what former senator Trillanes has to say.)

“Unfortunately, masyadong technical ang presentation or the ruling of the presiding officer. Mukhang mayroong kaunting heeding si dating senator Trillanes na mukhang hindi siya papayagan even assuming na siya ay sinubpoena o hindi sinubpoena,” he added.

(Unfortunately, the presentation or the ruling of the presiding officer is too technical. It seems former senator Trillanes has a sense/apprehension that he won't be allowed to speak, even assuming he was subpoenaed or not.)
Moreover, Domingo said Escudero should have allowed the House prosecution panel to present Trillanes as a witness.

“Kung hindi sila tugon sa ruling ng presiding officer, for example in this particular case whether to present Senator Trillanes at that time, sana pinagbigyan na 'yun because after all, after juris prudence ang panel, the prosecution panel, has the right to present the witness at its own, hindi dapat papakialaman ng presiding officer,” he said.

(If they do not agree with the ruling of the presiding officer, for example in this particular case on whether to present Senator Trillanes at that time, hopefully that would have been granted because after all, according to jurisprudence, the panel—the prosecution panel—has the right to present witnesses at its own discretion, and the presiding officer should not interfere.)
However, Senator-judge Panfilo "Ping" Lacson earlier said the decision not to subpoena Trillanes as a witness in the trial did not rest solely with Escudero.

Impeachment court spokesperson Regie Tongol also said it was the prosecution which did not name Trillanes in time for the issuance of a subpoena. He reiterated that despite this, Trillanes still would have been allowed to appear as a voluntary witness. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: In southern Philippines, Tawi-Tawi builds feasts to be shared
articles.summary: Food becomes art, memory, and hospitality in Bongao during the Kamahardikaan sin Tawi-Tawi celebrations

items: Marilyn Jimlan, a municipal registrar in Bongao, Philippines, participated in the Kamahardikaan sin Tawi-Tawi celebrations by preparing a maligay display, showcasing local delicacies and family traditions.
The festival features two main elements: the dulang, a feast platter for sharing food, and the maligay, an architectural structure made of food that highlights creativity and local culture.
The event emphasizes the importance of food in cultural transmission, as Jimlan's cooking knowledge has been passed down through generations, and the shared meals foster community and connection.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
BONGAO, Philippines – Marilyn Jimlan was standing beside what looked less like a food display and more like an edible house.

Crabs, prawns, mantis shrimp, rice cakes, eggs, seafood, and native delicacies covered its tiers. Bills were tucked among the food. Darkened chickens sat high on the structure, while pastries hung from its sides. Around us, dozens of similarly elaborate creations filled the hall in Bongao on September 27.

Jimlan, 58, the municipal registrar of Bongao, had helped prepare one of the entries for the Maligay and Dulang displays, part of the Kamahardikaan sin Tawi-Tawi celebrations marking the province’s founding anniversary.
She has been cooking for most of her life.

“I started really cooking when I was about 14,” she said, speaking mostly in Filipino. Before that, she had already spent years watching and helping in the kitchen, learning the way many family recipes survive in the Philippines, through mothers, elders, repetition, and taste.

blocks.caption: A house-shaped food display rises with seafood, native delicacies, and other local produce, turning Tawi-Tawi’s culinary traditions into edible art. All photos by Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

blocks.text: Jimlan eventually taught her own children to cook. That detail explained much of what I was looking at. The festival was not simply about displaying what Tawi-Tawi could produce. It was also about knowledge passed from one generation to another, then placed proudly on a table for everyone to see.
At the center of the tradition are two things that can be confusing to someone seeing them for the first time.

The dulang is the feast platter, traditionally a large serving tray around which food is arranged and shared during gatherings, celebrations, religious occasions, weddings, and the welcoming of guests.

The maligay is the house-like structure built to hold and display food. Decorated with local delicacies and whatever imagination its makers can bring to it, the maligay turns the feast into architecture.

blocks.caption: Bongao municipal registrar Marilyn Jimlan explains the dishes and ingredients in a festival spread, many of them recipes and food traditions passed down through families.

blocks.text: During the festival, the distinction becomes obvious. One is the spread. The other rises from it.

Some maligay were almost architectural in scale, built with bamboo, trays, baskets, food, and ornamentation. There were crabs with brilliant orange shells, rock lobsters, mantis shrimp, clams, sea urchins, fish, fruits, root crops, eggs, and sweets.
Panyalam, a deep-fried rice cake, and other rice-based delicacies appeared again and again. Some displays carried cash bills, another expression of prosperity and generosity.

Several were crowned with blackened chickens. The dark color comes from the preparation associated with piyanggang, a Tausug chicken dish flavored with coconut that has been charred before being ground with spices.

Jimlan moved easily through the display, naming food and explaining preparations. She spoke about rice, native chicken, seafood, sweets, and coconut. Cooking, to her, did not sound like a special skill she had decided to acquire. It sounded like part of growing up.

That may be why the displays felt different from the food competitions I had seen elsewhere. Yes, there was artistry, and yes, there was judging. But the food was never meant to remain untouched after the photographs were taken. It would be eaten.

blocks.caption: Prawns, crabs, shellfish, eggs, and other ingredients crowd one of the elaborate displays at the Maligay and Dulang Festival in Bongao.

blocks.text: Once the judging was finished, people gathered around the displays. Food that had taken hours to cook and arrange was opened, passed around, and shared. The exhibition disappeared the way a feast is supposed to disappear, one helping at a time.
Jimlan made sure I did not leave empty-handed either. She gave me crab, bread, and okó-okó, the Sama-Bajau delicacy of rice cooked inside a sea urchin shell.
There was no ceremony to it. She simply packed food for me. Very Filipino. Very Mindanao. You visit, therefore you must eat. And chances are, you are not leaving empty-handed.

That gesture captured what the enormous maligay and dulang could easily obscure with their spectacle. Behind every arrangement were people who cleaned the seafood, cooked the rice, fried the pastries, prepared the chicken, tied the decorations, and decided where each piece should go.

blocks.caption: Piyanggang chicken and Philippine peso bills crown a maligay display, where food, artistry, and symbols of abundance come together during Tawi-Tawi’s provincial anniversary festivities.

blocks.text: The province’s geography explains much of what appears on the table. Tawi-Tawi is an archipelago, and life here is intimately tied to the sea. Seafood was not an accent in these displays. It was everywhere.

But food tells more than geography. It carries family history, trade, religion, and the relationships among the Sama, Sama Dilaut, Tausug, Jama Mapun, and other communities that have shaped Tawi-Tawi.

By then, I had spent days seeing the province through its festivals, dances, music, islands, and people. The Maligay and Dulang displays were the last major event I attended before leaving. Perhaps, that was why it stayed with me.

There are easier ways to explain culture. You can read its history, photograph its landmarks, watch its dances, and listen to its music. But sit beside its food, ask someone who cooked it where she learned, and watch that food passed from hand to hand, and something else becomes clear.
Culture is also what people decide is worth preparing again.
Marilyn Jimlan began cooking seriously at about 14. Decades later, she still cooks, and her children know how because she made sure the knowledge continued.
Around her stood houses made of food and great platters waiting to be shared. By the end, much of the feast was gone. Which, I realized, was exactly the point. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
articles.summary: Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.

blocks.text: Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.
Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.
Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.
On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel.

Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.
The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.
But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.
Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both.

The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers.
Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023.

"I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.
Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.
We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.
Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves.
"Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.
The new rules have divided opinion.

Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.
One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.

''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''
In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board.
"Get down, I say get down," he shouts.
But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world, external, others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.
Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent.
"The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.
Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption.
"We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says.
"The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.
For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income.
"I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."
Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety.
Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison.
But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.
Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.

The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.
He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message.
"There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.
For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.

articles.title: Cornell president says university 'must do better' after frat house rape allegations
articles.summary: Michael Kotlikoff described the allegations of a woman who says she was drugged and gang raped as "deeply disturbing".

blocks.text: Cornell University's president says the school "must do better" after a woman alleged she was drugged and raped by a group of men at a fraternity house.
In an eight-minute video statement released Saturday evening, Michael Kotlikoff described the allegations raised by the woman, identified only as Jane Doe, as "deeply disturbing".
The alleged incident has raised questions around the culture on campus of drug and alcohol use, and the way investigations were conducted in the case, Kotlikoff said.

Jane Doe was a 20-year-old student at the university when she says seven men from its Chi Phi fraternity assaulted her for hours in an incident involving alcohol and the drug ketamine on 19 October 2024.
She said she had reported the incident two weeks after it happened to Cornell University police, which investigated, but no charges were laid.
Last month, Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university, in which she alleged Cornell had failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved.
Kotlikoff said Cornell was "committed to investigating" the way the case was handled, and said the school administration and community "must do better".
"We must foster a culture in which sexual assault is inexcusable and ensure our community is empowered and understands informed consent," he said.
He added that university leaders need to create an environment where victims of sexual assault "feel safe coming forward and are treated with compassion and dignity".
As part of "broader work" that needs to happen, Kotlikoff said there should be a "serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life".
"Being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility for our own actions, for how we treat others, or for speaking up when someone may be at risk," he said.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul has said she was "deeply disturbed" by how the investigation was handled, and has appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James to lead a review of the case.
Kotlikoff said he supported the decision to appoint James to leaddddd a criminal investigation, and welcomed an independent review by a law firm of how Cornell has handled the matter.
Jane Doe said in her lawsuit that she was intoxicated during the alleged incident and could not provide consent.

articles.title: Why Canada is preparing for a (long shot) US invasion
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the military is running scenarios in the unlikely case the US invades Canada.

blocks.text: Prime Minister Mark Carney admitted last week that he has prepared for a once-unthinkable scenario - a US invasion.

Noting the risk was low and the likelihood highly improbable, he told the New York Times he had a responsibility to consider all possibilities as the US-Canada relationship is redefined under the Donald Trump presidency.
"That's just risk management," Carney said.
Trump's global tariffs and his often-repeated desire to make Canada the 51st state has led Canada to war game an attack by the Americans.
In 2025, the US president said it was "highly unlikely" that the US would ever use force against Canada. Instead he said, he would continue to exert economic pressures to obtain political aims.
"President Trump has done more than anyone to protect the great people of Canada," the White House told the BBC in a statement this week.
Military experts who spoke to the BBC also think an invasion is a long shot, pointing to the multiple ways the two countries work together on defence.
But the issue is clearly weighing on Canadians' minds.
In January, after the US captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, a Leger poll suggested that over 30% of Canadians believed that a US invasion was likely.

A war between Canada and the US would be complicated and almost difficult to imagine, said Lt-Gen Christopher Coates, a former military officer of 34 years with the Royal Canadian Air Force who held various senior positions.
"I was involved in military operations for my whole career, and we never considered the possibility that there would be a military attack coming from US territory," he told the BBC.
Coates, who had served on Nato missions, noted that Canada and the US collaborate on many aspects of military defence.
They are both members of the north Atlantic defence alliance, which mandates members to defend a fellow member-nation should they be attacked.
The two countries also conduct joint Arctic defence missions under the North American Aerospace Defence Command (NORAD), and frequently share intelligence.
Because of this, Coates said he believes an attack by the US on Canada would not begin with an armed assault, but rather with more discreet means like cyberwarfare.
After World War II, Canada and the US became natural allies for the latter part of the 20th Century, and have become heavily integrated economically, militarily and culturally.

But it wasn't always this way. In fact, a core tenet of Canada's identity is its resistance of US expansionism in the 18th and 19th Centuries, said Tim Foran, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum.
"Fear of the United States is foundational to the political project that is Canada," he said.
Canada was formed as a collection of British North American colonies who remained loyal to the British Crown when the colonies in the modern-day US rebelled.
Before the formation of Canada, the US had attempted to invade British North American colonies, taking control of Montreal in 1775 and nearly conquering Quebec City.

In the war of 1812, the Americans invaded what was known then as Upper Canada, Lower Canada and the maritime colonies repeatedly, resulting in a stalemate. During that war, British troops famously burned down the White House in retaliation.
Foran said that at the time, the colonies that later became Canada relied on Great Britain and its Royal Navy for its defence, as well as indigenous peoples who served as generals in major battles.
Canada again contemplated war with the US post-World War I in response to its growing power and influence.
It drafted a plan that was informed by secret trips to border cities made by Canadian army generals, who would pose as tourists and snap photos of bridges and highways for intelligence.
They also spoke to local residents to better understand their enemy.
A war was an unlikely scenario then, said Andrew Burtch, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum with expertise on Canada in the 20th Century, but the Canadians still wanted to be prepared.
"That's part of what militaries do," he said. "They envisage all sorts of different scenarios."

Even if a US invasion is extremely unlikely, Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor of national security at the University of New Haven in Connecticut, said the fact that Canadians were preparing was a sign of just how drastically the global order has shifted.

He added Canadian leaders do have hard questions to ask about how closely they want to continue working with the American military - a partnership that gives them valuable information should they want to harm Canada in any way.
"It's really doing harm to relationships with the United States, and there's a certain amount of legitimate fear," he said.
Americans might not take Trump's comments about making Canada the 51st state seriously, he said, but Canadians clearly do - and are prepared to defend themselves if needed.
So what would it be like if it happened?
The first phase of a war could be quite short.
According to the model used by the Canadian military, as reported on by the Globe and Mail newspaper earlier this year, a US attack would see Canada's strategic positions overwhelmed within a week
Its military would quickly be outnumbered, forcing Canadian forces to resort to guerilla-type warfare to try to suppress their enemy.
Allied nations like France and Britain would be called on to provide support and defence for Canada, the newspaper reported in January, citing senior government officials.
The theoretical model is believed to be the first time in a century that Canada planned for an American assault.
The modelling is on the lighter end of military combat planning, Coates said.

He said that Canada, unlike its Nato allies, was lagging behind when it came to having a response plan in place in the event of any ground invasion, and that it was now playing catch-up in this era of unpredictable geopolitics.

Part of that, he said, was made evident by a recent call by Canada's defence chief to drastically increase the size of its military, including the addition of as many as 300,000 lightly trained citizen soldiers.
An invasion of Canada might not be straightforward from the US point of view either.
Even with its outsized military, the US would have a difficult time getting buy-in for a fight with Canada, said Schmidt.
"I think you would have a large number of American officers who would resign if given the order to invade Canada," he said.
"They would see it as an illegal and immoral order."
Schmidt said Canadian soldiers and American soldiers routinely train together, and share a mutual respect.

But in the unlikely scenario that relations would deteriorate to the point of combat, Schmidt said the US would likely focus on acquiring valuable Canadian resources like oil and minerals, and political decapitation.
"You would see a a kind of operation that would mirror perhaps what you saw in Venezuela," he said, referring to US military action earlier this year to capture former Venezuelan President Maduro.
Although he acknowledged the US has greater military capacity, he said that "pound for pound" Canadian soldiers would be able to put up a fight.

articles.title: Pete Lacaba for National Artist. My mother would have approved.
articles.summary: Jose “Pete” Lacaba will be honored by fellow writers and artists in a tribute on October 10

blocks.text: One of my fond memories of my friend Jose “Pete” Lacaba, who will be honored by fellow writers and artists in an October 10 tribute, featured my late mother, Isabel Impelido Pimentel.

One morning in the ’80s, Pete stopped by our house in Cubao for a work meeting. Mommy invited him for lunch even though she didn’t have time to prepare. Lunch that day meant rice and boiled fish with saluyot (jute mallow) leaves, the type of food Mommy grew up with in Sinait, Ilocos Sur.
Pete sat down to eat with us and he appeared to enjoy the meal. After he left, Mommy told me: “He’s a good man. He ate our food.”
She shouldn’t be surprised, I explained. Pete may be a famous writer, but he is a down-to-earth guy who would enjoy a simple Ilocano meal.
Mommy eventually became a fan of Pete’s poetry. She even read them aloud to me one time — which worried me a little bit.
She thought “Paksiw na Ayungin” (Ayungin fish cooked in vinegar) was wonderful. But as she began reading the first two verses of “Pasyong Mahal ni San Jose” (The Holy Passion of Saint Joseph)…
“Pait, katam at martilyo, (Chisel, plane and hammer)“Ibubulong ko sa iyo (I will whisper to you)“Ang masaklap kong sikreto…” (My terrible secret)
…I knew I had to distract her and stop her from reading further ..
“Ah, Mommy, have you heard anything from Auntie Cadie?”

It worked. And I felt relieved. A devout Catholic, and a lay Carmelite, she probably would not have appreciated the rest of Pete’s poem, a meditation on exploitation (divine or otherwise) through the eyes of Saint Joseph.
“Hindi ko pa inaano (I haven’t even touched her)“Buntis na ang nobya ko.” (And my girlfriend’s already pregnant)
When my parents celebrated their 50th wedding anniversary in 2003, Mommy insisted that we invite Pete. He and Marra Lanot, who passed away recently, celebrated with us that evening.

blocks.caption: The personal is political: Honoring Marra PL Lanot

blocks.text: I was a UP student when I first met Pete in 1982 at the Galian ng Arte at Tula studio in Cubao at the launch of Days of Disquiet, Nights of Rage, his classic account of the First Quarter Storm.

Many of us were so impressed with the book that my friends Bertrand Quesada, then editor of Sinag, the paper of the UP College of Arts and Sciences, and managing editor Gani De Castro (and now a Rappler editor), decided to publish a full-page comic strip version of Days of Disquiet, Nights of Rage.
The next time I saw Pete was in the streets.

We were marching toward Liwasang Bonifacio during one of the countless protests after the assassination of Ninoy Aquino. It started to rain. When some protesters took out umbrellas, the more unruly rallyists started taunting them. “No umbrellas. We march in the rain!”
Pete didn’t appreciate that.
“Hindi problema ang payong (Umbrellas are not the problem),” he told the anti-umbrella marchers.

By then, Pete was a major collaborator with one of our best film directors, Lino Brocka. He wrote some of the best and most memorable Brocka films. Kapit sa Patalim (Clinging to a Knife) and Sister Stella L helped define what was then a vibrant protest culture. We were inspired by them, and even moved to action.

I remember how we marched toward Malacañang and passed a giant movie poster of Sister Stella L showing Vilma Santos with a raised fist. Fellow marchers yelled out the line from the movie: “Katarungan para kay Ka Dencio! (Justice for Ka Dencio!)”

I finally got to work with Pete after the EDSA revolution when I joined Midweek. I had just graduated from UP Diliman and actually had a choice. Work for a mainstream newspaper or TV station. Or join a small magazine few people had heard of, but led by two of the best writers in the country: Pete Lacaba and the late Greg Brillantes.
Choosing the latter was one of the smartest decisions I ever made. Until now, I remember what I learned from Pete and Greg whenever I’m writing.

blocks.caption: MIDWEEK. Pete Lacaba (3rd from right) and Greg Brillantes (partly hidden, seated next to him) with Neng Torres Yabut, Vivian de Lima, Melanie Manlogon (2nd from left) and the author.

blocks.text: Working with Pete and Greg wasn’t just about work of course. I will always treasure memories of our inuman (drinking sessions), especially at Davao Inihaw on Tomas Morato Avenue and later, at Pete’s house on Mother Ignacia Avenue in Quezon City.
Greg passed away last year before he was finally named National Artist for Literature, an honor that he should have received decades ago.

blocks.caption: Pareng Greg: Remembering the great Gregorio Brillantes

blocks.text: It’s Pete’s turn. Many of us believe that. Including the many artists and journalists who will be gathering at My Brother’s Mustache Bar in Quezon City for “Salinawit ni Pete: A Tribute” on Saturday, October 10.
Other important writers should be named with Pete, including great writers who have also passed on, Lualhati Bautista and Rogelio Sikat.
I hope it happens the way it happened for Greg.

blocks.caption: ARTISTS. The author with Pete Lacaba and Marra Lanot in 2013.

blocks.text: Jose F. Lacaba, my friend and mentor, poet, journalist, screen writer, translator and editor more than deserves to be our next National Artist for Literature or our next National Artist for Film.
Mommy would have agreed. – Rappler.com

Benjamin Pimentel is the author of ‘U.G. An Underground Tale’ published by Anvil Publishing which just released the 2nd printing of the 3rd edition. He is also a journalist and technology editor based in the San Francisco Bay Area, California, USA. Royalties from ‘U.G.’ are donated to Bantayog ng Mga Bayani.

articles.summary: Montreal Canadiens defenceman Lyle Odelein, who won a Stanley Cup with the team in 1993, has died at the age of 58. The Canadiens confirmed Odelein's death in a statement Saturday.

image.caption: The Montreal Canadiens confirmed the death of former player Lyle Odelein, pictured in 2009, in a statement Saturday. (Richard Wolowicz/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Sports
Montreal Canadiens defenceman Lyle Odelein, who won a Stanley Cup with the team in 1993, has died at the age of 58. The Canadiens confirmed Odelein's death in a statement Saturday.
Quill Lake, Sask., native scored 20 goals, 75 assists in 420 games with Montreal
Montreal Canadiens defenceman Lyle Odelein, who won a Stanley Cup with the team in 1993, has died at the age of 58.
The Canadiens confirmed Odelein's death in a statement Saturday.
The Pittsburgh Post-Gazette also reported Saturday that Odelein died of a heart attack. He played the last of his 16 NHL seasons with the Pittsburgh Penguins in 2005-06 and lived in the area.
Odelein from Quill Lake, Sask., scored 20 goals and had 75 assists in 420 games with Montreal between 1990 and 1996.
He ranked second in franchise history with 1,357 penalty minutes, and led the team in that category in each of his six seasons with the team.
The seventh-round pick of the Canadiens in 1986 played a career 1,056 NHL games with Montreal, New Jersey, Phoenix, Columbus, Chicago, Dallas and Pittsburgh.
"The entire Canadiens organization is saddened to learn of the passing of Lyle Odelein, who passed away Friday at the age of 58," the Canadiens said in a statement.
"The organization wishes to offer its most sincere condolences to Lyle Odelein's family, friends and close ones."

The Canadiens are saddened to learn of the passing of Stanley Cup champion Lyle Odelein.

News release ↓https://t.co/n2M44SKx7O—CanadiensMTL
Odelein was the first captain of the Columbus Blue Jackets when the team joined the NHL in 2000.
"Lyle is a significant part of our history, serving as our first captain and helping us celebrate our 25th season in March," the Blue Jackets wrote in a social media post on X on Saturday.

"He left an indelible mark on our organization and on our community. On the ice, Lyle was a fierce competitor and a Stanley Cup champion. Off the ice, he was warm, kind and quick with a smile and a kind word. He was a friend to all who knew him and will be sorely missed."
The Penguins also lamented Odelein's passing Saturday in social media posts.
"Lyle was known for his tough exterior on the ice, but we will always remember his generous heart and enormous laugh," the team wrote.

articles.title: Philippines voices concern over Myanmar airstrike deaths, injuries
articles.summary: The Philippines, chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), expressed concern over an airstrike in Myanmar's Rakhine state that caused deaths, injuries and destruction, and stood…

blocks.text: Published October 4, 2026 6:11am

Smoke rises as fire burns following a Myanmar military airstrike, according to a rebel group that controls the area and a local aid worker, in Kyauktaw, Rakhine State, Myanmar, in this screen grab obtained from a social media video released September 28, 2026. Social Media/via REUTERS

The Philippines, chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), expressed concern over an airstrike in Myanmar's Rakhine state that caused deaths, injuries and destruction, and stood ready to facilitate discussions within the regional bloc on how best to assist Myanmar.

"The Philippines is closely monitoring developments and expresses concern over the attacks which resulted in destruction, loss of lives and injuries to those affected," Foreign Affairs Assistant Secretary for ASEAN Affairs Ana Marie Hernando said in an email response on Saturday.
As ASEAN chair, Manila said it remained mindful of the views of all member states and would continue to be guided by the regional bloc's consensus-based approach.
The Philippines said it stood ready to facilitate discussions within ASEAN on ways to assist Myanmar, in line with the common aspiration of finding a solution that is "Myanmar-owned and led."
Monday's Kyauktaw airstrike, Rakhine's deadliest such attack since a December hospital bombing, killed 50 people and wounded dozens more.
Myanmar has been locked in a nationwide civil war since a 2021 coup, with an alliance of armed groups, including the Arakan Army, fighting against the military.
The protracted conflict has since killed around 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million in the impoverished Southeast Asian nation. —Reuters

articles.title: Met launches murder inquiry after man shot dead at London memorial service
articles.summary:
Forty-year-old victim declared dead at the scene in East Acton in a ‘senseless act of violence’

A murder investigation has been launched after a 40-year-old man was shot dead in a “senseless…

blocks.text: A murder investigation has been launched after a 40-year-old man was shot dead in a “senseless act of violence” during a memorial service in west London, police have said.
Police were called on Friday at 7.47pm after multiple shots were heard in East Acton.
Officers attended alongside the London ambulance service. The victim was treated at the scene on the junction of Braybrook Street and Erconwald Street, however, he was pronounced dead.
The Metropolitan police said about 40 to 50 people were at the scene, including children. The man’s family have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers.
A postmortem examination is scheduled to establish the cause of death, but the victim is believed to have sustained a gunshot wound, the force added.
No arrests have been made.
DCI Brian Howie, who is leading the investigation, said: “Our thoughts are with the family and friends of a man whose life was taken in a senseless act of violence.
“We understand a large number of people had gathered for a memorial service and what should have been a time to come together in remembrance has instead left a family devastated.
“We believe between 40 and 50 people, including children, were present when this incident occurred. Someone knows what happened and we need them to come forward.

“If you were around Erconwald Street, Braybrook Street, the surrounding roads or Wormwood Scrubs playground between 6pm and 8pm, please think carefully about what you saw. Did you see anyone carrying or concealing weapons, people on bicycles acting suspiciously or vehicles being driven at speed?
“We also want to hear from anyone with photographs, video, dashcam, doorbell or mobile phone footage or who has seen anything relevant on social media.”

articles.title: AI giants 'not being nearly careful enough,' warns outgoing OpenAI safety engineer
articles.summary: Days after President Donald Trump signed a voluntary pact with artificial intelligence giants, a former OpenAI worker said his industry needs the same safeguards as nuclear power or aviation.

image.caption: OpenAI has delayed plans for a public listing this year due to safety concernsImage: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: A safety engineer who recently quit ChatGPTcreator OpenAI warned Saturday that artificial intelligence (AI) firms were "not being nearly careful enough."
David Robinson's comments come amid growing concerns about AI becoming too powerful — a threat that US President Donald Trump has labeled a "hoax."
OpenAI and Anthropic recently disclosed cases in which their AI models slipped past safety controls, hid mistakes and hacked systems they were not meant to access.
How US, China could end the AI race
What did David Robinson write?
In an op-ed for The Atlantic, Robinson said AI needs guardrails similar to those for nuclear power and aviation, adding, "The time for trial and error is over."
He called for more emphasis on safety and research before US Big Tech develops more advanced AI models "so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster."
Robinson, who oversaw safety reports for 12 frontier AI-model launches, said the recent errors were typical because tech giants are prioritizing "speed and flexibility."
"An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to."
The former OpenAI employee noted that the firm relies on "iterative deployment." It releases new AI models first and only tightens safeguards after problems show up.
"As ​the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the ​level of care ‌that I believe is needed," Robinson, who worked at OpenAI for 3 1/2 years, added.

blocks.caption: Activists have staged protests calling on AI labs to slow developmentImage: Karl Mondon/AFP

blocks.text: ChatGPT creator insists AI is safe

OpenAI reacted to the latest criticism in a statement, "We're making sure our models don't become more capable than we can safely manage ​and secure, and ⁠we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down."
In recent months, there have been repeated warnings from technology experts and policymakers that AI models are advancing so fast they could take control and possibly wipe out humanity.
Despite those fears, US President Donald Trump is vehemently against stronger regulation, insisting that it will slow down innovation and make it harder for US AI models to beat Chinese rivals.
This week, Trump announced a voluntary safety pact with six companies — Nvidia, SpaceX, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Alphabet's Google.
The president described the deal as "morally binding,” even if it is not legally enforceable.
He also directed his administration to rename AI as "Super Intelligence" or SI.
A survey by Reuters/Ipsos last month found that three-quarters of Americans worry that AI giants are not doing enough to stop AI from causing serious harm to society.

articles.title: Tories plan to expand free childcare to high earners to end ‘cliff edge’
articles.summary:
Kemi Badenoch says those earning more than £100,000 should not be discouraged from working more

The Conservatives have unveiled a proposed £700m childcare giveaway for high earners ahead of…

blocks.text: The Conservatives have unveiled a proposed £700m childcare giveaway for high earners ahead of their annual conference, saying they would end the “cliff edge” where free entitlement ends at salaries above £100,000.

The plan, set out the day before the event begins in Birmingham, follows the earlier proposal by Kemi Badenoch’s party to abolish most stamp duty, another change to taxation that would disproportionately benefit wealthier people.

Under the current system, put in place under Rishi Sunak’s government, families with young children in England are eligible for 30 hours a week of free childcare, but this cuts off if one parent earns more than £100,000, irrespective of another parent’s salary.
Under the Conservative plans, this limit would be abolished, with all parents working 16 or more hours a week able to claim the childcare.
The party says it would cost aabout £700m a year, which it says would be paid for by cutting jobs at organisations such as Arts Council England and the Environment Agency.
In comments released to promote the idea, Badenoch said the current system was “absurd” and a disincentive to work more.
She said: “Conservatives believe that you shouldn’t be punished for working more, but this childcare cliff edge does exactly that.
“I’m a mum-of-three and I’ve had to make the same choices many families have had to make on work and childcare. Those choices are difficult already, government should not be making them harder.
“No one should be turning down a promotion or a pay rise because they literally cannot afford to earn more.

“It is often women who end up carrying more of the childcare responsibility so a system that makes it harder for them to progress in their careers is not helping families, it is not helping women and it is definitely not helping the economy.”

A Labour spokesperson said: “It tells you everything you need to know about the Tories that the first of their own tax policies they want to unpick is one helping higher earners. They clearly don’t want to admit that they set the thresholds in the first place.”
The idea of abolishing stamp duty on people’s primary residences in England and Northern Ireland was unveiled by Badenoch at last year’s conference, costing an estimated £9bn a year.

While some economists have argued that stamp duty can have a drag on the housing market and even the economy, as it disincentivises moving, scrapping it rather than reforming the tax would disproportionately benefit better-off people and those in London and south-east England.
The other main policy set out ahead of the conference was a plan to build 50,000 new prison spaces in England and Wales, a 50% expansion in capacity.

This would be paid for in part by slashing overseas aid to £1bn a year, a 90% cut on current plans. Under Keir Starmer, Labour said they would reduce aid from 0.5% of GDP to 0.3% by 2027, but even that lower proportion would still amount to £9bn a year.

When Reform UK announced plans to cut aid to £1bn a year, aid groups warned that this would not cover existing contributions to global bodies such as the UN and World Bank, shredding Britain’s international influence.

articles.title: UP, Manila HealthTek sign deal for telemedicine expansion
articles.summary: The University of the Philippines (UP) and Manila HealthTek Inc. have signed an agreement allowing the company to use the RxBox trademark for a biomedical telemetry device designed to support remote…

blocks.text: Published October 4, 2026 4:33am

The University of the Philippines (UP) and Manila HealthTek Inc. have signed an agreement allowing the company to use the RxBox trademark for a biomedical telemetry device designed to support remote medical consultations and patient monitoring.

The agreement covers the use of the RxBox trademark for a device that measures vital signs and transmits patient data over the internet, allowing healthcare workers in underserved areas to seek assessments and referrals from doctors remotely.

According to a press release, RxBox can measure and record blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, electrocardiogram (ECG) readings, and maternal-fetal data. The system also supports electronic health records, initial patient assessment and referrals to specialists.
UP President Angelo Jimenez and Manila HealthTek CEO and founder Dr. Raul Destura signed the trademark licensing agreement on Sept. 29, 2026, at the UP Manila Museum of a History of Ideas.

The RxBox project previously manufactured and deployed 1,000 units to local clinics in selected local government units, including in the CALABARZON region, where the devices were used to help healthcare workers assess patients and determine whether they needed referral to higher-level facilities.
The units were also deployed to referral centers during the COVID-19 pandemic to support remote patient monitoring and help inform treatment decisions.

Destura said Manila HealthTek is preparing to develop a new version of the device, called “RxBox Next Gen,” with the goal of expanding its use in support of the government’s Universal Health Care program.
“We are celebrating a Filipino innovation that has evolved and continues to find its purpose serving our world,” Jimenez said during the signing ceremony.

The project was developed by Filipino engineers and medical experts, with researchers from UP’s College of Medicine and Technology Transfer and Business Development Office among those involved in its development and technology transfer.
In his speech, DOST Secretary Renato Solidum Jr. said the DOST supported the RxBox project as part of efforts to develop technologies addressing healthcare needs in communities.
“This is Agham na Ramdam — science you can feel. Science that reaches the grassroots, answers our people’s needs, and makes a tangible difference every single day,” Solidum said.
The parties said they intend to continue working with government, academe and industry partners to expand the adoption and commercialization of the technology.

“Let us be relentless in developing this technology. Today, we recommit ourselves until RxBox reaches more communities and until Filipino innovation stands confidently before the world,” de Guzman said. — MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Trump urges calls to Arkansas senator in push for permanent daylight saving time
articles.summary:
President appeared to share phone number of Tom Cotton for people to call to push him to support measure

Donald Trump on…

blocks.text: Donald Trump on Saturday put pressure on the US senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas to support a bill to make daylight saving time permanent, urging Americans to call what appeared to be the personal cellphone number of his fellow Republican and the chair of the Senate intelligence committee.

The Sunshine Protection Act passed the House in July, but it faces roadblocks in the Senate, where some Republicans are strongly opposed to it. Proponents, including the president and his administration, argue that the change would provide more daylight during the times that Americans are most active. Detractors said permanent daylight saving time would lead to darker and potentially more hazardous winter mornings when children will be waiting for school buses and parents will be driving to work in darkness.

Daylight saving time is that period between spring and fall when clocks in most parts of the US are set one hour ahead of standard time. Not all states observe it – and under the bill, states can opt out of the change if their respective legislatures act to do so before the bill’s enactment.

“For some reason, Tom is stopping the Bill,” Trump wrote on social media, noting that passing the proposal would give professional golfers more time on the greens. “So, everyone in Arkansas … tell Tom to, GET IT DONE! It will be appreciated by all.”
Trump included a phone number with an Arkansas area code. The Associated Press called the number, but no one answered – and the voicemail box was full.
The Guardian also called and was greeted with a message from the service carrier saying, “The wireless customer you are calling is not available. Please try again later.”

Cotton, a member of Republican leadership, reiterated his opposition to permanent daylight saving time in a social media post of his own on Saturday afternoon, though he is not the only Republican who opposes it.

“No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent daylight saving time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” he wrote. “Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first.”

Cotton wrote that many Arkansans wouldn’t get sunrise until 8am or 8.30am during the dead of winter if daylight saving time was permanent. In that case, at the height of winter, those in Seattle wouldn’t see sunrise until 9am; and in Williston, North Dakota, the sun wouldn’t rise until nearly 9.45am, Cotton wrote.
But Trump, who is spending the day at his northern Virginia golf club before traveling to Ohio later Saturday, promptly fired back.

“If Tom Cotton were putting Arkansas first, he would give them an extra hour of daylight and, more importantly, they wouldn’t have to run all over their houses, farms, work places, and everywhere else, twice a year, having to change their Clocks, and often forgetting to do so,” Trump said. The president added that he believed “that is really putting Arkansas FIRST”.
This is not the first time Trump has released personal information about a US senator.

While competing for the 2016 Republican presidential nomination, the US senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina described Trump as “unfit for office” after Trump denigrated the military service of the US senator John McCain of Arizona. Trump then released Graham’s personal cellphone number. That prompted a viral video in which the senator dramatically destroyed a series of flip phones. Graham later became a close ally of Trump before dying in July. McCain died in 2018.

A 2025 poll from the AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research shows that if forced to choose, most Americans would prefer to keep that extra hour of daylight in the evening. Only 12% of US adults favor the current system of daylight saving time, which requires people in most states to reset clocks twice a year, while 47% are opposed and 40% are neutral.

Members of Congress have long been interested in the potential benefits and costs of daylight saving time since it was first adopted as a wartime measure in 1942 during the second world war. The Senate passed a bill in 2022 to make daylight saving time permanent, but it stalled in the House.

articles.title: Pakistan vs. Afghanistan: From allies and neighbors to war
articles.summary: For years, Pakistan supported the Taliban in Afghanistan. But now Pakistan is bombing its neighbor. How the former allies became adversaries and why negotiations keep failing.

image.caption: Taliban security forces after a Pakistani airstrike in Khost, September 2026Image: AFP

blocks.text: On Thursday night, Pakistan attacked targets in Afghanistan. The results of that attack are disputed. The Taliban, the Islamic fundamentalist nationalist movement that controls Afghanistan, says that between nine and 10 civilians were killed, including women and children. But Pakistan claims the strike killed 22 militants and destroyed weapons and ammunition depots.
These early October attacks are just the latest escalation in a conflict between the two countries that reignited mid-September, after months of comparative calm.

The conflict was sparked again after a series of attacks on Pakistani security forces. On September 18, an attack on a police compound in the northwestern city of Kohat resulted in the deaths of 31 people and more than 100 injured. A splinter group belonging to the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, claimed responsibility for the attack in Kohat, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, bordering Afghanistan.
Pakistan accused Afghanistan of providing the TTP with a safe haven. Afghanistan denies this but clashes at the border and then airstrikes by Pakistan followed.

blocks.caption: Pakistani security officials inspect a mosque destroyed in an attack in the border town of Kohat, September 2026Image: Hussain Ali/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: TTP and Taliban: A complex relationship

The TTP in Pakistan is not the same as Afghanistan's Taliban. Although it does have close ideological and personnel ties to the Afghan Taliban, it is an independent organization that fights the Pakistani state.

Many of its fighters sided with the Taliban during that country's long-running insurgency against international and US troops. This is why, after the Taliban returned to power in 2021, the TTP gained more room and more leverage. This has meant that Afghanistan — a former ally of Pakistan — has increasingly become a threat to its neighbor.
Pakistan has asked the Taliban to take action against the TTP, but the close connection between the two make this difficult.

"Because of these personal connections and networks, it is extremely difficult for the Afghan Taliban to break away," says Conrad Schetter, director of the Bonn International Center for Conflict Studies, or BICC.
How 5 years of Taliban rule have changed Afghanistan

The connections don't mean that the Taliban has any control over the TTP. There are certainly historical connections between the two, but Schetter doesn't believe that equals any sort of strong, direct influence.

"The Taliban are simply not prepared to take orders from Islamabad," adds Thomas Ruttig, co-director of the Afghanistan Analysts Network, a think tank working between Kabul and Berlin. "They won't let anyone outside interfere."
This means the Pakistani policy of supporting the Taliban in order to gain influence in Afghanistan hasn't worked.
Difficult borders

There's also another older conflict that has an impact on the current situation. This involves what is known as the Durand Line, drawn in 1893 by a British diplomat and an Afghan emir to mark spheres of influence between British India and Afghanistan.

The current border between Afghanistan and Pakistan follows the Durand Line and also divides an area on both sides, homeland to Pashtuns, who make up the largest ethnic group in Afghanistan and second largest in Pakistan.
So the border dispute here isn't just about territory, it's also about identity.
"Ethnic and nationalist elements play a significant role in the conflict," Schetter tells DW. Many Pashtuns still refuse to accept the border that the Durand Line created.

In Pakistan, the country's long-running rivalry with India also plays a part. A friendly Afghanistan would have been advantageous for Pakistan. But India has also strengthened its ties to the Taliban.

"While Islamabad once viewed Afghanistan as a source of 'strategic depth' in its rivalry with India, it now increasingly views its north-western neighbor as a liability," an analysis by British think tank Chatham House notes.
Pakistan exerts pressure

Pakistan still has power over Afghanistan, though. As a landlocked country, Afghanistan relies on trade routes through neighboring countries, and Pakistan in particular. Pakistan can use border closures and trade restrictions to exert pressure even as the Taliban regime is trying to reduce dependence on Pakistan and find new economic and political partners.

blocks.caption: A Taliban soldier with an anti-aircraft gun on the border with Pakistan in April 2026Image: AFP

blocks.text: Trade and security considerations are now becoming tangled. Pakistan has held talks with the TTP that were mediated by the Taliban and ceasefires were agreed upon. Talks between Pakistan and Afghanistan also took place. But none of the temporary agreements resolved the crucial question of how to prevent attacks on Pakistan from Afghan territory.

So in parallel with diplomacy, Pakistan has also been relying on economic and political pressure, for example, by closing borders and restricting trade and by sending Afghan refugees back into Afghanistan.

An analysis by the US-based Council on Foreign Relations notes that the Taliban are worried that if they crack down on the TTP too hard, they will drive the group towards another extremist militant group, the Islamic State in Khorasan Province or IS-K. This group opposes the Taliban.

The conflict recently escalated to another level. At the end of September, Kabul reported 28 killed and 32 captured fighters who had infiltrated Afghanistan from Nuristan province, Pakistan. The Taliban accused Pakistan of supporting its armed opponents, something Pakistan has denied.

"It is known from past decades that Pakistan has regularly supported armed groups on the Afghan side — for example, the Mujahideen during the Soviet occupation and later the Taliban," Ruttig points out. "What's new though is that Pakistan apparently also supports parts of today's armed anti-Taliban opposition."
Significant escalation
This is turning the dispute over the TTP into a larger conflict in which both sides accuse each other of supporting armed groups from the other's territory.

British think tank Chatham House speaks of a significant escalation compared to previous border skirmishes. Worryingly, a conflict over armed groups and border incidents is turning into a direct confrontation between the two nation states.
Ruttig believes that it would be possible to contain the spiraling violence if both sides return to negotiations.

"If both sides were willing to return to the negotiating table — perhaps with international mediation —there would be ways to contain the conflict and, above all, to protect the civilian population on both sides," he argues.
Militants kill dozens of security officers in Pakistan

In a late September commentary in Pakistani weekly magazine The Friday Times, Pakistani analyst Saqib Ali Khan advocates for several things that could ease the tensions. That includes a reliable channel between Islamabad and Kabul, a separate approach for armed groups and greater involvement of the population along the border.
The conflict, he argues, is not merely a dispute between two governments but also a security, border, economic and regional conflict.
"Along those lines, there would have to be a shift in perspective on both sides," Schetter concludes.
In the long term, greater economic integration is also needed, he adds, so that Pakistan and Afghanistan do not define their relationship solely through security and power issues.
This story was originally published in German.

articles.title: Tennessee's prison chief resigns after botched execution of murderer Christa Pike
articles.summary: Prison commissioner Frank Strada insisted his team followed protocol, even after two doses of anesthetic failed to kill convicted murderer Christa Pike.

image.caption: Christa Pike was 18 when she killed a fellow student in 1995 [FILE: December 2007]Image: J. Miles Cary/Knoxville News Sentinel/USA TODAY NETWORK/REUTERS

blocks.text: The head of the prison system in the US state of Tennessee is resigning after the execution of convicted murderer Christa Pike went wrong, the state governor said Saturday.
Witnesses said Pike was still breathing and moaning after two doses of the anesthetic pentobarbital failed to kill her during Wednesday's procedure.
The attempt was halted and she was transferred to hospital in critical condition.
It was the second time this year that an execution in the southern state had to be halted.
What do we know about the resignation?
Governor Bill Lee said in a statement that prison commissioner Frank Strada would leave his post sometime this month.
Lee said he thanked Strada for "his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment."
In the same statement, Strada acknowledged that: "Stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward."
He said the department had carried out its responsibilities in accordance with established protocol, but called the review "entirely appropriate and necessary."
The state has halted further executions until the review has been completed.
Strada took on the role in January 2023. Nearly two years later, he announced that Tennessee would, from then on, only use pentobarbital for lethal injections of death-row inmates.
What went wrong?
Tennessee authorities have yet to explain why Pike survived.
Her attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.
Pike's lawyers said Friday that she is unconsciousand on a ventilator in hospital.
While they welcomed Strada's departure, her legal team said, “It does nothing to help Christa now.”
"What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," the four-lawyer team said.
"We hope the governor's call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system," it added.
Had the drugs killed Pike, she would have been the first woman executed by the state since 1820.
Pike was sentenced to death in 1996, aged 20, for the murder of Colleen Slemmer, whom Pike was convinced was trying to steal her boyfriend.
Slemmer, who was 19, was tortured and killed in a remote area near the University of Tennessee in Knoxville.
