articles.title: Ombudsman Remulla flags lack of data sharing with Customs in anti-smuggling campaign
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Saturday said the lack of data sharing with the Bureau of Customs (BOC) has hampered efforts to build strong anti-smuggling cases.

blocks.text: Published October 3, 2026 9:30pm
Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Saturday said the lack of data sharing with the Bureau of Customs (BOC) has hampered efforts to build strong anti-smuggling cases.
In his radio program, Remulla said the BOC has failed to provide complete documentation needed to file or investigate cases.

“Nagkaroon kami ng meeting ng Customs tsaka DOJ para tumigil na ang kalokohang ito sa smuggling. Ang problema mo lagi 'yung sa Customs, ayaw nila kumpletuhin ‘yung documentation para ma-dismiss ang kaso. Ifa-file namin 'yung kaso, o kaya imbestigahan namin. Sabay kapag hinihingi na namin 'yung dokumento ayaw dumating ng ibang dokumento,” Remulla said.

(We had a meeting with Customs and the DOJ to stop this smuggling nonsense. The problem is always with Customs—they do not want to complete the documentation, so the case will be dismissed. We will file the case, or we will investigate it. But when we ask for the documents, some of them do not arrive.)
“Walang data sharing. At least ang DBM [Department of Budget and Management] pumayag na sa data sharing. Ngayon Customs ang icha-challenge namin,” he added.
(There is no data sharing. At least the DBM has agreed to data sharing. Now we will challenge Customs.)
Earlier, the Department of Justice (DOJ), National Bureau of Investigation (NBI), and BOC signed a memorandum of agreement (MOA) aimed at combating economic sabotage.
Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida, BOC Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno, and NBI Director Melvin Matibag signed the agreement, with Remulla serving as a witness.
“Under this agreement, we commit to the timely exchange of information so that what one agency discovers, the others can act on,” Vida said in his speech.
According to Vida, the agencies will form a joint task force and technical working group within 30 days. — Jamil Santos/VBL, GMA News

articles.title: UK-Iran national arrested over alleged bomb plot at RAF Fairford released on bail
articles.summary:
The 25-year-old was the sixth man detained as counter-terrorism police investigate ‘possible foreign state involvement’

A sixth man who was arrested in connection with a suspected terrorist…

blocks.text: A sixth man who was arrested in connection with a suspected terrorist plot at RAF Fairford has been released on bail.
The 25-year-old, a dual UK-Iranian national, was arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts under section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006.
He was detained on Thursday in the borough of Westminster, London, where searches of two properties have now concluded.
The investigation into the incident is still under way, counter-terrorism police said.
Last weekend, five British nationals, all in their mid-20s, were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and terrorism and then bailed.
The arrests were made after three suspicious vans were spotted near the military site in Gloucestershire.

blocks.caption: Five men were arrested last weekend after police were alerted to suspicious vans near RAF Fairford. Photograph: BBC

blocks.text: Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, previously said the investigation was “hugely complex”, adding that specialist teams were “interrogating multiple lines of inquiry”.
She said: “As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement.”
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said there were “strong indications” Iran played a part in the incident near the Gloucestershire military base.
RAF Fairford has been used in recent months by US bombers after former prime minister Keir Starmer granted Washington permission to use British bases for “defensive” strikes against Tehran.

blocks.caption: A B‑1B Lancer bomber departs RAF Fairford airbase after police declared a major incident at the base last weekend. Photograph: Toby Shepheard/Reuters

blocks.text: Counter-terrorism police have said a quantity of petrol, but no explosive devices, was found in the vans that had sparked the security alert near the airbase.
On Thursday, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, claimed Israel handed Britain intelligence about the suspected terror plot.
Netanyahu said his country warned UK authorities about the “Iranian-sponsored attack” shortly before Britain’s announcement of a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

articles.title: B.C. lawyer found to have misappropriated $117K from dementia-stricken client
articles.summary: Leonard Hil Marriott also prepared documents to give himself 50 per cent ownership of the woman's condo and 75 per cent of her estate.

image.caption: A Law Society of B.C. tribunal says disgraced Vernon lawyer Leonard Hil Marriott misappropriated $117,000 from a dementia-stricken client. (Manjula Dufresne/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Leonard Hil Marriott also prepared documents to give himself 50 per cent ownership of the woman's condo and 75 per cent of her estate.
Tribunal defines misappropriation as 'tantamount to theft' in ruling against former lawyer Leonard Marriott
A Vernon lawyer already banned from practicing law for improper dealings with elderly clients has now been found to have misappropriated $117,000 from a female client with dementia.
The ruling against Leonard Hil Marriott is detailed in a Sept. 24 decision of a Law Society of British Columbia tribunal. The Society defines misappropriation as "tantamount to theft."
The decision says Marriott used the woman's money to buy an apartment for himself and to pay out another client's estate.
"The purported loan was contrary to [Marriott's] duty of loyalty and duty to not use his position for personal advantage," reads the decision.
It says Marriott has not repaid the money.

items: Law practice of disgraced Vernon lawyer seized by B.C.'s legal regulator

blocks.text: Last year, the Law Society banned Marriott for 10 years after he was found guilty of professional misconduct in cases involving two unrelated elderly clients.
The newest decision concerns a third client, a woman who was 84 when Marriott began acting on her behalf in 2017.
It says in 2018, Marriott prepared a power of attorney agreement that authorized him "to make decisions and do anything on the [woman's] behalf in relation to her financial affairs."
50% of her condo, 75% of her estate
In addition to the misappropriated funds, the Law Society says Marriot arranged paperwork to give himself a half ownership stake in her condo, worth almost $400,000 at the time.
Once he was on the property title, a maintenance enforcement order for unpaid child support was registered against the property by his former spouse. The order was eventually removed.
In March of last year, Marriott transferred legal title back to the woman at the request of the Law Society.

items: White collar criminals try to justify their actions to themselves, experts say

blocks.text: Marriott also created a will for the woman, naming himself executor and recipient of 75 per cent of her estate, according to the decision.
The disgraced lawyer said that he was aware the woman suffered from progressive dementia and claimed to have developed a "close familial-like relationship" with her.

While he admitted to the majority of the facts in the case, he argued unsuccessfully that the Law Society should deem the $117,000 an "improper withdrawal of funds," a less serious finding than misappropriation.
'Leaves people frustrated'

Speaking generally, B.C. forensic accountant and certified fraud examiner Marilyn Mellis said the findings of a regulatory body like the Law Society would not trigger a criminal charge or investigation because determining criminality is outside its scope.
Mellis said in her experience, it is rare for police or the Crown to pursue prosecution in cases of alleged white collar wrongdoing.
"They just don't," said Mellis. "They're just not interested in it, and it leaves people frustrated."

items: Edmonton man arrested in grandparent scam also charged with sex assault of teen girl: Winnipeg police

blocks.text: Mellis, who is based in Peachland, says regulatory bodies do not have the power to seek repayment for victims.
"They have no right to demand it, that's up to the court if the process goes through either civil or criminal [proceedings]," she said.

items: Disgraced former Manitoba law dean racked up millions in Swiss debt ahead of France arrest, documents suggest

blocks.text: Three years ago, the woman's family filed a civil suit in B.C. Supreme Court alleging Marriott conspired to divert her money for his benefit and to gain control of her property.
Marriott denied the allegations, stating in a response that he "always followed the instructions … while she had capacity to give such instruction and otherwise always acted in her best interest."
In a separate petition, family members have asked the court to appoint them as the woman's legal guardians. The case is still before the courts.
After his ban in 2025, Marriott's North Valley Law practice was seized by the Law Society after he was found to still be controlling solicitor trust accounts.
CBC News attempted to reach Marriott for comment, but did not hear back.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Karin Larsen is a former Olympian and award-winning sports broadcaster who covers news and sports for CBC Vancouver.

articles.title: Greece returns remains of Czar Samuel to Bulgaria
articles.summary: A warrior emperor who ruled the Bulgarian Empire in the Middle Ages, Czar Samuel is a symbol of Bulgarian national identity. But his remains have been in Greece for decades – and he is also claimed…

image.caption: A warrior emperor who ruled the Bulgarian Empire in the Middle Ages, Czar Samuel is a symbol of Bulgarian national identityImage: ArTo/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: The remains of one of Bulgaria's most important medieval rulers were set to arrive in the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, on Saturday after decades of negotiations with neighboring Greece.

Czar Samuel ruled the First Bulgarian Empire from 997 to 1014, gradually extending his authority over a swathe of the Balkans as far south as Lake Ohrid, now in North Macedonia on the border with Albania.
But Samuel's rule was also characterized by conflict with the Byzantine Empire which ultimately defeated his army at the Battle of Kleidion in 1014.
Samuel is said to have died of shock when thousands of his defeated soldiers returned home having been blinded by order of Byzantine Emperor Basil II, known as Boulgaroktonos – the "Bulgar Slayer."

The Bulgarian lands fell under Byzantine rule four years later but Czar Samuel is still considered a symbol of Bulgarian national identity today, and his remains – discovered in a Greek border area 60 years ago – are set to be received with full state honors.

They are set to be flown to Sofia aboard a military aircraft accompanied by a fighter jet escort before a 21-gun salute and a procession to the Church of St. Sophia, where the public will be able to pay respects.
Free trains to the capital are being provided for the occasion, with some 750 police on duty during the handover ceremony.
Through the ages in Sofia
Bulgaria: 'Czar Samuel unites us'

"These are items that belong to both our peoples; they constitute our memory and our bond, and our compatriots and future generations deserve and must have the opportunity to pay tribute to their ancestors," said Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev at a ceremony held at Museum of Byzantine Civilization in Thessaloniki, Greece, ahead of the handover.
Bulgaria officially opened talks on the return of the remains in 2007, and they became a major issue in relations with their southern neighbor.

"If, in the past, Czar Samuel divided us, I can say that today he unites us," said Radev. "He strengthens our strategic cooperation and makes the historical relations between our states and peoples even stronger."
Greece hopes for return of Parthenon Marbles

Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis, speaking alongside Radev, acknowledged that the remains of Czar Samuel have "incalculable cultural and spiritual but also emotional value" for Bulgaria, adding: "The global community is re-evaluating its long-standing stance on protecting cultural heritage."
In return, Greece is set to receive 48 sentimental objects pillaged by Bulgarian troops from churches and monasteries in northern Greece during the First World War.

Some prominent Greek academics and religious leaders have criticized the exchange as inadequate on the Bulgarian side, but Mitsotakis said he hoped Saturday's ceremony would bolster Greece's international campaign to return the Parthenon Marbles, a collection of 2,500-year-old marble sculptures taken from the Acropolis in Athens and later displayed in the British Museum.

"This shift is embodied by today's initiative, which rests on the obvious principle that monuments and historical heirlooms cannot be treated as spoils of war, nor as the result of circumstances subsequent to their creation."
Greece: How the Jewish cemetery in Thessaloniki disappeared
Czar Samuel: does North Macedonia also have a claim?
However, Bulgaria is not the only country to claim Czar Samuel, who is also celebrated with a huge statue in Skopje, the capital of North Macedonia.

"The bones return, the conflict remains! Samuel once again [contested] between Skopje and Sofia!" declared the Albanian-language newspaper Koha, while Skopje daily Sloboden Pechat called the handover another "battle over history."

In 2022, a bilateral commission recommended that Samuel be presented as the head of a state that "most contemporary historiographers consider to be the Bulgarian Empire" – territory which is now North Macedonia.
"Samuel occupies an important place in the historical narrative both in Bulgaria and in North Macedonia," Dimitar Bechev, a researcher at the Carnegie Europe think tank, told the AFP news agency.

Indeed, history has been playing a major role in the run-up to this month's Bulgarian presidential election, with incumbent President Iliana Iotova, backed by Prime Minister Radev, promoting a more neutral position between the European Union and NATO – both of which Bulgaria belongs to – and Russia.

"Radev is looking to attract the patriotic electorate," said analyst Bechev, adding that the return of the remains to Sofia "aims to underline the Bulgarian character of the Slavic population of Macedonia."
Gen Z leads Bulgaria's mass anti-corruption protests

articles.summary: Authorities in Spain rescued some 90 people after heavy rain sparked flooding in the town of Madrigueras. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez expressed his condolences to the family of a 102-year-old woman…

image.caption: The flooding wreaked havoc on the town of Madrigueras in Spain's Castilla-La Mancha regionImage: Eva Manez/REUTERS

blocks.text: Floods in the Spanish southeastern town of Madrigueras have killed an 102-year-old woman, regional authorities said.
Madrigueras, which has a population of around 4,000 residents, is located near the city of Albacete in the Spanish autonomous community of Castilla-La Mancha.
Authorities said 90 people had to be rescued due to flooding in the town.
Local Spanish media said the elderly woman was found dead in her home after the floodwaters had reached a depth of one meter (3.2 feet).
The floods in the region were caused by persistent torrential rainfall on Friday. Spanish authorities said around 140 liters of rainfall per square meter came down in Madrigueras.

blocks.caption: The flooding in Madrigueras also damaged vehicles in the town Image: Eva Manez/REUTERS

blocks.text: Sanchez: Spanish government monitoring flood situation

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, in a post on X, said his government is monitoring the situation. He also expressed his regards to the family of the woman who died in the flooding in Madrigueras.
Spanish meteorological authorities said heavy rainfall is expected to continue in eastern Spain through Sunday.
The torrential rain and flooding comes after the Mediterranean country witnessed its hottest summer on record this year.
Deadly wildfires were reported in Spain's north and south in recent months due to frequent hot, dry conditions.

articles.title: Protesters across Spain demand action over housing crisis
articles.summary: More than 50 protests are planned to take place on Saturday after the government failed to get emergency legislation through parliament.

blocks.text: The legislation put forward in Congress on Friday was divided into two separate decrees.

The first decree included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by so-called "vulture funds".
The second decree included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Tenant's Union.
MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166.

Prior to the vote, the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country.
However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure.
Sánchez's ruling coalition hurriedly drew up the decree laws in an effort to defuse the housing protests that were sparked when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted in September.
The social backlash led to the company that owns Abascal's flat, Urbagestión, negotiating her return to the flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued.

articles.title: City of Saskatoon cancels in-person count of unsheltered people over safety concerns
articles.summary: The point-in-time count was scheduled for Tuesday, and about 250 volunteers had been trained.

image.caption: One of the tents at an encampment in Saskatoon along Avenue K between 19th and 20th Streets on Sept. 23, 2026. (Jeremy Warren/CBC)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan
The point-in-time count was scheduled for Tuesday, and about 250 volunteers had been trained.
Concerns are 'related to protest activity,' city says
The City of Saskatoon says it won't fully conduct its in-person point-in-time count of people experiencing homelessness this year.
The count was supposed to happen Tuesday, with about 250 trained volunteers attempting to quantify the number of people in the city who don't have homes.

In a Friday news release, the city said the decision to cancel the in-person count was made due to "safety concerns related to potential protest activity which may affect the safety of volunteers, staff and community partners participating in the count."
The city said safety concerns have been heightened in recent weeks.

The fire department had warned that it planned to remove a west-side encampment occupied by more than 100 people, but the removal was paused after protests from those living there and the people who support them.
“If they want to say that, it’s like a kick in the head,” said David Fineday, an advocate who lives in the encampment.
“It’s giving these people a negative message … It’s not a protest, we’re not marching anywhere, we’re standing up here for our rights.”
Advocates filed an application for a court injunction to stop the fire department from removing part of the encampment, but that was rejected by a judge.

items: Judge reserves decision on injunction against Saskatoon clearing homeless encampment

blocks.text: “The safety of volunteers, community partners, staff and people experiencing homelessness must come first,” Lesley Anderson, the city's director of planning and development, said in Friday's news release.

“We are grateful to everyone who was prepared to take part in this year’s Point-in-Time Count. Their continued commitment helps Saskatoon better understand homelessness and advocate for the coordinated supports our community needs.”

The release said the city will work with the fire department to estimate the number of people living in Saskatoon's various encampments and will also count the number of people staying in emergency shelters, transitional housing and other systems.
“Why are they studying us?” Fineday asked. “Maybe instead of doing a PiT count and spending a quarter of Saskatoon’s budget on the police, maybe they should spend that much on affordable housing.”

items: Saskatoon tent encampment eviction delayed until Thursday

blocks.text: The primary limitation to the change of plan is that the 2026 count will not include information collected directly from unsheltered people.
The city's release said a more comprehensive version of the point-in-time count, including a full enumeration and survey, is already planned for 2027.
The 2025 count identified 1,931 homeless people in Saskatoon.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Halyna Mihalik is a journalist and weather specialist for CBC Saskatchewan. She holds a degree in journalism from the University of Regina. Halyna enjoys stories about advocacy, local politics and rural communities. Send Halyna news tips at halyna.mihalik@cbc.ca

articles.title: UK-Iranian dual national bailed after RAF Fairford incident arrest
articles.summary: The 25-year-old man was arrested in the London borough of Westminster on Thursday.

blocks.text: A UK-Iranian dual national arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with an incident at RAF Fairford has been released on bail.
The 25-year-old man was arrested in the London borough of Westminster on Thursday. Searches of two properties in the same area have now finished.
A major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated after police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase in Gloucestershire last weekend.
Five other men in their twenties were arrested and were subsequently released on police bail. All five were UK nationals from London.
The investigation into the circumstances surrounding the events are continuing, police said.

Last weekend, the five men aged between 23 and 25 were arrested in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF), sparking a major security incident.
The BBC understands that one of the men had dialled 999 himself, about an hour before a local farmer alerted police to a "large group" of masked men near the vehicles.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail on Monday in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a Cobra meeting that afternoon in response. He later said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident, but did not provide any more details.

Tehran has strongly denied any involvement. The Iranian embassy in London said on Monday that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident.
RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.
In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
Late on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a TV show that it was clear a "foreign actor" had been involved in events over the weekend.

Without providing evidence or giving further details, he told Fox News network's "Hannity" programme: "What happened, what almost happened, what could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation. It's one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor."
Speaking earlier at the Oval Office, US President Donald Trump said he would not have let the five men arrested out on bail, and that he was "surprised" they had been released.
"We know everything about them, we would not have released them," he said, adding that the UK had worked with the US "very closely" on this.

articles.title: Teodoro to Trillanes: Submit evidence on Sara Duterte-China claims so it could be investigated
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Gilberto "Gibo" Teodoro said allegations that Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband Mans Carpio received money from the Chinese government "raise serious implications for…

blocks.text: NATIONAL SECURITY IMPLICATIONS
Published October 3, 2026 6:52pm

Defense Secretary Gilberto "Gibo" Teodoro said allegations that Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband Mans Carpio received money from the Chinese government "raise serious implications for national security."

The allegation was made by former senator Antonio Trillanes, who said the couple got hundreds of millions from the Embassy of the People’s Republic of China through the foundation of the Vice President and Carpio's company.
Teodoro urged Trillanes to submit evidence, so it could be "thoroughly investigated."

"The allegations of Fmr. Senator Trillanes, if substantiated, raise serious implications for national security. He should submit the evidence in his possession, if any, to our law enforcement authorities so the matter can be thoroughly investigated," Teodoro said in a statement on Saturday.
Duterte’s camp has denied Trillanes’ claims, calling them "malicious and fabricated."

“The Vice President would gladly sue him for these endless fabrications, but we have already witnessed how those who actively peddle malicious lies against her and her family are openly protected and propped up by this administration," Duterte's spokesperson Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr. said.
He also slammed Trillanes for not stating these claims in the Senate impeachment court, where he could have been under oath. The vice president's defense team also was not able to question him.

"This sudden retreat is absolute proof that his claims cannot survive real legal scrutiny, and are nothing but black propaganda, which is par for the course for a professional character assassin," Panelo said.
Trillanes was withdrawn Thursday as a witness for the prosecution in the Senate impeachment trial of Duterte.
The former senator said he requested House prosecutors to withdraw him, as he would conduct a press conference wherein he would reveal everything that he would have disclosed in the trial.
Trillanes also claimed that he was unwelcome in the impeachment trial, but the impeachment court spokesperson Regie Tongol dismissed this. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Remains of medieval tsar return to Bulgaria after decades-long dispute with Greece
articles.summary:
Greek PM hopes handover of Tsar Samuel will help persuade Britain to return Parthenon marbles

The remains of medieval ruler Tsar Samuel will arrive in Bulgaria on Saturday amid great pomp…

blocks.text: The remains of medieval ruler Tsar Samuel will arrive in Bulgaria on Saturday amid great pomp and ceremony, after decades of negotiations with neighbouring Greece.

The remains – discovered in a Greek border area 60 years ago – are to be flown to the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, onboard a military aircraft to be received with full state honours, including a fighter jet escort, a 21-gun salute and a procession to the Church of St Sophia, where the public will be able to pay respects.

The Greek prime minister, Kyriakos Mitsotakis, said he hoped the handover would bolster Athens’s campaign to persuade Britain to return the Parthenon marbles, a collection of 2,500-year-old sculptures taken from the Acropolis and held by the British Museum.

“The global community is essentially re-evaluating its longstanding stance on protecting cultural heritage,” he said. “This shift is embodied by today’s initiative, which rests on the obvious principle that monuments and historical heirlooms cannot be treated as spoils of war, nor as the result of circumstances subsequent to their creation.”

blocks.caption: Bulgaria’s military personnel carry a coffin with the remains of medieval ruler Tsar Samuel during a handover ceremony in Thessaloniki. Photograph: Giannis Papanikos/AP

blocks.text: Samuel was a warrior ruler who battled the Byzantine empire to expand his kingdom, but was ultimately defeated and died shortly afterwards in 1014. He is considered a symbol of Bulgaria’s national identity.

The handover of his remains follows an agreement earlier this week between the two countries’ culture ministers, under which Bulgaria will return religious relics taken from Greek monasteries during the first world war.
Several prominent Greek academics and religious leaders have raised concerns about the adequacy of Bulgaria’s contributions.
Mitsotakis and his Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, attended a ceremony at Thessaloniki’s Museum of Byzantine Civilization, where the remains were kept, before the handover.

“These are items that belong to both our peoples; they constitute our memory and our bond, and our compatriots and future generations deserve and must have the opportunity to pay tribute to their ancestors,” Radev said, speaking at the ceremony held at the museum.

“If in the past Tsar Samuel divided us, I can say that today he unites us. He strengthens our strategic cooperation and makes the historical relations between our states and peoples even stronger,” Radev said.

articles.title: ‘I have to dodge them all the time’: Rome locals incensed by rise in golf cart tours
articles.summary:
Authorities crack down on trade they says risks spiralling out of control – but operators say they are being targeted unfairly

On the edge of Piazza Navona, one of the grandest squares in…

blocks.text: On the edge of Piazza Navona, one of the grandest squares in central Rome, Barry and Linda, visitors from Texas in the US, stepped out of a golf cart. They planned to cross the square on foot, perhaps stopping to admire Lorenzo Bernini’s 17th-century Fountain of the Four Rivers, before being picked up by their driver at the opposite end.

The couple had already done a walking tour on day one of their trip, and had been so exasperated by a stifling three-hour shuffle along a corridor towards the Sistine Chapel on day two that by the third day they wanted to give their tired feet a rest.

blocks.caption: American tourists Barry and Linda on foot in Piazza Navona. Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian

blocks.text: “When I first heard you could do golf cart tours in Rome, I thought to myself: that sounds a little weird,” said Barry. “But then we decided to try it out.” He said the most enjoyable thing about the experience was “feeling the breeze”.
Rome is a difficult city to navigate, noted Linda, especially its ancient narrow streets in the centre. “There are no sidewalks,” she said. “Our feet were hurting and we needed a break.”

For visitors, golf cart tours offer respite from the heat, crowds and cobbles. For residents, however, their proliferation in recent years has become another source of frustration in a city already wrestling with traffic and overtourism.

blocks.caption: Rome’s leaders are pushing for regionwide measures to properly regulate the carts. Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian

blocks.text: Taxi drivers are especially incensed, accusing golf cart operators of stealing their business, while one local newspaper said the city had been “taken hostage” by the vehicles.

Now Rome authorities are cracking down on the burgeoning trade. Police intensified checks this week after the news agency Adnkronos reported that 90% of the roughly 500 golf carts circulating in the city were operating without authorisation.

In recent days, police stopped 131 carts around Piazza Navona, the Pantheon, Circo Massimo and the Spanish Steps, issuing €38,000 of fines for offences ranging from unlicensed driving to illegal parking.
Rome’s leaders are pushing for regionwide measures to properly regulate an activity that “risks spiralling out of control”, Eugenio Patanè, a councillor for mobility, told the news agency Adnkronos.

blocks.caption: A golf cart in traffic in Rome. Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian

blocks.text: Prices vary based on the type of tour and duration, but the cost per person can start at €100 and exceed €400 for a half-day trip. Barry and Linda paid €310 for their three-hour ride. “But it’s worth it,” said Barry.

Rome’s traffic problem is hardly new. Julius Caesar tried to tackle the issue more than 2,000 years ago by banning private vehicles and commercial carts from the city’s streets during the day. Today, pedestrians, cars, scooters, delivery vans and the occasional rogue horse-drawn carriage all jostle for space.

blocks.caption: Nora and Carlo outside their shop Trevimage near the Pantheon. Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian

blocks.text: Tourists can also take tours in Fiat 500s, on Vespas with sidecars, and even in tuk-tuks. But the golf carts seem to have drawn a special kind of wrath.

“There are too many of them,” said Nora Fahmi, who works at Trevimage, an art photography shop behind the Pantheon. “We’ve had this shop for 13 years and have seen all sorts of things, but the golf cart situation is kind of wild.”

Nearby, two teenagers from Israel were taking a rest on a parked cart. “We just want a lift to the Colosseum but you have to book online,” said their mother, Miri. “Rome is too crowded and it’s difficult to walk.”

blocks.caption: Two young tourists rest in a golf cart parked in the town centre. Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian

blocks.text: Elisa Isacco, who lives in the Monti area, spares no sympathy for the weary tourists. “What do they actually see or learn about Rome when they are on one of these things?” she said. “I find myself having to dodge them all the time – Rome is chaotic, it’s like a jungle.”

Amid the clampdown, several golf cart tour operators have banned staff from speaking to the press. But Leo Pavoncello, a driver for an operator in the Jewish Ghetto area, was happy to publicly defend the trade.

“Golf carts are silent and eco-friendly,” he said. “Rome is not an easy city to visit but these vehicles allow people with disabilities and families with children to see the sites in a comfortable way. On top of that, they provide jobs for young people.”

blocks.caption: A golf cart waiting for a group of tourists in Piazza Navona. Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian

blocks.text: Pavoncello, who was subjected to the police checks and was found to be operating fully legitimately, argued that a few rotten apples were giving the business a bad name.

“I don’t understand why they are targeting us,” he said, although he suspects “taxi lobbies” are piling on the pressure. “But Rome is a touristic city that has always been full of traffic, and the golf carts are simply another mode of transport.”

articles.title: MAP: Where have system losses been highest from 2021 to 2025?
articles.summary: Explore this interactive map to see how high the system losses have been in your area

blocks.text: System losses remain the talk of the town months after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. promised to remove them in his 2026 State of the Nation Address last July.
Starting this billing cycle in October, consumers will no longer have to pay value-added tax on the system loss charge.
But that is only 12% of the charge, with the Department of Energy initially saying back in July that the government would need about a year to fully remove the system loss charge.

This means the Marcos administration has a long way to go before its vow is fulfilled — and with power rates continuing to be sky-high in many parts of the country due to thin electricity supply, the continuing charge has only become more controversial.
So, what are these losses? In short, system loss refers to the cost of power that is wasted as it travels from generation sources to homes and buildings.
Currently, this cost is solely paid for by consumers, which means we are paying for electricity that we did not consume.

These losses can be categorized into three types. Some come from the physics of electrical transmission through metal wires, transformers, and gears that convert a small fraction of that power into heat. Others are the result of human interference or error.

So, how bad have system losses actually been? They differ depending on your distribution utility (DU). Explore this interactive map to see how high the distribution system loss has been in your area from 2021 to 2025, based on annual data the ERC required distribution utilities to submit in August 2026.
Rural DUs record highest system losses
Many of the DUs that consistently recorded the highest annual system losses are rural electric cooperatives on the outskirts of Mindanao, Mimaropa, and Bicol regions.

The Philippine Rural Electric Cooperatives Association (PHILRECA) said high system losses in these rural distribution networks can be traced back to extended feeder lines and challenging terrain that are “governed by the law of thermodynamics rather than inefficiency.”

Aging infrastructure also plays a role in these losses, with electric cooperatives long suffering from this problem. But modernizing these assets is not so simple, since PHILRECA had previously said these cooperatives suffer from delays in disbursing capital expenditures and fiscal challenges.
Feeder losses most common, but non-technical losses preventable
While feeder technical loss makes up the largest share of system losses overall, individual DUs with some of the highest losses also have a large percentage of non-technical losses.

Advocate groups such as the Institute for Climate Sustainable Cities (ICSC) have long pointed out that these non-technical losses are preventable — and even the unavoidable technical losses can still be managed.

For them, resolving the system loss issue lies in balancing two objectives. The first is to make sure the DUs can recover prudent and efficient costs necessary to provide safe, reliable, and continuous service. The second is to protect consumers from costs coming from inefficiency, inadequate controls, or preventable losses.

“Cost recovery should follow performance,” the ICSC said in a separate position paper. “Persistent underperformance, weak loss prevention efforts, or failure to address preventable losses should not automatically result in recoverable charges.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Libyan unity talks upended as warlord’s son linked to drone attacks on fuel facilities
articles.summary:
Western Libya’s GNU say working with Saddam Haftar ‘impossible’ as US-backed merger plan breaks down

Allegations that the son of the Libyan warlord Khalifa Haftar oversaw a “terror cell”…

blocks.text: Allegations that the son of the Libyan warlord Khalifa Haftar oversaw a “terror cell” that launched drone attacks on fuel storage facilities and power stations in western Libya have upended plans for the Tripoli-based government of national unity (GNU) to continue cooperating with Haftar on a plan to unify the country.

Saddam Haftar, the deputy commander of the so-called Libyan National Army (LNA), has increasingly been seen by the US as an important figure in its plans to unify Libyan security, judicial and political institutions.
But a round of drone attacks in August worsened electricity blackouts in the west of the country, putting intense popular pressure on the GNU led by the prime minister, Abdul Hamid Dbeibah.

Libya has been split between the east, dominated by Haftar, and the west, governed by the GNU, since the fall of Col Muammar Gaddafi in 2011, leaving the oil-rich country at the mercy of corruption, militia, migrant traffickers and myriad external actors.

blocks.caption: Khalifa Haftar. Photograph: Esam Omran Al-Fetori/Reuters

blocks.text: Donald Trump’s Africa adviser, Massad Boulos, has hatched a plan to unify the two Libyan governments in which Haftar from the east would take on the role of president and a member of the Dbeibah family from the west would become prime minister.

Boulos has insisted he is not trying a quick fix that entrenches family elites in Libya. “It’s not about families or names,” Boulos said when asked about the reported Haftar-Dbeibah deal, before adding: “At the end of the day, those are individuals that have to be in one position or the other.”

But the drone strikes, it is claimed, were prompted by Haftar’s anger at Dbeibah apparently stalling on the Boulos merger plan and by Tripoli allegedly encouraging tribes in southern Libya to attack and kill his forces.

Over more than five days in August, drones attacked the Zawiya oil station and fuel storage facilities in western Libya. The drone strikes hit the gasoline-storage tank at the Zawiya oil complex, west of Tripoli, causing a large fire and the tank’s collapse. The tank held approximately 4.5m litres of fuel when it was struck, according to Libya’s National Oil Corporation.

On 5 September, three Libyans and one Spanish citizen were arrested in southern Tripoli by the GNU for their alleged role in a plot that was intended to include an attack on Tripoli airport. It was thought the whole group involved five Spaniards and four Libyans. The three arrested Libyans were allegedly affiliated with the Tareq ben Ziyad brigade, an LNA formation. Information that has emerged from interviews about the plot, and Saddam Haftar’s alleged role, not just in Libya, has been described as a goldmine, capable of weakening Khalifa Haftar.

Sources in the GNU said the alleged plotters were working for Saddam Haftar. “No formal decision has been made, but in light of what has been discovered it is impossible to work with Saddam,” the sources said.

The claims not only damage Saddam Haftar’s role in the Boulos plan but also the parallel UN sponsored 4+4 talks involving the main four political institutions in Libya that led to an August agreement to stage elections within two years. The deal endorsed by the UN security council overcomes previous obstacles to elections, and had been backed by the main actors capable of delivering the change.

Walid Ellafi, minister for state for political affairs in the UN-backed Libyan GNU and an enthusiast for elections, said: “Our support for the 4+4 process is rooted in its role as a UN sponsored framework offering a new approach to achieving practical results that pave the way for elections and institutions whose political legitimacy derives from the will of the people – not as a political settlement that overlooks violations or sets aside the rights of those affected.”
He opposes an elite east-west political deal that brushes aside longstanding grievances such as the displacement of 9,000 families in Benghazi during the 2014 war.
The allegations about the sabotage operation may intensify a power struggle between the three sons of Khalifa Haftar in the east.

Saddam Haftar is seen as his father’s most likely heir, possesses the most resources, enjoys the backing of the United Arab Emirates and has so far dominated the political tracks. But his brothers, Khaled and Belqasim – more allied with Egypt than the United Arab Emirates – have recently started to challenge his dominance.

articles.title: These former inmates turn life behind bars into art
articles.summary: For the formerly incarcerated members of the Bagongbuhay Group of Artists, art becomes one way of confronting the difficulty of rebuilding life after release

blocks.text: At the UP College of Law, a mural tells a story that cannot be found in a case file.

Painted by members of the Bagongbuhay Group of Artists (BAGA), a collective of former Persons Deprived of Liberty (PDLs), the artwork brings their experiences of detention, change, and life after incarceration into a place where law is taught and practiced.

The painting, Buyon, was formally turned over to the UP College of Law on September 18 as part of the UP Law Class of 2001’s 25th anniversary celebration. It was unveiled alongside a wider exhibit of works by BAGA, a group founded in 2021 that brings together former PDLs and marginalized communities through art.

But before it became a mural hanging inside Bocobo Hall, “buyon” was a word rooted in the everyday reality of life inside detention. It refers to a shared space where PDLs bathe, wash their clothes and dishes, and wait for their turn to use the limited water available.
And behind the painting are the stories of the men who created it — what they remember, what they experienced, and what they are trying to communicate through art.
The mural began last year, when Joey de Leon, 57, the founder and president of BAGA, was called to a meeting through Justice Karl Miranda.
Alumni of the UP Law Class of 2001 wanted a large, painting-style mural about the country’s criminal justice system for their legacy project, and they wanted BAGA’s help bringing it to life.
De Leon, who has lived through incarceration himself and would later become one of the five BAGA artists credited on the finished work, proposed starting somewhere the public rarely thinks to look.

“Ang buyon ay isang facility sa loob ng bawat brigada sa kulungan. Doon kayo naliligo, doon rin kayo naglalaba, doon rin dumudumi. Hindi siya katulad ng normal na comfort room o bathroom, pinagsama-sama lahat doon,” De Leon said.

(The buyon is a facility inside every brigada in a detention center. That’s where you bathe, where you wash clothes, and where you relieve yourself. It isn’t like a normal comfort room or bathroom. Everything happens in the same space.)

In the mural, that cramped space is filled with the routines PDLs share. Men bathe and wash clothes beside basins and buckets, against tiled walls and beneath a small barred window. The exhibit’s description also presents the buyon as a place of connection and shared experience among the people who use it. Still, De Leon is careful about what the painting is and is not trying to say.
“Hindi namin sinasabi na, ‘oy, eto kami, bigyan niyo kami,’ kasi may problema ang gobyerno,” he said. “Kami ay pangkaraniwang inmate na naranasan mismo iyon. Pinapakita lang namin, we are humans.”
(We’re not saying, “hey, here we are, give us something,” just because the government has problems. We’re ordinary inmates who lived through it ourselves. We’re just showing that we are humans.)
For Danilo Faustino, 65, the harder question came after his release. What happens after you have served your sentence?

Faustino spent around two decades in the New Bilibid Prison. For him and other members of BAGA, art became one way of confronting the difficulty of rebuilding life after release. Finding regular work can be difficult for former PDLs, particularly for someone his age, and painting offered another way to earn and help support his family. He wants the same for those still in detention, which is why he encourages them to learn art.
“Para paglaya nila, meron silang, ika nga eh, panghanapbuhay o diskarte,” said Faustino.
(So that when they are released, they will have, so to speak, a livelihood or something they can do.)

Of all the images Faustino could have painted, he chose Lady Justice, a figure closely tied to the justice system he once passed through. His version shows her blindfolded, holding a set of scales in one hand and a sword in the other. After all those years in Bilibid, Faustino has not given up on what she stands for. In his reading of the figure, her balance remains, and justice is still something she is bound to give.
“Katarungan, kailangan niyang ibigay (Justice is something she has to give),” he said.

blocks.caption: LADY JUSTICE. Danilo Faustino stands beside his painting of Lady Justice at Bocobo Hall.

blocks.text: Faustino also sees art as something that helps people get through their time inside. BAGA teaches PDLs so they have something to focus on while serving time.
“Para meron silang mapaglibangan,” he said. “Yung artwork na ’yan, hindi sila ma-homesick sa loob. Hindi sila maburyong.”
(So they have something to keep them occupied. With art, they don’t get homesick inside. They don’t go stir-crazy.)

Leo Eroja, 49, is one of the five BAGA artists behind Buyon. He began making art in 1996, the year he was imprisoned, and most of his works are mixed media, often with embossed details. His piece in the exhibit, titled Tree of Life, carries a meaning he explains in simple terms.
“Simbolo siya ng pag-asa at kasaganahan (It’s a symbol of hope and abundance),” he said.
Inside, art also became how he got by. With little else to fill his days, painting gave him something to focus on and something he could sell to support himself.
“Sa loob, matutukan mo talaga ang art. Wala ka namang ibang gagawin. Magpipinta ka para maibenta mo at maka-survive ka sa pang-araw-araw,” Eroja shared.
(Inside, you can really focus on art. There’s nothing else to do. You paint so you can sell your work and survive day to day.)

blocks.caption: TREE OF LIFE. Leo Eroja stands beside his mixed media work ‘Tree of Life’ at Bocobo Hall.

blocks.text: What Eroja wants people outside to understand is how much of ordinary life continues behind bars. Many do not realize there are schools inside, he said, and apart from limited movement, the main difference is that family cannot always come to visit.
“Hindi nila alam na may school din pala doon. Parang nasa loob ka, parang nasa laya ka rin. Ang kaibahan lang, nakakulong kayo, limited ang galaw mo,” he shared.
(They don’t know there’s a school there, too. Life inside has some of the same routines as life outside. The only difference is that you’re locked up and your movement is limited.)

For the lawyers behind the mural, Buyon also carries a message for their own school. Professor Oliver Xavier Reyes, a member of the UP Law Class of 2001, admitted during the turnover that he felt some apprehension when a painting was first proposed as the batch’s legacy project, since everything depended on what it would show. Buyon answered that question for him.
“The painting is all about the stakes as we practice law in the grand manner,” he said.

Reyes compared law school life to a cloister, where concerns beyond its walls can sometimes feel like distractions. That distance can be useful, he acknowledged, but it also risks separating legal study from the lives affected by it.
“It is helpful still, for the law student or the lawyer, to be served on occasion the clarifying reminder that the lives embedded in the law are not as sterile as the texts we read,” Reyes said.

One detail in the mural stood out to him, the daylight entering through its barred window, which he called a reflection of “the best of the human spirit.” He also found it fitting that Buyon now hangs in Bocobo Hall, home of the UP Law Center, the government’s legal policy and research arm.
Anyone who walks in, he said, may be reminded that the people lawyers serve include “those who have been rendered least capacitated.”

Each of the artists asks for something small and concrete. Faustino wants PDLs to leave detention with a skill they can live on. Eroja wants people outside to know that schools and daily routines continue behind bars. For De Leon, what matters most is trust, which he said remains the hardest thing to earn back, even years after release.
He credits organizations and members of the judiciary, like those behind the mural, for giving BAGA’s members another chance, and he hopes the rest of society will follow.
“Ganoon din sana in general, hindi lang itong mga judiciary institution natin. Bigyan niyo kami ng second chance,” De Leon said.
(We hope it’s the same in general, beyond our judiciary institutions. Give us a second chance.) – Rappler.com
Arabella Grace Sta. Ana is a Rappler intern studying BA Philosophy at UP Los Baños.

articles.title: 3 Cape Bretoners were hit and killed by a train in Maine in 1970. Some want the case reopened
articles.summary: Kenny Novak, 15, David Burrows, 17, and Terry Burt, 20, were in sleeping bags on a rail track west of the border town of Houlton, Maine, when they were struck early on the morning of July 10, 1970,…

image.caption: Kenny Novak, David Burrows and Terry Burt were 15, 17 and 20, respectively, at the time of their deaths in Maine in July 1970. It's unclear why they were in Maine and not camping in Cape Breton as planned. (Galen McRae/CBC)

blocks.text: Every morning, 78-year-old Richard Novak hears a passing train from his apartment in Bedford, N.S., and thinks of his late brother, Kenny.
Kenny, 15, was one of three Cape Breton youth who inexplicably ended up in Maine in July 1970 after deviating from a planned camping trip in Cape Breton Highlands National Park.
Kenny, David Burrows, 17, and Terry Burt, 20, were in sleeping bags on a rail track west of the border town of Houlton, Maine, when they were struck by a train early on the morning of July 10.
Novak, who has Parkinson's disease and is in failing health, has the same thought every morning as he lies in bed and hears the train.
"The first person I think of [is] Kenny, Terry and David, and what it would be like under that train and why would you choose the tracks?" said Novak.
The deaths were ruled accidental, with the Sydney-area youth believed to be asleep at the time of the collision.
Novak would like to see the case reopened, even though documentation from the time is sparse.
"What I'm trying to do is unite with the people from Maine and clear this up once and for all, so we can put it to rest and have some peace," he said.
At the time of the incident, Novak was living in Ontario.
"I've never felt so much pain in my life," he said of learning of the deaths.

Novak said Kenny was the youngest of six boys and one girl in the family. The 5-7, 145-pound teen with black hair collected comic books, loved music, skating and swimming, and had been studying Latin for three years.
Novak believes the group may have been going to a concert in the U.S.
It's a case with many unanswered questions, but here's what's known.
Timeline

On Friday, July 3, 1970, Kenny Novak and Burt were driven to the Highlands by Novak's mother, she told the Bangor Daily News, according to a July 19, 1970, article. She told the paper she believed Burrows joined them on July 5.
The three were last seen in Ingonish, N.S., on July 6, the newspaper reported, citing the RCMP.

It's believed they hitchhiked to the U.S. and entered illegally on Thursday, July 9, from Woodstock, N.B., which Houlton borders. There was no record of youths matching their description crossing officially that date, the Bangor paper reported in its July 11-12 edition.

The newspaper also reported that a border patrolman tried to stop three hitchhiking youth in Houlton, but they fled. The patrolman also tried to find the youths later using an unmarked vehicle, but was unsuccessful.

It was around 11:30 p.m. ET when 20-year-old college student Royden Hunt was at a dairy bar in Houlton, around a mile from the border. The business was closed and he was hanging around outside with some friends.
"Those three come along and were walking, and they stopped and talked to us and they asked us how they could get to [Interstate] 95," Hunt told CBC News.
Interstate 95 is a highway that runs from Maine to Florida.
How the trio ended up at the rail line

Hunt said he didn't usually pick up hitchhikers, but the trio seemed pleasant. And while the original plan was to drop them off a few kilometres away at the nearest spot on the interstate, Hunt let it slip that they were going to be travelling to his hometown of Island Falls, Maine, almost 50 kilometres from Houlton.
The trio asked if they could be taken there, but Hunt and his friend, Mike York, said that wouldn't make sense as there wouldn't be much traffic for hitchhiking options.
"Well, is there any place we can get on the railroad tracks?" asked one of the Cape Breton youth.
Hunt knew of a place called Smyrna Mills about halfway between Island Falls and Houlton that fit the bill.
"So that's what we did. We stopped, let them out … and it was only like 50 feet to the railroad tracks and they went to the railroad tracks and we left," said Hunt.
He believes they wanted to walk the tracks so they could stay out of sight.
Besides the circumstances, the timing stands out for Hunt because he had to drop off his friend York for a midnight shift at the gas station where he worked.

Hunt later learned that after they left the dairy bar, a border patrol agent showed up asking the people who remained outside whether they had seen the three youth. The people who were still there were friends of his and relayed that detail to him. (It's unclear if this was separate from the second effort made by the border patrol agent to find the youth, as referenced in the July 11-12 Bangor Daily News.)
Hunt and York, who is no longer alive, were the last people known to have spoken with the trio.
The day of the crash

The following day around 7 a.m., a 19-car train weighing about 725 tonnes was headed toward Houlton when it rounded a sharp turn. The engineer spotted what he thought was a rubber raft on the tracks, the July 11-12 edition of the Bangor Daily News reported.
"They're sleeping bags!" said the train's fireman, with the trio about 50 metres away.
The engineer tried to stop the train, but it was too late.
The trio did not move before being struck by the train, the engineer said.
Newspaper accounts report that Canadian cigarettes, canned goods, and maps of the Atlantic provinces, Maine, New England, Pennsylvania and New Jersey were among the possessions found on the trio.
The Cape Breton Post reported one of the sleeping bags had the name and address of one of the three youth, while other newspapers said the words "Sydney, N.S." were marked.
The Biddeford-Saco Journal reported a wallet found on one body contained a small sum of money but none of the individuals had identification. The article doesn't state how much money was found.
One of Hunt's memories of the trio is that one of them had a roll of cash, perhaps around $100 to $150 worth.

On the day of the crash, 18-year-old David Sjoberg of Houlton was working at a local funeral home doing odd jobs such as property maintenance, washing hearses and helping with visitations. It was his second year there as a summer job and he was off to college in the fall.
He recalls his boss telling him the bodies of the trio would be arriving.

"I remember they arrived in the morning because before I went to lunch that day, he said, 'When you come back, I'd like you to go down and help them out in the morgue,' sort of tending to what they needed to do with those bodies," said Sjoberg, who later became a pastor.
Besides the circumstances surrounding the deaths, the day stands out to Sjoberg because a cousin of his got married that night.
Autopsies
Autopsies by Aroostook County's medical examiner found the trio died from severe head and body injuries. Testing later conducted at a state lab found no alcohol or drugs in the bodies.
Sjoberg said he was not present in the morgue for the autopsies, but his boss had a request for him: Would he transport the bodies back to Cape Breton?
"As an 18-year-old kid, I think that sounded like a pretty exciting adventure," said Sjoberg. "Thousand-mile round trip, be gone two or three days, so I didn't hesitate to say yes."
By Sunday the 12th, according to newspaper accounts, the fathers of the three youth were in Houlton to confirm the identity of the bodies.

"[Frank] Novak, middle aged and with a crew cut, and Gordon Burt of Sydney and James Burrows of Sydney River agreed that their visit to the funeral home and personal belongings they were shown had convinced them their sons had been killed by the train," reporter Dean Rhodes wrote in the July 13 Bangor Daily News.
"I couldn't ask for nicer people," Frank Novak told the reporter. "Everybody made everything as nice as possible for us."
He didn't have an answer for why the trio ended up in Maine.
"We haven't got a clue," he said.

With the identities confirmed, Sjoberg started driving to Cape Breton on Sunday, overnighting at a motel along the way. He arrived in Cape Breton on Monday the 13th and brought the bodies to a funeral home. After a quick stop there, Sjoberg returned home.
He doesn't remember the incident being the talk of the town.

"I thought the story had died decades ago," said Sjoberg, who learned in recent years about a Facebook page dedicated to the case and concerns from family members about the investigation. There's also a petition calling for the case to be reopened.
One of Richard Novak's criticisms of the investigation is that it wasn't thorough enough. He believes the deaths involved foul play, with the bodies placed on the rail track to cover up for murder.
Sheriff department's investigation
Aroostook County Sheriff Darrell Crandall, who oversaw the investigation, died in 1996, but newspaper accounts from 1970 provide some insight into the investigation and his thinking.
The July 17, 1970, Cape Breton Post noted Crandall had not closed the investigation as he was still awaiting an autopsy from the state lab in Augusta, Maine.
Crandall, a former railroad brakeman, believed the incident was an unfortunate mishap with one fundamental question.
"Why did they lay down on the railway tracks?" he told the newspaper.
The sheriff said he had 70 men at his disposal in the surrounding area and "if there's anything we'll know about it."
Less than a week later, Crandall ruled the deaths did not involve foul play.
It had rained on the day of the crash, meaning the ground was damp, "which may have led them to decide on the rail bed as a dry sleeping area," according to the July 23, 1970, Cape Breton Post.
The Aroostook County Sheriff's Department did not respond to interview requests for this story.

In an email shared with CBC News, an Aroostook County official told Novak the department was "not in possession of … case reports, statements, forensic findings, evidence, case files, or any other records dating back to 1970."
Hunt said he's hunted in the area and you can hear the train from miles away.

"Where we let 'em out, that's in the middle of nowhere," he said. "I can't imagine that they run into anybody that would have brought any harm to 'em, a mile and a half up that track at 11:30, 12 o'clock at night. There'd be nobody out there. And to lay across that track, with their head on the track, and not hear that train coming … I don't know."

items: More stories from Cape Breton

blocks.text: At the time, the rail line was lightly used, the Cape Breton Post reported, with an average of one train moving in each direction per day.
Hunt said he was interviewed twice by police officials, including once at a golf course.
Richard Novak said his late brother Lorne led the charge to get answers, but died last year. As a result, Novak has now been thrust into the role.
"Justice has not been served," he said. "They did not die accidentally."

articles.title: Green party conference continues with cost of living on the agenda – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Green conference enters its second day, while Tories prepare for theirs on Sunday

Meanwhile, Reform leaders this morning have been speaking about the fact that the man acccused of murdering…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 4m agoFarage has 'not been believed' on safety fears, says Tice
14m agoOpening summary

blocks.text: Farage has 'not been believed' on safety fears, says Tice

Meanwhile, Reform leaders this morning have been speaking about the fact that the man acccused of murdering former party spokeswoman Ann Widdecombe has also been charged with a terror plot against Nigel Farage.
Deputy leader Richard Tice told the BBC Radio 4’s Today programme his party leader has “not been listened to” over his safety concerns.
Farage has repeatedly raised the threats against his personal security before, often in the context of justifying or explaining why he’s received significant financial donations.
Tice said: “(Farage’s) security and the risks to it, he’s talked about over over many times, many occasions, over many years.

“And I think what’s particularly upsetting for those of us in and around him is sometimes he’s not being believed, not being listened to, and you know we have just got in a sense, deep regret over everything that’s happened over a long period of time.”

Police charged Joshua Kerry, 28, with the terror plot on Friday. He already stands accused of the brutal murder of Widdecombe, 78, a former Reform representative and Tory minister, who died on 8 July at her home in Devon.
Opening summary
Good morning and welcome to the UK Politics live blog where cost-of-living issues are top of mind as diesel surges past £2 a litre for the first time.

That’s a 40% increase since the start of the year, meaning the cost of filling up an average family car is now £110, nearly £32 more than before the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran in late February.

The eight-months long war now has choked off key global shipping routes, blocking supplies from Gulf oil producers. On Friday, G7 countries including the UK bowed to pressure from US President Donald Trump and released 100 million barrels of oil and diesel.
But there are still spiralling ramifications on the cost of energy, food, transport and housing.

Greens leader Zack Polanski yesterday used his party conference speech yesterday to call for an emergency brake on rent rises. Party deputy leaders today will announce a policy to provide guaranteed jobs for 18-24 year olds.
Tory leader Kemi Badenoch, ahead of the Conservatives party conference kicking off tomorrow, will also anounce later today a childcare benefit for those on over £100,000.

Meanwhile early word of the flavour of Chancellor John Healey’s first Budget, to be delivered in a few weeks time, suggests it will be a careful one aimed giving reassurance households and businesses, with targeted assistance, as opposed to any major tax or spending hikes.
Stick with us and we’ll bring you the latest updates from the ongoing Green party conference, as well as wider political developments.

articles.title: ‘The enemy is tearing our city apart’: terror in Kyiv as Russia ramps up attacks
articles.summary:
Mayor Vitali Klitschko says Kyivans can no longer pretend it is ‘peacetime’ amid strikes on school, hospital and bridge

Valeriya Tkachenko was dropping her son off at school in central Kyiv…

blocks.text: Valeriya Tkachenko was dropping her son off at school in central Kyiv when the air raid alert sounded. Staff hurried the children and parents into the shelter, where the frightened lawyer spent the next two hours with her son.
“I’m scared to death all day about what could happen to my son,” she said as she emerged from the shelter, already late for work.
A day earlier, a Russian jet-powered drone had struck a school nearby. “And I can’t plan anything any more,” she said. “It’s not sustainable like this.”

blocks.caption: Smoke rises after a Russian drone hit the Academy of Sciences building in Kyiv on Monday. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian
Firefighters tackling a blaze in the city centre. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian

blocks.text: Across the city on Friday morning, Artem Marchenko, an IT worker, was forced to abandon his car and walk for 20 minutes across the Pivdennyi, or Southern, Bridge on his way to work after repeated Russian strikes damaged the crossing.
He feared Russia would soon target Kyiv’s other bridges, paralysing movement across a city of about 3 million people, the two halves of which are divided by the Dnipro.
On Saturday morning, Russia targeted a second major bridge connecting Kyiv, damaging the road surface on the Northern Bridge and temporarily halting traffic.
Kyiv is entering its most difficult period since the early days of the invasion, as intensifying Russian attacks reshape everyday life in a capital that Moscow is seeking to plunge into darkness.

For weeks, the main worry in the capital had been the coming winter, when Russia is expected once again to try to plunge Ukraine into darkness and cold. But a sharp escalation in Russian attacks has left many residents feeling that some of the hardship they had been bracing for is already here.

blocks.caption: Rescue workers running to a shelter during an air threat. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian

blocks.text: “The capital is in a very dramatic situation. And it’s no longer possible to pretend that we can live now as we do in peacetime,” the Kyiv mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said on Friday. “The enemy is tearing Kyiv apart.”

This week alone, Russian missiles and drones have struck offices, datacentres, a school and hospital and one of Kyiv’s main bridges. Moscow has also started its attacks on Ukraine’s energy, targeting a thermal power plant and other energy facilities, leaving several neighbourhoods without power and water by morning.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy underlined the apparent shift in Russian tactics in an interview with the Financial Times this week, saying Vladimir Putin had recently ordered his commanders to abandon the rules of war.
“They want Ukrainians to leave the capital … and show that if you don’t have the capital you don’t have the country,” Zelenskyy said in separate comments to reporters.

blocks.caption: A volunteer medic crew on patrol in Kyiv. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian

blocks.text: Until recently, Kyiv had retained a deceptively normal rhythm, while cities closer to the front, including Kharkiv and Dnipro, absorbed the brunt of daily missile and drone attacks. Now, residents joke grimly that the balance is beginning to shift, with those cities at times feeling safer than the capital.

The city is confronting a particularly dangerous combination of an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors for ballistic missiles and a new generation of faster, jet-powered Russian drones that are harder to shoot down.

Kyiv is racing to fast-track a new generation of interceptor drones capable of taking down the jet-powered models. Several are already in use, according to three defence industry sources, though they said it could still take weeks or months to deploy them at a scale sufficient to provide meaningful protection for the capital.
At the same time, Russia’s advances on the battlefield remain relatively slow and are coming at enormous cost.

Moscow captured about 361 sq km in September, according to the military analyst Konrad Muzyka, an increase on recent months but still far short of the pace needed to seize the rest of the Donbas before winter, when offensive operations typically become more difficult.

blocks.caption: A man with a tattoo reading ‘immortal’ standing near the site of a Russian drone strike in Kyiv. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian

blocks.text: Ukraine, meanwhile, has clawed back about 126 sq km in a series of counteroffensives in the east, being conducted under the codename Vivaldi. That slower-moving battle on the ground is increasingly at odds with what is happening far behind the front. The contrast reflects a broader shift in the war, as Ukraine’s major cities come under growing pressure.

“You can be quite successful in the land domain, but if you are vulnerable in the air, especially in the rear, that is the vulnerability your opponent is going to exploit,” said Mykola Bielieskov, a military analyst at Ukraine’s government-run National Institute for Strategic Studies.

Ukrainian officials have been warning their European counterparts about the scale of the looming threat. According to the New York Times, Ukraine’s energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, recently briefed European counterparts on an intercepted Russian plan to use as many as 1,000 missiles, drones and bombs against the country’s energy system. The targets included electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants and boiler houses, in what appeared to be an effort to plunge Ukrainian cities into darkness and cold and create a humanitarian crisis.
“Russia plans to freeze Kyiv out, to throw it back into the stone age,” said one senior western diplomat in Kyiv, speaking on condition of anonymity.

Western diplomats say publicly that they intend to remain in Kyiv, mindful that leaving would hand Moscow a propaganda victory and risk creating the impression that Ukraine was being abandoned. However, privately two senior diplomats said contingency plans were being drawn up to relocate embassies to Lviv or eastern Poland if Russia began deliberately targeting foreign missions.
“The situation is obviously deteriorating fast,” the diplomat said.

articles.title: Kim wins Asian Games gold to secure military exemption
articles.summary: Golfer Tom Kim wins gold at the Asian Games to secure an exemption from mandatory service in South Korea's military.

blocks.text: Asian Games - final round
-18 T Kim (Kor); -15 K Higa (Jpn), W Ding (Chi), S Kaewkanjana (Tha); -11 W-H Wang (Tpe)
Tom Kim won gold at the Asian Games to secure an exemption from mandatory service in South Korea's military.
The 24-year-old led going into the final round and produced a brilliant six-under-par 64 to finish 18 under and claim victory by three strokes.

There were signs of nerves with a bogey on the 17th but, after five birdies and an eagle prior to that, Kim had the margin for error and tapped in for par on the last before letting out a roar, his relief clear to see.
Able-bodied South Korean males are usually required to undertake between 18 and 21 months of military service before the age of 28.
However, the government rewards Asian Games champions and Olympic medal-winners of any colour with a service exemption bar basic training, which lasts less than a month.

Athletes who have previously secured the exemption include former Tottenham footballer Son Heung-min, who served for only three weeks in 2020 having won the Asian Games with his country two years earlier.
Kim rushed from the Presidents Cup in the United States to tee off at the Kasugai Country Club in Japan, having to manage on just six hours of sleep and a 14-hour time difference.
His efforts were worth it as the world number 32 can now continue his career, in which he has already won four PGA Tour titles and triumphed at the Scottish Open in July, with minimal disruption.
Kim had previously come close to securing an exemption at the Paris Olympics in 2024, finishing day one tied for third before ultimately finishing eighth.

However, his compatriot SH Kim, 28, missed out on a military exemption as South Korea could only win silver in the team event, alongside Tom Kim and Mun Do-yeob, who has already completed his service.

articles.title: Flydubai co-pilot attempted 'terrorist attack,' UAE says
articles.summary: The man, who stabbed his fellow pilot on an Israel-bound Flydubai flight, was reportedly barred from flying in his native Oman over security concerns.

image.caption: A replacement Flydubai aircraft landed in Tel Aviv, carrying passengers from the flight on which a pilot stabbed another [Photo: September 30, 2026]Image: Gil Cohen-Magen/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The co-pilot accused of stabbing his captain during Flydubai Flight 1073 was wielding a crash ax and attempted to carry out a "terrorist attack," UAE investigators said Saturday, according to Emirati state news agency WAM.
A crash ax is typically stored in the plane's cockpit for use in case of an emergency.
Western and Gulf officials cited by Reuters and AP news agencies named the co-pilot as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami. Emirati authorities have not publicly commented on his identity.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Friday that he had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns that he had adopted radical ideological views.
The attack that took place on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv has raised many questions about how the incident unfolded as well as about background checks in aviation hiring.
There were 182 people on board, including four pilots.
After the co-pilot stabbed the captain in an apparent attempt to crash the plane, two other pilots in the cabin took control and landed the aircraft safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
Flydubai co-pilot was barred from flying by Oman over security concerns
The Wall Street Journal report said the co-pilot was hired by Flydubai despite the ban by Oman, allowing him to fly the jet on a sensitive route connecting the UAE and Israel.
Israel and the UAE, which includes Dubai, signed the Abraham Accords normalizing relations in 2020.
The newspaper said it could not be determined whether Oman shared concerns about the pilot's radicalization with other countries or airlines.
The nature of his radicalization was also not clear.
US broadcaster CNN cited two sources saying the co-pilot was removed from a job at Oman's national airline last year over concerns about extremist views.
Saudi broadcaster Al Arabiya, also citing an informed source, reported that Omani authorities determined that the co-pilot held extremist views.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Thursday in a video statement that they know the co-pilot "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination" and intended to crash the jet.
Netanyahu also said they were also looking into whether the co-pilot had acted under anyone's direction, warning that whoever was involved would pay a "heavy price."

The investigation is ongoing. A Gulf diplomat, in comments to AP, said authorities were attempting to find out whether the Omani co-pilot was a "lone wolf or has any connection with any extremist groups."
