articles.title: Morocco's first female head of government: Symbol or real reform?
articles.summary: Fatima Zahra Mansouri has been chosen as Morocco's first female prime minister. Is her appointment a kind of symbolism, to show Morocco in a positive light? Or could Mansouri bring genuine changes…

image.caption: Mansouri has been nicknamed the "pasha's daughter" because she comes from a prominent Marrakesh family and her father was formerly a pasha or municipal governorImage: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP

blocks.text: After the announcement that Morocco would appoint its first female head of government – Marrakech mayor Fatima Zahra Mansouri – citizens interviewed by local television reporters were mostly enthusiastic.
"It would be great if we had a female prime minister for a change. She'd lift our spirits a bit," one woman said.
"Why don't we give women a chance? We've never had one [a female head of government] before," said another. "May God bless her and help her stay on a straight path."
"Regardless of who takes on the role, it should be a change for the better in Morocco," a man added.

blocks.caption: Morocco's King Mohammed VI chose Fatima Zahra Mansouri to be the country's first female prime minister following September's parliamentary electionsImage: Mosa'ab Elshamy/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: But there were also naysayers. Some locals questioned how she would take part in official events where tradition and protocol dictate that only men attend.

"People are saying that a nation cannot succeed if a woman is in charge, even if she's only half in charge," one man told a television reporter, referring to the fact that Morocco's King Mohammed VI has the final say in national politics.

Morocco is a constitutional monarchy so elections are held but the king has ultimate executive power. The head of the country's government, or prime minister, leads the cabinet and administration and executes public policy.

The king chose Fatima Zahra Mansouri, minister of planning and mayor of Marrakesh, over Fouzi Lekjaa, head of Morocco's football federation and budget minister. The pair are senior members of the Authenticity and Modernity Party, or PAM, which won the most seats in the country's parliamentary elections in September.

"If you talk to Moroccans, there are some who are really proud of having a woman at the top and they see a chance for her to have impact on women's representation in society," confirms Anja Freudenreich, who heads the Morocco office of Germany's Friedrich Ebert Foundation (FES) in Rabat. "But others see her appointment as bare symbolism."

Mansouri will lead what is colloquially being called the "World Cup government" as Morocco prepares to invest billions before it hosts the 2030 football World Cup along with Spain and Portugal. Mansouri is seen to have shown leadership after the devastating 2023 Morocco earthquake.
Her appointment makes her the third woman to lead a government in the Arab world.

blocks.caption: Morrocan women have become more visible in local politics in recent years. Casablanca and Rabat both have female mayors, and there are a number of female cabinet ministers Image: Abu Adem Muhammed/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Will Mansouri improve the lot of Moroccan women?
There is no doubt that Mansouri's appointment has important symbolic value, observers say.

Two Tunisian women, Najla Bouden and current prime minister Sara Zaafarani, became heads of an Arab government before Mansouri's appointment. A 2022 surveyby polling organization Arab Barometer found Tunisian attitudes towards women in power had changed as a result.

Researchers from Arab Barometer believed the change — with only 40% agreeing that "in general, men are better at political leadership than women" in 2022 compared to 56% four years earlier — was the result of a "role model effect." Before the appointment of Bouden and Zaafarani, there had been no major changes, they pointed out.
According to a 2025 survey by the organization, attitudes toward women's roles have also been changing in Morocco. Mansouri could accelerate that.

"We've already noticed how impactful this [appointment] is in terms of social and cultural norms," said Stephanie Willman Bordat, co-founder of Rabat-based advocacy organization, Mobilizing for Rights Associates (MRA).

"People in public spaces, in cafes, on trains on their commute and just regular folks are having conversations about women's leadership and the taboo that says women can't be heads of government or women can't be bosses of men. There's good public debate and dialogue on this."

"And on a global level, in terms of women's participation, this is really something to encouraging," Bordat, who has lived in Morocco for two decades, told DW. "Especially when you look at the global climate of backlash and regression in women's rights."

Mansouri's prime ministership "is certainly notable as female leadership in the region is rare," Freudenreich of FES agreed. "It does have a highly symbolic character and I'm sure she does, or she will have, a role model function for women and girls in Morocco as well as in the region."
No major changes from past
However, Mansouri is unlikely to initiate a major change from past politics, Freudenreich suggested.

She's more of a pragmatist than a rebel — a quality that's likely to see her navigate the much-discussed issues of protocol — and her party's electoral manifesto doesn't go into any major detail on women's issues, she pointed out.
Before the September elections, MRA looked at which parties had women's issues in their electoral manifestos. Mansouri's party, PAM, appeared to offer only three such policies.

blocks.caption: PAM said it wanted to increase female economic activity, increase vulnerable widows' pensions and ensure better obstetric care.Image: Jalal Morchidi/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Other parties were more vocal on women's issues than PAM, with some saying they would push for updates to the Moroccan family code, or "moudawana." This sets rules on all-important aspects of Moroccan women's lives like custody of children, divorce, property rights, marriage, polygamy and domestic violence. It has not been updated since 2004.
Did the king pick a symbol or is he genuine?
In 2023, King Mohammed VI asked the then-prime minister to look into further updates to the family code. Discussions around that are ongoing and reforms are still pending, MRA's Bordat said.
"But what's really interesting is that now we can say, well, women can be heads of government so women can also be heads or co-heads of family," she argued.

The Moroccan king, who took the throne in 1999, has been broadly supportive of women's rights, Ahmed Benchemsi, advocacy and communications director for Human Rights Watch's Middle East and North Africa division, confirmed. Still, his organization would like to see things improve further.
"With regard to women's rights, a symbol won't serve women's rights as much as legal reform," Benchemsi told DW.

blocks.caption: Morocco is generally considered comparatively progressive in women's rights and the 2011 Constitution guarantees equality between men and womenImage: Moe Zoyari/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Activism around women's rights remains relatively permitted — an exception to the heightened governmental scrutiny and judicial proceedings against other areas of activism in Morocco," the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace wrote in a July 2025 commentary. "The king's leadership on gender reforms creates space for this activity, as advocates are often working in conjunction with parts of the government rather than against it."

Given popular discontent with the economy and high youth unemployment and protests, "improving women's status is a promise the government can deliver on in a challenging period," the organization noted.
But right now, Bordat argued that Mansouri's appointment shouldn't be seen as "something to be either celebrated or criticized."

The country is still waiting to see how Mansouri will form a governing coalition, she argued. How many female ministers the new government appoints, and what powers they are granted, will also be closely observed.

After that, "the real question is what civil society organizations, NGOs and citizens will do with this opportunity?" Bordat concluded. "That is, how do we hold all of the political parties and all of the newly elected representatives accountable and engaged … so we can continue to advance women's rights in Morocco?"

articles.title: Internal documents show why Ottawa is worried about the Alberta referendum, even if the province votes to stay

image.caption: Alberta separatists rally outside the offices of Elections Alberta in May. Documents obtained by CBC News show the potential risks that the federal government is evaluating ahead of this month's referendum. (Todd Korol/ Reuters)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Internal federal documents offer insights into how Ottawa is assessing the economic fallout from the possibility of Alberta separating from Canada and becoming an independent state.
Briefing notes outline potential fiscal shocks, population outflows, head office exodus
The documents from Finance Canada and the Justice Department also shed light on the consequences being considered from the uncertainty caused by Alberta separatism.

Finance Canada briefing notes, released to CBC News through access to information legislation, detail the federal government has been quietly studying the impact of a possible $18-billion fiscal shock, corporate head office flight and a mass exodus of Albertans to neighbouring provinces if Alberta exits the federation.
It also flags that federal pension laws are "flawed" and might not be up to the task of dealing with the possibility of Alberta exiting the Canada Pension Plan.
Much of the documents were redacted but still shed light on a range of outcomes the government is considering this fall.
The documents are dated June 2026.

Alberta's Oct. 19 referendum asks voters whether the province should remain in Canada or hold another vote at a future date to leave. Up until now much of the analysis of the economic hit of Alberta potentially separating has focused on the impact on the province instead of Canada as a whole.
Although polling indicates more Albertans want to remain in Canada than leave, the documents show even the possibility of a separation referendum could cause economic harm to Canada and the province.
Exodus of business headquarters
The analysis invokes the 1995 Quebec referendum which resulted in Quebecers voting to remain in Canada by a tight margin.
Data from bond and equity markets showed that vote coincided with "tightening in financial conditions both provincially and nationally," it states.
Businesses, it notes, delayed "investment decisions pending greater clarity regarding future economic arrangement."

items: Poll suggests slight majority of UCP voters favours separation
Everything you need to know about the Alberta referendum

blocks.text: Citing data from the Conseil du patronat du Québec during the late 1970s and early 1980s, it states that 263 major corporate head offices, including Sun Life, left Montreal.
"Lingering uncertainty in Alberta could trigger a similar exodus of headquarters, especially for non-resources sector companies," the documents state.

Under the heading "interprovincial population outflow," it notes that in 2021 Alberta saw nearly 17,500 net workers with post-secondary degrees move into the province — and suggests highly educated and highly skilled workers would leave an independent Alberta in large numbers.
CBC News asked Finance Canada for more details about the department's work studying the impact of the Alberta referendum.

Instead, the Privy Council Office responded with an emailed statement which said the federal government is "conducting its own study of various third-party economic analyses" on the potential costs of Alberta's separation from Canada.

"Alberta is an integral part of Canada and contributes significantly to the prosperity of Albertans and Canadians. Alberta is stronger as part of a united Canada," wrote Privy Council spokesperson Mélany Gauvin.
15% of national GDP
The analysis is also a reminder of how much the Albertan economy provides for the rest of Canada.
Between 2022 and 2024, Alberta's net fiscal contribution averaged roughly $18 billion annually.
With the province accounting for $475 billion in annual economic activity, Alberta represents 15 per cent of national GDP over the last decade.
Over the same time period the province also accounted for 31 per cent of Canada's exports. Most of this came from energy.
Stability or a fair shake: Ranchers' perspectives on separation

University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe has completed a similar analysis on the impact of separation. Tombe, who is part of the federalist group Lead Not Leave, notes that in 2024 Ottawa collected more than $19 billion than it spent in the province.

An independent Alberta would get to keep that money but Tombe's report found it would be quickly eaten up by NATO defence commitments, expenses related to assuming federal operations and falling revenues from a shrinking economy.

items: Establishing independent Alberta could cost up to $170B over 5 years: report

blocks.text: In an interview with CBC News, Tombe said although Canada stands to lose a lot from Alberta leaving, the real loser would be his province.
"Without doubt, it would be Alberta that would experience the largest economic disruption as a result of separation," Tombe said.
Canada Pension Plan impacts
Tombe has also done some number crunching on the impact of Alberta exiting the Canada Pension Plan.
The CPP was established in 1966 as a measure to provide retirement income to older Canadians and to make up for gaps in private pensions.

The plan has opt-out provisions and a formula to transfer assets, but the internal document notes the federal government's independent overseer of the CPP, the chief actuary, is concerned about the wording and payout formula set out in the federal law that governs the pension plan.
"In addition to the legislation being open to interpretation, the chief actuary has indicated that the formula it sets out is flawed," the documents state.

items: What to expect when you’re voting in the Alberta referendum and watching results

blocks.text: When the CPP and the legislation that came with it was set up in the 1960s, its assets were invested in provincial bonds.
But now the fund is invested in infrastructure like airports, equities and other global bonds — making divesting Alberta's share complicated.

"I would anticipate that if a province were to want to exercise their right to withdraw that the Supreme Court would have to make a ruling on what the language in the act ultimately means," Tombe said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

David Thurton is a senior reporter in CBC's Parliamentary Bureau. He covers daily politics in the nation’s capital and specializes in environment and energy policy. Born in Canada but raised in Trinidad and Tobago, he’s moved around more times than he can count. He’s worked for CBC in several provinces and territories, including Alberta and the Northwest Territories. He can be reached at david.thurton@cbc.ca

articles.title: Canada bet billions on an EV boom. Was it too much, too soon?
articles.summary: The federal and provincial governments bet billions on the rapid rise of the electric vehicle industry. But major EV and battery projects in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia have since been…

image.caption: The steel frame of PowerCo's battery plant rises from the construction site in St. Thomas, Ont. Volkswagen's battery subsidiary now says production at the plant will begin in 2029, two years later than originally planned. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

blocks.text: Canada·New

The federal and provincial governments bet billions on the rapid rise of the electric vehicle industry. But major EV and battery projects in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia have since been delayed, cancelled, suspended, substantially changed — and in one case, gone bankrupt — as automakers and suppliers adjust to weaker-than-anticipated demand.
Volkswagen battery plant in Ontario latest major project to be delayed
The latest is Volkswagen's massive PowerCo battery plant in St. Thomas, Ont., where production has been pushed back two years to 2029, because of "evolving market demand."

The setbacks are raising questions about whether Canada bet too big on how quickly the EV market would grow. Critics say demand may never reach the levels needed to support the scale of battery production governments sought to attract, while others argue these are temporary delays in the decades-long shift toward electrification.
A million batteries, but for what?

Grieg Mordue, a former Toyota executive and retired McMaster University professor who studied the auto industry, says the St .Thomas plant illustrates two problems with Canada's EV investment strategy: scale and location.
When the project was announced in 2023, PowerCo said the plant would eventually make enough battery cells for roughly one million EVs a year.

Mordue says that seemed inefficient since Volkswagen's major assembly operations are in the southern United States and Mexico, meaning batteries produced in St. Thomas would have to travel long distances to reach the vehicles they're intended to power.
Europe isn't the obvious destination either, he says, because Volkswagen (VW) already has battery production capacity there.
Even together, VW's North American plants don't produce enough vehicles to provide an obvious market for a million batteries a year.
"They got a million batteries," he said. "What are they going to do with them?"
VW and its PowerCo subsidiary did not respond to a request for comment.
VW has said the plant remains a cornerstone of its North American battery strategy and is continuing construction even as it pushes production back.
VW also said the delay will allow it to incorporate newer battery technology and scale production as demand develops.
It could also have an upside for taxpayers, Mordue said — in the form of a smaller subsidy bill.

Much of the support promised to Volkswagen is still tied to how many batteries the plant produces. With production now set for 2029 and with those incentives scheduled to start declining in 2030 and ending in 2032, Mordue says governments will likely pay "a whole lot less" than the original maximum.

Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada said in a statement that the federal government has so far contributed $700 million to the construction of the St. Thomas battery plant, noting Ontario is responsible for one third of the $13.2 billion governments have agreed to in production subsidies.
"The government remains engaged with PowerCo on their updated timelines," the statement said.
Ontario's Ministry of Economic Development Job Creation and Trade did not respond by deadline.
A bet on the long-term
Still, others argue that looking at today's EV demand misses the time scale on which investments such as St. Thomas were made.
"These investments are meant to last 50 to 70 years or more," Joanna Kyriazis, directory of policy and strategy at Clean Energy Canada told CBC News.
She said the current slowdown should be seen as growing pains in an industry that is still transitioning, rather than evidence Canada built too much battery capacity.
There are signs Canada's EV market may already be recovering after a slowdown.

New restgistrations of battery-only EVs rose 37.4 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, compared with the same time last year, according to Statistics Canada. When hybrids are included, Canadians registered 58,811 new zero-emission vehicles during the quarter, up 26.7 per cent.
Kyriazis says the investments are about keeping Canada relevant as the global auto industry undergoes a historic shift from gasoline-powered vehicles.
"It's not a question of maintaining a place in the North American auto indstury. It's — is Canada going to have an auto industry that survives in the 21st century at all?" she said.

"There's a clear direction that the global auto sector is going and if Canada wants to have a competitve auto sector into the future, we've got to be able to make and sell competitively priced electric vehicles and the parts that go into them."

Kyriazis says the potential market for these batteries also extends beyond electric vehicles. As electricity grids expand, batteries will increasingly be needed to store power and help balance supply and demand.

items: Gas prices and new incentives sparking more EV sales
Gas prices are dropping. You can thank the 'winter blend' for that

blocks.text: The St. Thomas site and a NextStar plant in Windsor, she said, "were looking at a short-term strategy of building batteries that would be used for grid-scale storage while EV update in North American started to sort of even out."

Kyriazis argues the current U.S. retreat from electric vehicles could prove temporary and that Canada shouldn't base a decades-long industrial strategy on policies that could change again under a future administration.
There is evidence the EV battery bet may have been early rather than fundamentally misplaced. The wider justification for building domestic battery capacity hasn't disappeared either.

China produced more than 80 per cent of the world's battery cells last year, according to the International Energy Agency, leaving governments in North America and Europe to build domestic supply chains in an industry that remains heavily concentrated in Asia.
Will buyers catch up?

University of Guelph economics professor Ross McKitrick is less convinced that time will solve the problem. He said EVs have an established market, but argues governments built their policy around expectations of demand far greater than what has so far emerged.
"What the government's been trying to do is force that market into existence," he said. "The numbers just don't add up."

McKitrick points to the billions governments offered manufacturers to build EVs and batteries, while simultaneously offering consumers incentives to buy the vehicles as evidence the industry wasn't able to sustain itself on the scale governments envisioned.

In a 2024 paper published in the Canadian Journal of Economics, McKitrick warned that if Canada's EV sales requirements rise faster than buyers' willingness to purchase them, it could hurt automakers and the wider economy.

items: Want to buy a used EV? Here’s what to look out for
As more EVs hit the road, will we have the mechanics to keep them running?

blocks.text: Ottawa scrapped EV sales requirements in 2026 and is moving repeal the broader federal mandate. It announced replacement emissions standards in February with consultations on the proposed regulations running until October 29.
Electric vehicles still account for a minortiy of new vehicle sales in Canada, despite years of government incentives aimed at encouraging consumers to buy them.
Electric vehicles accounted for 11.7 per cent of new light-duty vehicle sales in Canada in the first three months of 2026, according to Transport Canada, down from a peak of 15.4 per cent in 2024.
"At this point, it's a niche market," McKitrick said. "Some households like the product and are willing to pay for it."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Colin Butler is based in London, Ont., where he reports for Ontario and national audiences. He covers investigative, science, public policy and government accountability with a particular interest in using public records to uncover hidden stories.

articles.title: Sliding student scores spark fresh calls to revisit how we're teaching math
articles.summary: With recent high-profile assessments warning of sluggish and waning math skills among Canadian students, some experts say we need to revisit how we're teaching it, and to pay numeracy the same…

image.caption: Upper Grand District School Board teacher Kendra Corbett leads her Grade 3 students in a math lesson on Thursday, in Orangeville, Ont. (Deana Sumanac-Johnson/CBC)

blocks.text: Canada·New

With recent high-profile assessments warning of sluggish and waning math skills among Canadian students, some experts say we need to revisit how we're teaching it, and to pay numeracy the same attention we've shown literacy in recent years.
Vast research on how kids learn not always translating into classrooms, professor says

Earlier this week, Kendra Corbett stood at a blackboard breaking down an addition question for her Grade 3s, laying out step by step how to determine the answer and occasionally testing out suggestions her students called out.

A little later, she split her class into groups. Some youngsters played math games while others worked on an assignment using base ten blocks — manipulating the small plastic cubes, bars and squares (denoting units of one, 10 and 100, respectively). Corbett settled in with a handful of kids for a focused lesson on ordering numbers from least to greatest. All the activities allowed for practice learning three-digit numbers.

"We assume kids come in knowing what numbers actually mean. If they can count to 10, that doesn't necessarily mean they understand what 10 represents," said Corbett, a teacher in Upper Grand District School Board in Orangeville, Ont., some 60 kilometres northwest of Toronto.
"If they don't have the foundation of knowing what numbers actually mean and understanding of magnitude, then they're really going to struggle later on."

Knowledge and understanding of math rests on building blocks that students usually start developing in primary school. But with recent international and provincial assessments warning about sluggish and waning math skills among Canadian students — a slide that pre-dates the pandemic — some experts say we should revisit how we teach math and pay numeracy the same attention literacy has received in recent years.

What worries Canadian mathematician John Mighton are the changes happening over time, specifically the growth in students who are slipping to lower levels — where some can only handle basic math or are considered below functional numeracy — and the wider impact of that trend.

"That's a real threat to our country, to our economy, even to our political system. How can you think your way through problems that involve risk or probabilities or science if you can't do the simplest math?" said Mighton.
"It's a tragedy that we think math is not as important as it as and that we're not doing something about it."
Back in 2002, Mighton founded JUMP Math, an education charity that's grown to work with students and teachers in K-8 schools across Canada and abroad.

Teaching novices a new concept takes a different approach than teaching those already fluent in a topic, he says, yet much math instruction of the past 20 years has treated kids like experts before they're ready.

"From day one, you're given a lot of rich problems … highly contextualized, lots of complexity, lots of language. People don't feel they're really giving kids math unless they're doing that kind of problem," Mighton said.
"We mistake the end where we want to get kids to — we want them to be great chess players, great problem solvers — with the means to get them there," he said.
"Guide kids more, scaffold more, give more practice, build foundational knowledge, so the kids can become experts …When you do that, kids become much better problem-solvers."
LISTEN | Deep debate about teaching math:
The Current25:25Are your kids learning math the RIGHT way?
Building a solid foundation and then strong reasoning and problem-solving skills are especially important amid the rise of artificial intelligence, he says.
"It's a dangerous idea that kids are just going to be able to deal with all the challenges that are coming from AI … if they don't have any domain-specific knowledge, particularly in mathematics.
"You're going to be so easily fooled and misled and you'll make disastrous decisions if you don't understand the math."
Not a return to rote learning
As with the recent shift toward more explicit, structured and phonics-led literacy teaching, there's a growing call for more systematic, teacher-led, direct instruction in math.

That doesn't mean rote learning, Mighton says, but does mean relying on evidence-based practices. He encourages teachers to use screenings, for instance, and regular low-stakes assessments to help them to make adjustments that propel students' progression.
How to build math skills and student confidence: Mighton

There's a wealth of research about how children learn — on their attention spans, their ability to absorb information, barriers to that, and more — yet that research doesn't always translate into classrooms nor into the training that aspiring and working teachers receive, says neuroscientist Daniel Ansari, a professor of psychology and education at Western University in London, Ont.
He also advocates breaking up math learning into multiple, simplified steps, because it helps developing minds more readily pick up information.

"Sometimes teaching can assume that children start out as experts and they are required immediately to focus on their understanding, explaining their answers. And these sorts of things can overwhelm their cognitive systems and thereby prevent information making its way into long-term memory," he said.

Ansari says educators can absolutely strike a "balance between explicit instruction and letting children discover things working by themselves," but adds teachers must keep in mind what's developmentally appropriate and what learners are ready for.
Take timed practice — a.k.a. those "mad minute" sheets with rows of addition, subtraction, multiplication or division questions to be answered as quickly as possible — as an example.

Introduced too early, it overwhelms cognitive capacity, Ansari says. But once students have some time to learn and a bit of practice, "mad minutes serve as a way of increasing and deepening their fluency — and then it can also become something really fun."

items: OECD tests show sharp drop in math skills among Canadian teens
Alberta educators call mandatory screening tests time-consuming, ineffective, survey says

blocks.text: Rather than touting a "back to basics" mentality, Ansari instead suggests we consider "how can we improve things further, pick some things that we maybe discarded too early? Keep some things we're doing right now, but reassess some others."

Back in Orangeville, Upper Grand K-12 math lead Ashley Kozak has overseen a multi-pronged plan to improve early math learning. It includes central math facilitators, creating new teaching resources, employing an early math screener and, for the schools with the greatest need, sending in support teachers to deliver focused tutoring.
Updated math training for Grade 1 and Grade 3 teachers and principals has also boosted educator confidence, Kozak says, adding the board saw improvement in its latest EQAO results.
While she loves seeing kids' "a-ha" moments when visiting math classes, she says it's even better seeing students confidently approach the next questions.
"It's more than memorization. It's about problem-solving. It's about making those connections," she said. "Seeing that ... makes me feel like 'OK, we got this. We can do it.'"
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Based in Toronto, Jessica Wong covers stories about Canadian school systems and education for CBC News, with a particular interest in how technology impacts the lives and learning of students. Every so often, she revisits her previous life as a journalist covering the arts, entertainment and pop culture. You can email story tips and ideas to jessica.wong@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Hosting a radio show taught me immigrants came for Canada, not a separate Alberta
articles.summary: As the host of Red FM, Rishi Nagar has heard from many listeners who, like him, are immigrants to Canada and don't want Alberta to separate.

image.caption: As the host of Red FM, Rishi Nagar has heard from many listeners who, like him, are immigrants to Canada and don't want Alberta to separate. (Submitted by Rishi Nagar)

blocks.text: Canada·First Person
As the host of Red FM, Rishi Nagar has heard from many listeners who, like him, are immigrants to Canada and don't want Alberta to separate.
We do not have to choose between being strong Albertans and proud Canadians
This First Person is the experience of Rishi Nagar, who lives in Calgary. Also, check out our series on the Alberta referendum here and learn how we selected the writers.

My wife and I were working in India as teachers when we decided to immigrate to Canada. We were thinking of the future of our son, who was five at the time, and we felt he might get a better education in Canada.
At that time, I had no idea that Calgary — or Alberta — would eventually become the place my family and I would call home.

Like many Indians, when I thought about immigrating, I thought about Canada as a whole rather than any particular province or city. Of course, places like Brampton, Ont., and Surrey, B.C., are well-known in India because of their large Indian communities. But in conversations I've had with others who wanted to immigrate, the draw is simply Canada — a country of opportunity, diversity and new beginnings rather any specific city
For six long years, I waited. Then, in 2008, a letter arrived from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada asking me to prepare for a medical examination and other formalities.
The letter carried the maple leaf embossed therein. That very image became permanently etched in my mind as the symbol of Canada and of the new life awaiting my family.

When I finally landed at Pearson International Airport in Toronto, my heart was throbbing with excitement. Beside me was my equally excited wife and our 12-year-old son, almost dancing with joy. We had landed in our dreamland.

But dreams also demand struggle. The year 2009 was difficult because Canada was going through a harsh recession. I had moved to Toronto because some of my former students lived there. But I was advised to move to Vancouver because British Columbia was preparing to host the 2010 Winter Olympics and there might be more job opportunities there. I followed that advice and secured a security guard's licence.

items: Alberta referendum pitches more control over immigration. Here's what you need to know

blocks.text: I still remember my first day of work in Canada. My first assignment as a security guard was at the CBC building in Vancouver. For someone who had also previously worked as a television presenter in India, standing inside CBC was an extraordinary feeling. I thought: a former TV presenter from India is now at CBC. Wow! Suddenly, my dreams had wings again.
Soon, I joined Red FM as a news presenter, returning to journalism and broadcasting. When an opportunity arose in 2013 after Red FM established a station in Calgary, I chose to move here.

Alberta has given me tremendous opportunities. Here, I built my career as a journalist and broadcaster, raised my family, bought my first home and became deeply involved in the community. I had the privilege of serving two terms in the University of Calgary Senate and contributing to community initiatives, including anti-racism committees. These experiences taught me that citizenship is not only about what a country gives us; it is equally about what we give back.

Through all these moves, I never thought of myself as moving from one separate place to another. Toronto was Canada. Vancouver was Canada. Calgary was — and for me will always be — Canada. I was a proud Canadian in Toronto, a proud Canadian in Vancouver, and I remain a proud Canadian in Calgary. Had Red FM opened a new station in the U.S. or Alberta (if a separate sovereign country), I would never have opted to go there. My dreamland was Canada.

Recently, I held a radio talk show about the referendum question. Every caller who participated supported Alberta remaining part of Canada. The callers were all of South Asian background and represented different backgrounds: seniors, permanent residents who were not yet Canadian citizens, people with varying levels of education, working- and middle-class Albertans and university students.

items: Albertans divided on immigration, while half still undecided on 9 non-separation questions: poll

blocks.text: Yet their message was remarkably similar: Not one caller supported a separate Alberta. Many of them feared that separation would lead to increased racism against the racialized communities. Many of them also said that immigrants like them would not pick Alberta as a place to move because what they know about separation makes them concerned they won't be welcome.

Of course, one radio phone-in cannot represent the views of every Albertan. But listening to those voices reinforced something I have experienced throughout my Canadian journey: many people in my community do not see their Alberta identity and their Canadian identity competing with each other.
Neither do I.

Even sports reflect this Canadian feeling for me. I am an ardent Calgary Flames fan. But if the Flames fall behind and the Edmonton Oilers advance, I quickly start cheering for the Oilers. And I can equally enjoy a victory by the Toronto Maple Leafs. Ultimately, for me, it is Canadian success.

I understand many Albertans have genuine grievances with Ottawa. Concerns about federal policies, equalization, resource development, provincial jurisdiction and whether Alberta receives sufficient respect within Confederation deserve serious discussion. They should never simply be dismissed. On a personal note, the EV mandate by the Trudeau government never made sense to me for our brutal winters. Even in Calgary, my personal EV gives me a hard time at times and the long hauls would be a nightmare. These matters can be resolved amicably, and I appreciate it when Ottawa listened and repealed the EV mandate.
But separation is not the answer for me.

Canada is not perfect; no federation is. But disagreements within a family do not necessarily mean that the family should break apart. When an arm is broken, we don’t abandon it; we support it in a sling and keep it close to our heart.

items: Should Alberta separate? Here's why these Canadians feel the way they do

blocks.text: When Albertans make this historic choice, I will vote for Alberta to remain a province of Canada. I will also continue to support a stronger Alberta that confidently protects its constitutional rights and receives the respect it deserves within Confederation.
I arrived in this country carrying dreams beneath a maple leaf. That maple leaf still means something deeply personal to me.
We do not have to choose between being strong Albertans and proud Canadians. We can — and should — be both.
Do you have a compelling personal story that can bring understanding or help others? We want to hear from you. Here's more info on how to pitch to us .
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Bio: Rishi Nagar is a Red FM Calgary news director and host, a former senator at the University of Calgary and a former member of anti-racism action committees of the City of Calgary and the Calgary Police Service.

articles.title: Forgotten Island a 'love letter' to Filipino mythology, family and home
articles.summary: Forgotten Island is the first big-budget animated feature to place Filipino culture and mythology at its centre. It follows two childhood friends who are drawn into a fantasy world inspired by…

image.caption: Forgotten Island is a groundbreaking animated adventure rooted in Filipino culture and mythology, following childhood friends Jo and Raissa, as migration, separation and folklore intertwine in a magical world. (Universal Pictures)

blocks.text: Filipino Canadian Tricia Serdon grew up watching Disney movies and searching for a princess who looked like her. She never quite found one.
That changed with Forgotten Island.
"I think it’s such a great love letter to Filipinos," says Serdon, a marketing co-ordinator in Toronto.

The film, produced by Dreamworks Animation and released on Sept. 25, is the first major Hollywood animated feature to place Filipino culture and mythology at its centre. It follows Jo and Raissa, two childhood friends whose paths diverge when Raissa leaves the Philippines to attend college in the U.S., while Jo stays behind.

As the two friends navigate the pain of separation, they are eventually drawn into Nakali, a fantasy world populated by supernatural figures, adapted from folklore told in the Philippines for centuries. The name "Nakali" is a play on nakalimutan, or Tagalog for "forgotten."
Though inspired by ancient tales, the setting is a creative reimagining rather than a direct adaptation.

items: How the South Korean film Hope is making us think about the future
He’s won one of Canada’s top honours, but this Inuk filmmaker says his work is for his culture

blocks.text: A rich, lesser-known mythology

Nakali is not a traditional place from Filipino folklore. In the film, it is an imagined portal into the mythology itself — a place where Jo and Raissa encounter stories, creatures and memories carried across generations.
Among them are the manananggal, a vampiric creature whose upper body separates from its lower half and flies through the night, and the kapre, a dark, bearded giant that dwells in the forest.
Serdon, who was born in the Philippines, grew up hearing stories about these creatures. She says seeing them brought to life on the big screen was thrilling and deeply personal.
"The accuracy — I was very impressed," she told CBC News. "Sometimes it gets lost in translation, or even the pronunciation is never truly ... accurate. But this film I think did a really great job."

items: 'Through the Bamboo' is a play packed with Filipino folklore

blocks.text: The co-directors — Januel Mercado, who is Filipino American, and Joel Crawford — have wanted to tell a story about Filipino culture for years.
"We wanted to tell a Filipino story or make a movie set in the Philippines. We're like, 'Wow, they have this rich mythology,'" Mercado said. "And that's something we don't see that much."
Crawford says the creatures in the film are also metaphors for the characters’ emotional struggles, pointing to the weredog as an example.
A Filipino weredog is a mythical creature that transforms from a human into a giant, fierce dog at night. It is considered a type of aswang, a predatory monster.
The creature's involuntary transformation reflects the uncertainty of adolescence and the search for identity, Crawford says.
"In this coming-of-age story, we kind of treat it like puberty in a way," he said. "You can use this amazingly specific creature, the weredog, to go, 'Is he a human? Is he a dog? Is he a weredog?'"
With the support of his friends, the character eventually begins to understand who he is.
Mercado admits the film only scratches the surface of the Philippines' vast lore. He recalls earlier drafts that were "overstuffed" with creatures, eventually prioritizing story over spectacle.
The filmmakers hope the movie will inspire audiences to seek out more Filipino stories and encourage other Filipino creators to bring their interpretations to global audiences.
Familiar rhythms of family life
Beyond the magic, the film captures the familiar rhythms of Filipino family life.

One scene depicts a party where young children run around while relatives make sure everyone has enough food. Karaoke plays in the background, and titas and titos — aunts and uncles — trade jokes and observations.
For many viewers, this offers a rare portrayal of Filipino culture that isn't defined by hardship, but by humour, music and food.

Serdon says she was moved to tears by a sharp sense of recognition within the first 15 minutes, particularly struck by a scene where Jo’s lola, or grandmother, comforts her after she receives bad news.
She says she could also connect to the friendship at the heart of the film. Like Raissa, many Filipinos leave their home country to go abroad for new opportunities, often leaving behind loved ones.

"In the Philippines, you grow up being in the same class as everyone until you graduate," she said. "I miss my friends who I grew up with in the Philippines, and I just relate to the friendship [in the film] so much that I wish I could have watched it with my childhood friends that are back home."
Pop culture critic Rachel Ho says this kind of cultural specificity is what makes the film universal. "It makes the storytelling that much more authentic," she told CBC News.
Behind-the-scenes representation

The film's commitment to representation extended behind the scenes, as well. The voice cast features a powerhouse lineup of Filipino talent, including singers H.E.R. and Lea Salonga, along with actors like Manny Jacinto and comedian Jo Koy.
Manila-based Snipple Animation handled the 2D-animated flashbacks.
"It was important to us. We would love to have as many Filipino artists, Filipino Americans and homegrown artists from the Philippines be a part of this," Mercado said.

Michaelangelo Masangkay, co-founder of the Siné Institute, a non-profit organization in Toronto that champions Filipino cinema and filmmakers, emphasizes that representation must extend beyond the screen.
"It's really important for us to be able to get into that decision-making matrix to be able to say, 'Take a chance on this. This is what is authentic,'" he said.
Forgotten Island celebrates Filipino culture, friendship and 'girl power'

items: Is Forgotten Island the next sleeper hit for animated movies?

blocks.text: Reflecting on her childhood search for a Disney princess who looked like her, Serdon hopes the next generation of young Filipinos won't have to search so hard.
"To dress up as someone for Halloween, I want children to be inspired ... now, they can do Raissa and Jo for a costume or a manananggal, for example, if they want more of a villain," she joked.

That is the possibility Forgotten Island leaves behind — not simply that Filipino audiences will finally see themselves reflected on screen, but that the next Filipino story will not have to wait so long to be told.

articles.title: With celebs and influencers glamourizing 'cigs' online, experts are carefully watching smoking trends
articles.summary: Social media is filled with images of celebrities and influencers lighting up cigarettes and hyping the habit of smoking, suggesting it's experiencing a bit of a cultural resurgence. Though data…

image.caption: Images of celebrities, influencers and other content creators smoking are all over social media, and experts warn that they can have an outsize influence on young people picking up the deadly habit. (Guillaume Saligot/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Health·New

Social media is filled with images of celebrities and influencers lighting up cigarettes and hyping the habit of smoking, suggesting it's experiencing a bit of a cultural resurgence. Though data suggests tobacco use has long been trending downward, experts say if we want it to stay that way, harmful online content that glamourizes smoking shouldn't be ignored.
Experts say online content glamourizing cigarettes is harmful and no amount of smoking is safe
Dua Lipa in the streets of Italy. Charli XCX at her wedding. Singer Clairo snapping selfies. Heated Rivalry stars Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams out on the town.

These are just a few of the world's biggest celebrities who've recently appeared in dozens of photos on Instagram and TikTok, looking impossibly cool while doing something notoriously unhealthy: smoking cigarettes.
"It's almost like they're glamorizing smoking again," said Carolyn Baglole, an associate professor with McGill University's department of medicine.

But even with celebrities caught puffing and influencers hyping the habit, data suggests tobacco use has long been trending downward. Still, if we want it to stay that way, experts say online content glamourizing the habit shouldn't be ignored.
Global study found many people don't understand the dangers of smoking
No amount of smoking is safe: experts
Dedicated accounts to smoking culture have popped up online, including @cigfluencers, which boasts more than 100,000 followers on Instagram and posts pictures of celebrities smoking.
Meanwhile, posts normalizing "cigs" abound online.

Like the one that jokingly declares cigarettes don't count if you smoke them with your morning coffee or overseas. In another video, a woman defends influencer Alix Earle for smoking a cigarette with the caption, "Let a girl smoke a cheeky cig!" In another, the content creator says cigarettes don't count "if you're in the middle of writing."
However, experts warn that this is the kind of behaviour that can lead to addiction.

items: Q&A: This doctor says he's seeing the harms of social media on youth
Health officials trying to tackle massive and 'tragic' use of vapes among teens

blocks.text: "Nicotine is so highly addictive," said Rob Cunningham, a senior policy analyst with the Canadian Cancer Society. "A small number of cigarettes can lead to addiction and cravings."

According to Health Canada, tobacco use is the leading preventable cause of premature death in the country, and can lead to more than 40 debilitating and potentially fatal illnesses, including cancers and heart disease.

That hasn't stopped some people from posting about trends like "social smoking" — the practice of only smoking with friends or peers — while others even claim that smoking could "cure the loneliness epidemic" or help people make friends.
Though some of these posts may be facetious or played off as jokes, experts told CBC News no amount of smoking is safe.

"Even smoking socially, you don't want to risk a nicotine addiction," Baglole said. "If that happens and you become a life-long smoker, the risk of developing a chronic disease such as lung cancer, is so much higher."
Jared Oviatt is a smoker who runs the @cigfluencers account. Despite the popularity of his content, he previously told CBC Life that he doesn't believe we're in a smoking renaissance.
“I don’t see the comeback of cigarettes in celebrity culture as a true return to smoking as a mainstream habit,” Oviatt said.
“Are we seeing it more often? Yes. However, I also think we’re already nearing the peak of that trend."
Smoking on a downward trend
Cunningham confirmed that smoking isn't on the rise, at least not yet.
"So far, we have not seen an increase in smoking and that's good," he said.

Recent data from the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health shows a significant downward trend between 1999 and 2025. For students in grades 7-12 in Ontario, smoking tobacco cigarettes decreased from 28.4 per cent in 1999 to 3.5 per cent by 2025.

items: Drinking among Gen Z adults has gone up, busting the sober myth
New data shows 1 in 3 young Canadians have tried nicotine pouches

blocks.text: According to the federal government, smoking rates have steadily declined across the country. About 300,000 Canadians who smoked in 2023 reported that they quit smoking in 2024, with just 11 per cent of adult Canadians reporting smoking that year.
"We want to keep that trend going downward," Baglole told CBC News. "I would hate to see that trend reversed in any way and in any age demographic. Smoking is just so bad for you."
U.K. lawmakers approve lifetime tobacco ban for anyone born in 2009 or after
Cunningham says the habit damages teeth, skin and causes bad breath.
"It's also very costly once you're addicted," he said. In Canada, a pack of cigarettes can cost anywhere from $14 to $26 Cdn.

items: U.K. lawmakers approve lifetime ban on sale of cigarettes, vapes to anyone born after 2008
A 'smoke-free generation' tobacco ban is coming to the U.K. Could it also happen in Canada?

blocks.text: He also warned that the content on social media that glamourizes smoking is harmful.
"The positive depictions by influential people on social media is extensive and concerning," he said.
"Actors or influential people or celebrities do have influence — outsized influence — on the people they're exposed to."
Cunningham says he believes celebrities and influencers have a responsibility to protect their fans.
"They wouldn't want their kids or grandkids to smoke, and they should realize their behaviour can influence vast numbers of young people."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Anya Zoledziowski is a Peabody-winning multimedia journalist from Edmonton who's covered social and climate justice, Indigenous affairs, gender, politics and more, and has been recognized by several national and international awards. She’s currently pursuing her PhD in journalism studies.
With files from Trevor Risk

articles.title: Swiss scientist soils underpants, wins silly science prize
articles.summary: Franz Bender convinced a thousand people to soil their underwear. The Swiss soil ecologist and his team recruited 1,000 citizen scientists to bury and dig up underwear around Switzerland in an effort…

image.caption: Franz Bender, a Swiss soil ecologist, and his team of researchers recruited 1,000 citizen scientists across Switzerland and had them bury and dig up underpants to study soils. (Gabriela Braendle/Agroscope)

blocks.text: LISTEN | Why citizen scientists buried thousands of undies:
Quirks and Quarks9:24Why citizen scientists buried thousands of undies
Franz Bender convinced a thousand people to soil their underwear — and he wasn’t asking for bowel movements.

In 2021, the Swiss soil ecologist and his team recruited 1,000 citizen scientists to bury and dig up underwear around Switzerland in an effort to better understand soil and soil health. In September, the research won an Ig Nobel Prize, which is awarded annually for research that makes people laugh and then think.

The effort yielded some surprising results for the researchers — and the participants when they unearthed their underwear, which the hungry underground microbes had often consumed down to almost nothing.

“I think this moment when people dig out the underwear and look at it, it was really a revealing moment for many,” Bender, who works at the Agroscope agricultural research centre in Zurich, told Quirks & Quarks host Bob McDonald.
“It’s fascinating to see that, yeah, soil is really alive, and there’s a lot of life underground that we usually don’t think about.”
The research was published in Plants People Planet in Aug. 2026.
But Bender isn’t the first person to put underwear underground. In fact, the effort has roots in Canada.

The Innovative Farmers Association of Ontario started burying underwear in Ontario fields around 2015, farmer Alan Kruszel said. People had been burying cotton strips called assays for decades, but the farmers decided underwear was more fun.
It was so much fun, in fact, that Kruszel suggested taking it national. So, in 2017, the national “Soil Your Undies” campaign was born.
“It was just a marvelous hit,” Kruszel, a board member with the Soil Conservation Council of Canada, told Quirks & Quarks.
“It was to get people to think about soil as a living, breathing ecosystem, and to raise awareness of the importance about soil and soil health.”

items: Okanagan grape growers say crop insurance model failing amid wildfire smoke taint
This is how fast Swiss glaciers, the 'water tower of Europe,' are melting away

blocks.text: And it wasn’t just farmers and soil researchers who wanted to put what normally goes under our pants into the earth underneath our feet.
“I buried undies with all kinds of different people. We did it with senators, we did it with deans of universities, school kids, the Canadian Ag Museum in Ottawa did it with us,” Kruszel said.
“Garden clubs … you have no idea how much fun a group of little old ladies had with holding up soiled undies.”
A colleague of Bender's took notice, and suggested trying it in Switzerland. They hosted a small event where families buried underwear in the soil.

“The Swiss media just loved it. It was all over the place in the media,” Bender said. “Then another collaborator approached us [and said] ‘Hey, why don’t we start a citizen science project out of this and do something really big with it?’”

Bender and his research team needed 1,000 citizen scientists, but they got around 1,400 applications, so they had to select for geographically balanced distribution around Switzerland. Bender and his team shipped the volunteers two pairs of size small organic, cotton underwear, 12 teabags for comparison with the underwear, and some detailed instructions.
“So we drew clear pictures how they should be inserted in the soil, to which depth, and where the teabags should be placed,” Bender said.

The team also developed a smartphone app where participants could add additional information, such as pictures and geographical data, and answer questions about the land, such as whether it's fertilized or whether pesticides were used.
The citizen scientists dug up one pair of underwear and one set of teabags out after four weeks, and the second set of underwear and the rest of the teabags after eight weeks.
Hungry soil consumes underwear

Underwear doesn’t sound like an appetizing meal, but for the microbes and other life in fertile, biologically active soil, it was delicious. Uncovered from other kinds of soil, though, the uncovered underwear looked almost wearable.
“In some instances, there was only the synthetic threads at the waist band left. The underwear was completely eaten,” Bender said. “And in other cases, the underwear still looked like almost new.”
Generally, the underwear saw the greatest decomposition in private gardens and flowerbeds, and the least decomposition in lawns. Arable fields and grasslands were somewhere in between.

Bender explained that gardens often have a lot of compost and potentially also irrigation, which create soil conditions that have a lot of nutrients, organic matter and moisture. This promotes soil biological activity, which — in turn — leads to mangled underwear.

Lawns, in contrast, don’t have much species diversity above ground, and also get cut often. The soil system under lawns therefore isn’t nearly as alive and active as it is in gardens, and the result is that some underwear buried under lawns looks more dirty than consumed.

items: Here's why southern Ontario farmers are supporting a new bill to make soil a national asset
Sask. soil has improved by about 40% over the last 3 decades, study finds

blocks.text: There were some unexpected results, though. Bender said he was surprised by how high the nutrient contents were in private gardens, and also how little the underwear decomposed in farm soil compared to his expectations.
Bender also cautions that more active, fertile soil isn't necessarily "healthier." It can be, for example, harmful to biodiversity in a forest or nature reserve.
Bender said he hopes people understand how important soil is to us, especially as human activity such as chemical use affects it in uncertain ways.
"Soil is really important to keep the cycle of life going, and we all depend on soil," he said. "When we don't know enough about soil, it's also difficult to protect it."
Underwear boosts soil interest: profs

Asim Biswas, a professor and Canada Research Chair in digital agriculture at the University of Guelph, said that while the study is scientifically sound, its greatest value is the awareness it's brought to soil.
“It got major [media] coverage in 25 countries — that’s huge,” he said.
“The reason I feel like this was a very, very nice way of advocacy for soil, is that it’s something funny, and people tend to remember these sort of things."
Biswas seconds Bender's caution that more active, fertile soil isn't necessarily healthier, and adds there's a lot of research still to be done on the subject.
Joann Whalen, a professor at McGill University who studies soil, said the underwear method is a simpler, quicker and less costly alternative to chemical lab tests.
“We might see situations where somebody is interested in their soil, but they’ve never actually taken the time or had the opportunity to test it,” she said.
“With a visual test like this one, and you can just see the disintegration of the undies, you get a pretty quick idea of what’s going on in your soil."
The Soil Conservation Council of Canada also encourages it, and provides instructions.
And the exhumed Swiss underwear will see new life. Bender and his team have collaborated with a fashion designer who's already made a dress out of some of them.
"There will be more fashion items coming out of this," Bender said.

articles.title: Sara Duterte camp hits Trillanes over ‘desperate, tired narratives’
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte's spokesperson Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr. on Saturday, October 3, hit former senator Antonio Trillanes IV over allegations linking the vice president's family to Chinese…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte's spokesperson Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr. on Saturday, October 3, hit former senator Antonio Trillanes IV over allegations linking the vice president's family to Chinese funds, calling them “desperate and tired narratives.”
Panelo issued the statement a day after Trillanes alleged that a food company partly owned by Duterte's husband, lawyer Manases “Mans” Carpio, received more than P319 million from China.

“Since 2016, former Senator Antonio Trillanes IV has been peddling the same exhausted lies regarding Extrajudicial Killings (EJKs), fabricated drug links, imaginary unexplained wealth, baseless corruption allegations, and fictional China connections against the Duterte family,” Panelo said.
Trillanes' China allegations
Trillanes made the allegations at a press conference on Friday, October 2, a day after House prosecutors dropped him as a witness in Duterte's impeachment trial.
He said he had asked to be removed from the witness list to relieve the prosecution of further pressure and instead disclose publicly what he intended to present before the senator-judges.

Trillanes alleged that Chinese government-linked entities and corporations sent more than P319 million to Cale88 Foods Corp., a banana chip exporter where Carpio was an incorporator, director and shareholder from 2021 to 2024.

Securities and Exchange Commission Director Gerardo Del Rosario previously testified during the impeachment proceedings that Carpio's stake in Cale88 rose to 47.5% in 2024 before disappearing in 2025.
Duterte herself had no ownership interest in Cale88, but Trillanes argued that the company's ties to her husband were relevant to her liability.

He also presented records showing that the Tapang at Malasakit Alliance for the Philippines Inc., a nonprofit founded by Duterte, received P150 million from the Embassy of the People's Republic of China.

The group's financial statement showed that the money was a donation intended to build 13 classroom buildings in Davao City. The project was carried out under an agreement with the Chinese embassy and coordinated with the Department of Education.

On Thursday, lead prosecutor Rep. Jinky Luistro confirmed that Anti-Money Laundering Council records submitted to the impeachment court included summaries of remittances to Cale88 from China and other countries. She declined to disclose the amounts, citing the court's sub judice rule.
Panelo: Trillanes ‘folded’
Panelo, however, accused Trillanes of backing away when given the opportunity to defend his allegations under oath.

“Yet, the moment he was faced with the very first opportunity to test his wild claims against actual facts, verified records, and law through cross-examination by the Vice President’s defense team, Trillanes folded,” Panelo said.
“Instead of defending his claims under oath, he chose the comfort of a safe and scripted press conference where his lies could once again go unchallenged.”
Panelo also brought up Trillanes' previous allegations involving extrajudicial killings, alleged drug links and supposed unexplained wealth against the Duterte family.
He cited Peter Joemel Advincula, alias “Bikoy,” lawyer Jude Sabio and Arturo Lascañas, whom he described as people Trillanes previously relied on to support his claims.
Panelo claimed that Advincula had admitted being used in a destabilization plot and that Sabio had withdrawn his communication to the International Criminal Court.
He also said Lascañas' credibility had been “completely demolished” by contradictions in his statements.
Panelo described Trillanes' allegations as “black propaganda” and accused the former senator of being a “professional character assassin.”
Trillanes has maintained that the financial records he presented raise questions about the Duterte family's wealth and ties to China.

He said the alleged Chinese fund transfers to companies linked to the vice president's family had national security implications and could constitute grounds for her impeachment and disqualification from public office.
“Dapat kilabutan po tayo dito... Bawal po iyan. Bawal tumanggap from a foreign government, especially high-ranking official ang vice president,” Trillanes said.
Duterte has repeatedly denied allegations that she possesses unexplained wealth. In April, she accused Trillanes of reviving allegations he had made against her family since 2016.
Duterte camp: Evidence will speak
Panelo also accused the administration of protecting individuals who make allegations against Duterte and her family, citing Ramil Madriaga and Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.

“The Vice President would gladly sue him for these endless fabrications, but we have already witnessed how those who actively peddle malicious lies against her and her family are openly protected and propped up by this administration,” Panelo said.
He did not provide evidence in the statement to support his allegation of an administration plot against Duterte.
Panelo said Duterte's defense team would instead allow the evidence presented before the Senate impeachment court to speak for itself.
“Confident that the law, the facts, and the evidence are squarely on her side, the Vice President will let the evidence before the Senate Impeachment Court speak for itself,” he said.
“Her defense team stands ready to refute whatever Trillanes accusation the prosecution believes is even credible enough for the Court’s serious consideration.” — with a report from Cristina Chi

articles.title: COA flags P10.4-B terminated contracts of Leviste's Solar Philippines
articles.summary: The Commission on Audit (COA) has flagged a staggering P10.77 billion in uncollected financial obligations tied to 37 terminated solar energy contracts, reporting that a single corporate group…

blocks.text: Published October 3, 2026 3:54pm

The Commission on Audit (COA) has flagged a staggering P10.77 billion in uncollected financial obligations tied to 37 terminated solar energy contracts, reporting that a single corporate group founded by Batangas Representative Leandro Leviste accounted for 96% of the total defaults.

In its observations on the Department of Energy (DOE), state auditors said the government is at risk of non-collection following the widespread cancellation of Solar Energy Operating Contracts (SEOCs), "thereby underscoring the need for timely enforcement and close monitoring of contractual obligations of solar energy service contractors."

"Further, the termination of these contracts resulted in approximately 6.796 gigawatts-hour of unrealized potential generating capacity that could have contributed to the country's renewable energy supply," the COA said.

State auditors said that out of the P10.77 billion in financial obligations demanded across the 37 cancelled solar agreements, P10,389,331,719.44 is directly owed by firms under the Leviste-led Solar Philippines umbrella.

To put into context, state auditors said the sheer scale of the default at P10.39 billion demanded from Solar Philippines dwarfs the Solar Energy Management Division's 2025 operating budget of P21.02 million—representing roughly 494 years' worth of the division's annual funding requirement.

"This comparison highlights the significance of the outstanding obligations and underscores the importance of adopting timely and effective measures to ensure their collection in order to protect government interest and maximize the use of public resources," COA stated in its report.
The unpaid sums cover unfulfilled work commitments, training commitments, development assistance fees, and heavy contractual penalties.
The DOE has since escalated the matter to the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) to initiate legal recovery actions against Solar Philippines.
In particular, the Energy Department is demanding P24 billion in claims against Solar Philippines, which has been referred to the OSG.
The amount represents the P10.39 billion from the terminated solar energy contracts, while the remaining billions were related to their contracts terminated in previous years.

The Ombudsman is investigating Leviste and his mother, Senator Loren Legarda, in connection with P10-billion plunder and graft complaints, alleging that his renewable energy firm failed to provide solar power under its congressional franchise.
The mother and son lawmakers are currently outside of the country and are believed to be in France. Legarda is on medical leave, which she has repeatedly extended.
GMA News Online has reached out to Leviste for comment, but he has yet to respond as of posting time.

Earlier, lawyer Tony La Viña, spokesperson for Leviste and Legarda, said the Batangas congressman's companies did not have a monopoly, having only 5% of the total solar and 2% of the renewable energy contracts.
La Viña said not performing a service contract is normal since it is essentially a permit to explore.

He added that it was malicious to say Leviste did nothing, because President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. himself inaugurated the 3500 MW Terra Solar project in Nueva Ecija that was "conceptualized and implemented originally by Leviste, which the DOE boasted as the world's largest solar-battery project and the largest project of this administration."
The COA, however, recommend the following, which it said was agreed to by the DOE-SEMD and other concerned bureaus:

items: exhaust all available legal and administrative remedies to facilitate the collection of the outstanding financial obligations from the Solar Energy Developers concerned
strengthen the monitoring of compliance with the provisions of Solar Energy Operating Contracts to ensure the timely and effective enforcement of sanctions for contractual defaults

revisit existing policies and guidelines over the award and implementation of solar energy service contracts and cause reforms or modifications, if warranted, to minimize project cancellations and the resulting loss of potential generating capacity

blocks.text: Meanwhile, the DOE has assured state auditors that previously blocked project locations have been reopened for application to new, qualified developers under streamlined rules designed to fast-track real power output.
Furthermore, the Energy Department is finalizing a formal blacklisting policy for renewable energy (RE) developers.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – New online sellers and livestreamers can get a three-month break from commission fees under a new package launched by Converge ICT Solutions, the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI), and TikTok Shop.

Called SellerPlus, the package is aimed at micro, small, and medium enterprises, home-based businesses, and creators looking to build their businesses through livestream and e-commerce. It combines a 200 Mbps Converge fiber connection with TikTok Shop tools and other services.

Among its more useful features for sellers just starting out is 0% commission fees for their first 90 days on TikTok Shop, potentially allowing newly onboarded merchants to keep more of their sales while they establish an audience and test their products online.

The package also gives merchants access to vouchers and incentives through a gamified goal system called “seller missions,” promises dedicated customer service support, and traffic and voucher support through TikTok Shop’s monthly Sariling Atin campaign, which promotes local brands.

Converge said the 200 Mbps fiber connection is intended to support uninterrupted livestreaming, highlighting that disruptions with poor connections can lead to lost sales. The package also includes personal accident insurance from AXA.

SellerPlus is also tied to the DTI’s AI and Scale-Up Center in Makati, where entrepreneurs can access co-working facilities, training spaces, digital skills workshops, and demonstrations of tools such as content generators, customer-service bots, and inventory software.

SellerPlus also includes a mentorship component through BizFriend PH, a Facebook community where local merchants can exchange experiences, collaborate, and receive business advice. The program’s BizPro Rockstar Mentorship Program brings in experts in areas such as partnership law, digital marketing, tax compliance, business communication, and business growth.

The initiative comes as more small businesses use social commerce and livestreaming as lower-cost ways to reach customers. For newer sellers in particular, temporarily removing commission fees — alongside internet access, promotional support, and training — could reduce some of the upfront costs of experimenting with online selling. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe, UAE official says
articles.summary: The flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft two and a half hours into its journey before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker.

blocks.text: The co-pilot of the Flydubai plane travelling to Israel attacked the pilot with a crash axe in an attempt to take control of the aircraft, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.
The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv carrying more than 170 people plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two and a half hours into its journey.

Capt Smit Machchhar said he was lying on the cockpit floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside."
Passengers aboard the aircraft were then able to enter the cockpit and overpower the attacker, while on-duty crew travelling on the flight landed the plan safely.
A crash axe is usually kept ​in the cockpit in case of emergencies.
The UAE attorney general told state media that investigations were ongoing to determine the full circumstances and motives of the incident.
The co-pilot who launched the attack was an Omani national, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Netanyahu told Fox News on Thursday that, after being subdued, the attacker called out to the crew, "Kill me, kill me!"
He added: "So, it's clear that he was suicidal… It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane."
He also said the attacker "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination".
The UAE has begun investigating whether the "incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose", according to the country's state news agency.
Machchhar, who was stabbed in the attack, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.
He was in "good health and recovering well", the Indian embassy in the UAE said on Thursday.
The pilot said: "I am confident that the recovery will be there and I will become fit and healthy again."
