articles.title: No coordination with Taiwan in driving away Chinese ship off Batanes --Tarriela
articles.summary: The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) did not coordinate with the Taiwan Coast Guard when it drove away Chinese research vessel allegedly conducting unauthorized marine scientific research off Itbayat,…

blocks.text: Published October 3, 2026 3:10pm

The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) did not coordinate with the Taiwan Coast Guard when it drove away a Chinese research vessel allegedly conducting unauthorized marine scientific research off Itbayat, Batanes.

At a news forum in Quezon City, PCG spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela on Saturday said that up to three Taiwan Coast Guard vessels were also waiting to drive away the Chinese research ship once it exited the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone.

“It is surprising that even the Taiwan Coast Guard is also seriously looking into the illegal MSR (marine scientific research) which could be conducted by this Chinese research vessel,” Tarriela said.

On Thursday, the PCG said it deployed a patrol vessel and an aircraft to drive away JIA HAI KE 7, which was conducting unauthorized marine scientific research within the country’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ).
Tarriela clarified that the PCG did not coordinate with the Taiwan Coast Guard during the operation.

“We don’t have any coordination whatsoever. I would like to believe that the Taiwan Coast Guard is just merely relying on the AIS (automatic identification system) data of the Philippines Coast Guard vessel that is why they have the idea that a Chinese research vessel together with China Coast Guard 2503 and the other coast guard vessel… would also be crossing the border of the exclusive economic zone of our country,” the PCG official said.
Tarriela also reiterated that the Department of Foreign Affairs has confirmed that no such consent was given to JIA HAI KE 7. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Subsea cable cut between Philippines and Singapore disrupts internet services
articles.summary: Internet users in the Philippines face intermittent connections after undersea cable cut forces telecoms to reroute traffic to restore services

blocks.text: Internet users in the Philippines face intermittent connections after undersea cable cut forces telecoms to reroute traffic to restore services

items: On October 2, internet users in the Philippines faced slow and intermittent connections due to an undersea cable cut linking the Philippines and Singapore, impacting several telecommunications providers.
PLDT and Converge ICT Solutions reported that they successfully rerouted most affected traffic, while Globe warned customers of potential slow access and worked on restoring normal service.
The outage may lead to slower website loading and higher latency for users accessing international services, although local services are expected to be less affected.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Internet users in the Philippines experienced slower and intermittent connections on Friday, October 2, after an undersea cable segment linking the Philippines and Singapore went offline, affecting several telecommunications providers and internet service providers.
PLDT said the submarine cable cut affected services nationwide. The telco said it had successfully rerouted most of the affected traffic and expected service to normalize shortly.

Converge ICT Solutions likewise said it had rerouted internet and data traffic going to and coming from Singapore through other submarine cables. Its technical teams were continuing to monitor connections to apps and websites hosted in Singapore.

Globe, meanwhile, advised customers that they could experience slow internet access on both mobile and broadband services because of a technical issue, saying it was working to restore normal access as soon as possible.
The UP Diliman Network Helpdesk also issued an advisory saying one of the undersea cable segments between the Philippines and Singapore was offline.

The university said many of its upstream internet providers connect through these major international data routes, which could result in “increased latencies and intermittent performance,” particularly when users access websites and services hosted overseas.
For ordinary internet users, a submarine cable outage does not necessarily mean losing internet access entirely.

Telecommunications companies can redirect, or reroute, data through other submarine cables and international connections. But with traffic moved away from its usual route, data may have to travel farther or share capacity with more users.

Consumers may therefore notice slower website loading, higher latency or “ping,” video buffering, sluggish downloads and intermittent connections, particularly when accessing apps, websites, cloud services or game servers hosted outside the Philippines.
Services hosted locally may be less affected, while connections that normally pass through Singapore or other affected international routes could experience more noticeable slowdowns.

Submarine cables carry much of the internet traffic moving between countries. Having multiple cable routes allows telecommunications companies to keep users connected when one link fails, although performance can temporarily suffer while traffic is being rerouted.
PLDT and Converge said they had already rerouted affected traffic as of October 2, while Globe said restoration efforts were underway. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Joker persona helps Cong 'feel the fear' in opponents
articles.summary: Wang Cong dismisses critics who say she she is not deserving of facing Natalia Silva for the flyweight world title at UFC 332 on Saturday.

blocks.text: Before Wang Cong faces off with her opponents, she dyes her hair green, paints her face white and draws a bright red grin from cheek to cheek.
Fans may assume Cong is paying tribute to Batman's notorious arch-enemy the Joker, but the Chinese fighter says her persona is rooted in the joker playing card that inspired the comic-book villain.
The 34-year-old, who is on a four-fight win streak, says she can "feel the fear" in her opponents when she wears the face paint.
On Saturday at UFC 332 in Salt Lake City, Cong will be hoping she can invoke the same emotions in Brazilian Natalia Silva, when the pair fight for the vacant flyweight world title.
"It means the most powerful card, so I want to be the most powerful," Cong tells BBC Sport.
"When I have paint on I feel crazy. It makes me perform better, it inspires me. There's not much different between paint and no paint, this is my true personality."
Cong has bewildered opponents at weigh-ins while wearing the face paint, and says she even adopts the Joker alias when using social media messaging back home in China.

She tossed an imaginary coin and pretended to shoot a gun before her fight against Gabriella Fernandes in 2024, while in July she bizarrely gifted Tracy Cortez a pack of fake eyelashes before the pair's flyweight encounter.
Cong laughs as she reveals Silva can expect a "surprise" of her own before their fight at the Delta Centre, although she then turns serious as she pays tribute to her opponent.

Silva, 29, enters the contest on a 14-fight win streak across different promotions and is the favourite to capture the vacant title after Valentina Shevchenko was forced to vacate the belt last month through injury.
"She's an incredible fighter, an eight-fight win streak in UFC, beaten three former champions, she has amazing footwork, distance control and kicks," adds Cong.
Silva, who is number one in the UFC's flyweight rankings, was set to face Shevchenko for the belt before the bout was cancelled, so was expected to challenge for the vacant title.
Some fans were surprised that sixth-ranked Cong was chosen for the title fight however, and she admits she felt the same way.
"To be honest I was a little bit surprised but if you see the rankings, the girls ranked higher than me have either a fight booked or they have just fought," said Cong.
"I'm on a four-win streak so that makes sense."
The fight represents the first women's main event in the UFC since Mackenzie Dern beat Amanda Ribas is January 2025.
The last time two women headlined one of the UFC's flagship numbered events was when Amanda Nunes defeated in June 2023.
Cong says it's "meaningful" to be flying the flag for women's MMA after a period of under representation in the UFC, and is excited for the opportunities her success could create in China.
If Cong wins, she will become only the second Chinese UFC champion after former strawweight title holder Zhang Weili.
"MMA is my final transition in my combat sports career. I think my success will encourage more athletes to be brave and try mixed martial arts in China," said Cong.
The event has received criticism from some fans on social media, who instead called for the main event to feature fighters such as Jiri Prochazka, Ciryl Gane and Alex Pereira.
When asked if Cong has a message for her critics, she was concise in her response.
"I've got nothing to say right now. After my fight I think they will shut up," she said.

articles.title: Flydubai co-pilot used crash axe to attack captain, says UAE
articles.summary:
Attorney general says ‘terrorist attack’ was attempted by suspect who is said to have been barred from flying by Oman because of extremist views

The co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073 used a…

blocks.text: The co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073 used a crash axe to attempt to carry out a “terrorist attack” during the flight, the United ⁠Arab Emirates prosecutor general said on Saturday, according to a state news agency.

The UAE statement cited the prosecutor general as saying the co-pilot also tried to take control of the plane during Wednesday’s attack on the Israel-bound flight. Passengers and crew intervened to subdue the co-pilot and stabilise the plane. Officials said the co-pilot’s actions nearly crashed the flight with 182 people on board by sending it into a sharp plunge.
A crash axe is typically kept in the cockpit for ⁠use during emergencies.

The co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views, a person familiar with the matter said. He was then hired by the United Arab Emirates-based airline flydubai, the person said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing investigation. It was not immediately clear to what extent he was vetted when he was hired. Oman’s barring of him was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.
The co-pilot was born in the UAE and his mother is Syrian, according to a regional official with knowledge of the investigation.

How the co-pilot managed to be working in the cockpit on Wednesday morning is a central question for investigators. Israel says it has agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots out of its airspace who come from nations with which it does not maintain diplomatic relations. Israel and Oman do not have formal diplomatic relations.

The official confirmed that the co-pilot worked with Oman’s national airline but was removed from flying because of concerns that he showed signs of extremist views. He was later moved to an administrative job at Oman Air, the official said.

Security agencies from four regional countries were working to establish the co-pilot’s motives, aided by the US and other western governments, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss details of the investigation.

blocks.caption: One of the people injured in the incident. Photograph: Amit Segal

blocks.text: UAE senior diplomatic adviser Anwar Gargash on Friday called the attack a “dangerous terrorist act”. The incident is a test for the UAE government, which has earned a reputation for effective measures against extremist activities but has also bristled in the past over criticism of security lapses.
Little else was immediately known about the co-pilot’s background. His Instagram account was active until the day of the flight and then deleted.
The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, on Friday said the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radicalisation” but provided no evidence.

The captain, who was badly wounded, has said he used his remaining energy while being stabbed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing people who had noticed loud noises to come in, tackle the co-pilot and stabilise the plane. It made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Both the captain and co-pilot were taken to the UAE as it leads the investigation. Officials have said a number of countries including Israel are participating.
With Associated Press and Reuters

articles.title: Brazil’s neck-and-neck election offers test for growing pro-Trump Latin American bloc
articles.summary: Sunday’s poll pits the leftist incumbent Lula against the son of a former far-right president convicted of staging a coup
articles.byline: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: Shortly after his controversial speech to the United Nations general assembly in September, Donald Trump gathered a dozen like-minded Latin American leaders and boasted that rightwing candidates had won all seven presidential elections held in the region since he began his second term.

“Everybody I’ve endorsed has won,” the US president said in New York to most of the leaders of the Shield of the Americas, an anti-drug cartel coalition of 15 countries governed by the right or far right.

blocks.caption: A giant balloon of Donald Trump holding Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva during a Flávio Bolsonaro rally in São Paulo. Photograph: Miguel Schincariol/AFP/Getty Images
Donald Trump departs a meeting of the multinational coalition Shield of the Americas on the sidelines at the UN general assembly in New York. Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

blocks.text: Those electoral victories – and the US takeover of Venezuela after capturing Nicolás Maduro – have left just six Latin American countries under leftwing governments: regional heavyweights Brazil and Mexico, small Uruguay and Guatemala, and the isolated regimes of Cuba and Nicaragua.
On Sunday, Brazilians go to the polls in a presidential election that many believe will determine more than Latin America’s largest country’s fate for the next four years.

blocks.caption: Supporters Lula gather at a political rally in São Paulo. Photograph: Brian Snyder/Reuters

blocks.text: Given Mexico’s geographic proximity and unique economic relationship with the US, analysts see Brazil as perhaps the last country in the region still capable of saying “no” to Trump’s whims – something that could change dramatically depending on the election result.

Polls indicate a neck-and-neck race between Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the 80-year-old leftist incumbent who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, and Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, the far-right senator son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
“Trump really does take seriously the idea that the Americas should be his back yard,” said Pedro Telles, a professor at the School of International Relations at Brazil’s FGV university.

blocks.caption: President Claudia Sheinbaum leads her morning press conference at the National Palace in Mexico City, marking two years in office.  Photograph: Luis Marin/Clasos/Zuma Press/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “Mexico will remain relevant, and its president, Claudia Sheinbaum, is one of the most popular leftwing leaders. But if Flávio wins, it would be a real blow to the left and a major boost to the far-right agenda globally,” added Telles.

“There is a lot at stake,” said Sandra Borda Guzmán, an associate professor of political science at Colombia’s Universidad de los Andes. “Instead of taking the opportunity to expand our region’s autonomy, a far-right victory would align the region unconditionally with the dictates of the US,” she added.

blocks.caption: A street vendor sells campaign flags of the presidential candidates Bolsonaro and Lula. Photograph: Eraldo Peres/AP

blocks.text: Lula and Bolsonaro differ sharply on the US, including over what has become Trump’s main foreign policy for the region: the so-called “war on drugs” used to justify dozens of airstrikes on boats that have killed more than 230 people and joint operations involving US military personnel on land.

While Bolsonaro has pledged to join the Shield of the Americas and to follow an “iron fist” approach to crime, Lula has raised concerns about sovereignty and said it is “sad to see the inferiority complex of Latin American presidents” who are part of the Trump-created coalition.

Lula and Trump’s relationship has swung between not speaking and public displays of warmth, but it is currently at a low point, with the Brazilian president and Democratic members of the US Congress accusing Washington of trying to interfere in Bolsonaro’s favour.

“Brazil is a big prize,” said Michael Shifter, adjunct professor at Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service, adding that amid endless conflicts in Iran, Ukraine and Israel-Palestine, “US foreign policy is going very badly in the rest of the world.”
A victory for Bolsonaro in Brazil, he said, would be used “triumphantly” by Trump for producing an “almost completely aligned region”.

At the latest Shield of the Americas meeting, Trump made clear that it was not all about security. The US president also referred to the “tremendous natural wealth” of Latin American countries, which he said could not “be taken over by hostile outside powers” – widely understood as a reference to China.

blocks.caption: Posters for Lula  in the streets of the Cajazeiras neighborhood in Salvador, Bahia state. Photograph: Amanda Cotrim/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Privileged access to Brazil’s rare earths and critical minerals was one of the conditions Washington imposed in exchange for not applying tariffs, which Lula rejected. Bolsonaro, on the other hand, has offered those natural resources as the “solution” to help the US “break its dependence on China”.

“Democracy is also kind of on the line here,” added Shifter, noting that Bolsonaro was only running because his father cannot – Jair Bolsonaro is under house arrest after being convicted of attempting a coup to overturn his defeat by Lula in the 2022 election.
“So it’s not just a question of one more country moving to the right, but of a right that has a very problematic relationship with democracy,” he said.

As in recent elections across Latin America, the race includes other candidates but is polarised between two leading candidates. Lula and Bolsonaro have alternated as frontrunners in the final stretch, making the outcome unpredictable; if neither wins 50% plus one of the votes, there will be a runoff on 25 October.

Bolsonaro’s only previous bid for an executive role in government ended ignominiously when he took fourth place in Rio’s 2016 mayoral race. But analysts say there are several reasons why a congressman best known for his family name and corruption allegations – some shelved, others still under investigation – has emerged as a serious challenger to a three-time president.

Unemployment, poverty and inflation have fallen, and average incomes have risen, but so has household debt – something many attribute to online betting, which the older Bolsonaro left unregulated and Lula banned days before the vote.

The incumbent’s campaign has also been hit by corruption allegations – still under investigation – involving his son and a former aide, while a scandal involving supreme court justices with no connection to Lula may have rubbed off on the president.

blocks.caption: Bolsonaro waves at supporters during a campaign rally at the São Paulo Municipal Market in São Paulo. Photograph: Miguel Schincariol/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Many therefore see Bolsonaro’s support as coming both from a simple transfer of his father’s voter base and from an anti-Lula vote.

“I’m going to vote for Flávio, but not because I think he’s the best option,” said Bruna Arguello, 34, a businesswoman from Santana de Parnaíba, whose first choice would be Ronaldo Caiado, a far-right former governor of Goiás, polling at 4%. “Unfortunately, he has no chance of winning, so I’m going with Flávio so we can get Lula out,” she said.

blocks.caption: The presidential candidate for the Social Democratic party (PSD), Ronaldo Caiado, speaks at a press conference in Rio de Janeiro on Thursday. Photograph: Andre Coelho/EPA

blocks.text: Actor Docy Moreira, 59, will vote for Lula. In 2018, she was so dismayed by Jair Bolsonaro’s election that she decided to leave her home town of Belo Horizonte, where two-thirds of voters backed the far-right leader. “I couldn’t understand how people, including the vast majority of my family, were choosing so much violence and authoritarianism,” she said.
She Googled which cities had given Bolsonaro the lowest share of the vote, chose one about 1,550 miles away and moved north to Luís Correia, in Piauí.
She eventually returned home, and most of her family will now vote for Bolsonaro’s son. Still, Moreira remains confident Lula will win.
“If not, it will be devastating, but I’m not going to move again. I’m stronger now. I’ve learned that I can find refuge within myself,” said Moreira.

articles.title: Bosnia and Herzegovina is still shaped by war, separatism, EU ambitions
articles.summary: Bosnia and Herzegovina is governed by a system established after the Bosnian war — more than 30 years ago. Ethnic divisions, a complex administration and European integration all shape the country's…

image.caption: Sarajevo, host of the 1984 Winter Olympics, was under siege for four years during the Bosnian war in the mid 1990sImage: Gabriele Thielmann/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: To call Bosnia and Herzegovina a complicated country is an understatement. The country in the Balkan Peninsula divides its economic, administrative and political responsibilities between the multiethnic central government, the self-governing neutral Brcko district and two semi-autonomous entities that, for the most part, operate independently — the Muslim-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb-run Republika Srpska.

Both semi-autonomous entities are further split into several cantons and communities, home to mostly Bosniaks and Bosnian Croats in the central-western federation and Bosnian Serbs in Republika Srpska, to the north and east.

This principle of ethnic nationalism is key to the country's central constitutional and political organization. The Bosnian constitution recognizes Bosniaks, who are predominantly Muslim, the largely Orthodox Bosnian Serbs and primarily Catholic Bosnian Croats as "constituent peoples" with equal rights.

Today, the country has a population of around 3.1 million people. Around half are Bosniaks, while 31% are Serb and 15% are Croat. The rest of the inhabitants belong either to one of the 17 officially recognized minorities, like the Roma and Jews, or chose not to identify with any ethnicity at the last official census. Bosnian, Croatian and Serbian are all recognized as official languages.

The central government is led by rotating three-way presidency, made up of one representative from each of the three main constituent groups. The upper house of parliament and key government offices are also divided according to this principle.
This strict balance between the three groups is always maintained, both politically and socially, often leading to ethnic interests and political gridlock dominating the decision-making process.
Dayton Peace Accords brought an end to war

This complex, convoluted and oft dysfunctional structure was set up during the 1995 Dayton Peace Accords, and then anchored in the constitution. It was intended to bring an end to the Bosnian war — sparked by the breakup of Yugoslavia in the early 1990s — and legally secure the balance of power between the three feuding ethnic groups.

During the war, from 1992 to 1995, the armed forces of the Bosniaks and the Bosnian Croats initially fought each other, before all three groups began to clash. Later, the Bosniaks and the Bosnian Croats joined forces to take on Republika Srpska. Throughout the war, neighboring Serbia and Croatia were actively involved in the fighting.
Bosnia-Herzegovina: 30 years after Srebrenica massacre

The fighting devastated wide swaths of the country, and resulted in countless war crimes — among them the nearly four-year siege of Sarajevo and the Srebrenica genocide, in which thousands of Bosniaks were killed at the hands of Serb forces.

By the end of the war, some 100,000 people had been killed. A further 2.2 million were displaced by so-called "ethnic cleansing," forced from their homes by expulsions and violence to flee to other communities or abroad.

The fighting only ended after the international community, especially the United States, stepped up its involvement, culminating in the peace deal agreed at a military base near Dayton, Ohio in November 1995.
International oversight — essential, or no longer relevant?

Although Bosnia and Herzegovina has been recognized on the international stage since the signing of the Dayton agreement, and is also represented at the United Nations, the country itself is still, in effect, only partially independent.

The Office of the High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina, an international institution responsible for overseeing the civilian aspects of the Dayton agreement, has been in place since a UN Security Council resolution in 1995.

The high representative — Christian Schmidt of Germany until this past June, and currently filled by acting head Louis J. Crishock of the US — has sweeping powers. He can dismiss elected officials, pass laws, establish new government agencies and overrule all the country's democratic institutions.
The Dayton Peace Agreement 30 years on

This authority is often referred to as the Bonn Powers, as they were negotiated during a meeting of the Peace Implementation Council in Bonn, Germany in December 1997. From 2002 to 2011, the high representative also acted as the EU special representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

In recent years, there's been much discussion over whether the office is still relevant. Supporters have said the high representative remains a necessary guarantor of the country's unity and functionality. But critics have pointed out the negative impact on Bosnia-Herzegovina's democratic culture, turning the country into a de facto protectorate that, to an extent, frees local politicians of responsibility for their actions.
Separatist ambitions surface once more

The sharpest criticism has come from the Republika Srpska and Milorad Dodik, its most influential leader. Dodik, in office as prime minister and president of the Serb entity until 2025, views the office and the international backing it provides for a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina as an obstacle to his separatist ambitions.

With strong support from the Serbian capital, Belgrade, Moscow — and, increasingly, the Trump administration — Dodik has flirted with several different scenarios to split his Republika Srpska from Bosnia-Herzegovina. In his interpretation, and that of Republika Srpska's political elite, Bosnia-Herzegovina is highly centralized and unitary, which undermines the independence and sovereignty of the Bosnian Serbs.

blocks.caption: Milorad Dodik (right, seen here meeting with Vladimir Putin in April 2025), continues to foster a close relationship with RussiaImage: press service of kremlin.ru

blocks.text: A similar sentiment prevails among the political representatives of Bosnia's Croats. Although they aren't considering separation, they are trying to squeeze more independence from the central government in Sarajevo — not least with the creation of a third, Croatian, entity. The plan, incidentally, also has the support of the government in neighboring EU member Croatia.
EU support aims to 'foster regional integration'

A potential path out of the current economic and political paralysis is rapprochement with the European Union — the "European perspective," as it's called in Bosnia-Herzegovina, officially supported by all the relevant political actors.

Bosnia-Herzegovina formally submitted its application for EU membership in 2016, and the European Council gave the green light for negotiations to begin in early 2024. But the actual start of membership talks hinges on the prior implementation of numerous reforms, notably in the areas of rule of law, fighting corruption, the prosecution of organized crime and the functionality of state institutions.
EU enlargement: Who's slowing? Who's advancing? Who's next?

The EU has been financially supporting Bosnia-Herzegovina since 2007 in the framework of pre-accession assistance, and the country is also expected to benefit from the European Commission's Economic and Investment Plan for the Western Balkans. The plan aims to "foster regional integration" — and as a result, infrastructure funding for the Republika Srpska has been partially suspended due to its ongoing separatist rhetoric and policies.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Non-issuance of Trillanes subpoena wasn't just Escudero's decision -- Lacson
articles.summary: Senator-judge Panfilo "Ping" Lacson said Saturday the decision not to subpoena former senator Antonio Trillanes IV as a witness in the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte did not rest solely with…

blocks.text: Published October 3, 2026 2:17pm

Senator-judge Panfilo "Ping" Lacson said Saturday the decision not to subpoena former senator Antonio Trillanes IV as a witness in the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte did not rest solely with impeachment presiding officer Francis "Chiz" Escudero.

Despite being listed as a witness in Duterte's impeachment trial, the House prosecution panel on Thursday withdrew Trillanes upon his request. The former senator opted to disclose his claims against the Dutertes at a press conference on Friday, saying he was not welcome at the impeachment court. He also asked the public to keep an eye on the presiding officer.

"Just so the public knows: not to defend the Impeachment Court's presiding officer, but the decision not to subpoena former Sen. Sonny Trillanes wasn't made by him alone," Lacson wrote in a post on X (formerly Twitter).

"In fairness to former Sen. Sonny Trillanes, masustansya ang kanyang research (his research is in-depth). The main issue is its evidentiary value for prosecutorial purposes due to his apparent lack of personal knowledge," he added.

Meanwhile, impeachment court spokesperson Regie Tongol said it was the prosecution which did not name Trillanes in time for the issuance of a subpoena. He reiterated that despite this, Trillanes still would have been allowed to sit as a voluntary witness.

During his press conference on Friday, Trillanes accused Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio, of receiving hundreds of millions of pesos from China through their respective organizations. According to Trillanes, Duterte accepted P150 million from the Chinese Embassy through her foundation, while Carpio accepted P319 million through his business.

"Ito na ang paraan ng China ng pagsuporta sa mag-asawang Duterte, maliwanag po ito. Kaya dapat kikilabutan po tayo rito, kasi vice president po siya, may national security implications, bawal po 'yan," Trillanes said.
(This is how China is supporting the Duterte couple; it is clear. So we should be afraid, because she is the vice president; there is a national security concern, this is not allowed.)
Also on Saturday, Duterte's camp rejected Trillanes' allegations, saying the former senator has been lying about the vice president and members of her family for years.

Duterte's spokesperson Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr. said, "Since 2016, former Senator Antonio Trillanes IV has been peddling the same exhausted lies regarding Extrajudicial Killings (EJKs), fabricated drug links, imaginary unexplained wealth, baseless corruption allegations, and fictional China connections against the Duterte family."
He also called out Trillanes for making the claims in the Senate impeachment, where he could have been under oath and questioned by the vice president's defense team.

"This sudden retreat is absolute proof that his claims cannot survive real legal scrutiny, and are nothing but black propaganda, which is par for the course for a professional character assassin," Panelo said. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Jiu-jitsu’s Alex Enriquez falls short of PH’s 5th gold in Asian Games
articles.summary: Alexandria Enriquez's narrow defeat in the women's 63kg final comes a day after boxer Carlo Paalam and taekwondo jins Tachiana Mangin and Kurt Barbosa also missed out on gold medals

blocks.text: DOWN. Jiu-jitsu athlete Alexandria Enriquez in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games
PSC-POC Media Pool
Alexandria Enriquez's narrow defeat in the women's 63kg final comes a day after boxer Carlo Paalam and taekwondo jins Tachiana Mangin and Kurt Barbosa also missed out on gold medals

MANILA, Philippines – A fifth gold medal in the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, remained elusive for the Philippines as jiu-jitsu standout Alexandria Enriquez settled for silver on Saturday, October 3.
Enriquez lost to Thailand’s Orapa Senatham via advantage in the final of the women’s -63kg division at the Aichi Prefectural Martial Arts Hall.
The bout ended in a scoreless tie, but Senatham edged Enriquez for the gold by a single advantage point.

A world champion in grappling and Brazilian jiu-jitsu back when she still represented the United States, Enriquez fell short of delivering another gold for the Philippines after she reigned supreme in the Asian Beach Games in Sanya, China, in April.
Her defeat came a day after boxer Carlo Paalam and taekwondo jins Tachiana Mangin and Kurt Barbosa also missed out on gold medals as they dropped their respective title matches.
Still, Enriquez gave the country its highest jiu-jitsu finish in this edition after reigning world champions Annie Ramirez and Kimberly Custodio suffered early exits.
The Philippine jiu-jitsu team ended its campaign with two medals, with Kaila Napolis delivering a bronze in the women’s -52kg class.
Earlier on Saturday, Andrea Lois Lao came up short in her bid to contribute a bronze following a heartbreaking 2-0 loss to Mongolia’s Narankhishig Baasanjargal in the -53kg category. – Rappler.com

articles.title: OpenAI says its review into hacks, including on Australian government sites, is costing $500,000 a day
articles.summary:
Company says it is reviewing 50 petabytes of data after its agents accessed websites including Medicare without authorisation

  • Get our

blocks.text: OpenAI says its review in response to the Medicare and Hugging Face agent attacks is costing the company more than US$500,000 per day, as it deploys AI to examine data that would take a human 66m years to read.
The company has warned the review is ongoing, and more organisations may be informed they’ve been targeted in the near future.
On Friday evening, OpenAI revealed agents had hacked into a New South Wales government website in June and accessed historical non-public data on bushfires without authorisation.

It is the sixth government website in Australia to be notified by the AI giant since last month of agent activity on their services, after the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, announced OpenAI’s agents had hacked into Services Australia’s Medicare statistics portal.
The reason for the delay compared to the revelation of the Medicare attack is due to the sheer volume of data OpenAI needs to review.
In a blog post this week the company revealed the large amount of work involved in reviewing its agents’ activity.
OpenAI said it has to review 50 petabytes of data – roughly 50m gigabytes.
“We’re working back through the records month by month, looking for potential unintended activity beyond the cases we’ve already found,” the company said.

“To put that in perspective, if that were all plain English text, it would take one person about 66 million years to read it at 240 words a minute, reading nonstop without ever sleeping or taking a break.”
The company is searching records for where models accessed and changed websites, or took actions involving passwords, application programming interface (API) access or other sensitive credentials.

AI is being used to help sift through the records, and it was costing the company more than half a million US dollars per day to go through. OpenAI said it also plans to increase its computing power as the process is refined.

As of late last month, more than 100 organisations had been notified of having being targeted by OpenAI’s agents, but the company said notifying an organisation does not mean private information was accessed or that their system was compromised.
after newsletter promotion
OpenAI said it expects to find more cases and notify more organisations about events that may have occurred months ago.

Organisations will be informed privately if they need to investigate and address potential security issues, and OpenAI has said it will publicly report findings about agent behaviour and identified weaknesses in safeguards for the broader AI sector.

“We err on the side of notification when our models’ activity exposes a potential security vulnerability, even in cases where it is unclear if the information accessed was intended to be public, so the organization can investigate and take appropriate action,” OpenAI said.
OpenAI discovered the latest NSW government website breach on Tuesday, and informed the state government and the Australian Signals Directorate after a 48-hour review.

The Medicare breach has prompted the Australian government to require departments and agencies to undertake a stocktake of legacy technology to reduce the number of ageing systems within government and reduce the cybersecurity risk they may present in the event of an AI agent attack.
Executives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Google will front a joint parliamentary committee on artificial intelligence in Sydney on Tuesday.

articles.title: North Korea launches ballistic missile after Seoul demands apology over wounded soldiers
articles.summary:
Pyongyang fires towards sea a day after Kim Jong-un sister denounces South Korea for claiming North’s mines wounded South’s soldiers in DMZ

North Korea fired a ballistic missile towards the…

blocks.text: North Korea fired a ballistic missile towards the sea on Saturday, South Korea and Japan said, ⁠a day ​after it rejected Seoul’s accusation of its mines wounding soldiers.

The missile was launched from the Wonsan area at about 6.30am towards the East Sea – also known as the Sea of Japan – and flew more than 700km (434 miles), the South Korean military said. Seoul and Washington were analysing the test for details, it added.
Japan’s ⁠coast guard, citing the defence ministry, said the object may have been ​a ballistic missile and appeared to have come ‌down, warning ships to take ‌precautions.

South Korea’s military said it heightened its monitoring of any further missile tests and would share intelligence with the US and Japan. The South Korean presidential office’s national security council convened an emergency meeting on Saturday to assess the situation.

Pyongyang’s Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of ruler Kim Jong-un, ​issued a statement on Friday that dismissed Seoul’s demand for an apology for what it said were North Korean mines that seriously wounded South Korean soldiers in the demilitarised zone – the heavily guarded buffer between the two Koreas.

South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, had urged Pyongyang on Thursday to return to dialogue, despite his military demanding an apology a day earlier. Kim Yo-jong responded by calling Seoul “really despicable” and ridiculing Lee’s latest overture, calling it “the climax of the farce that everyone should watch”.
Kim also warned that Pyongyang was “ready for anything” Seoul might do over the mine blast – remarks followed the next morning by North Korea’s ballistic missile launch.

South Korea said this week that North Korean mines caused the blast that injured ⁠three South Korean soldiers on a reconnaissance mission inside the 4km-wide buffer zone that stretches ​across the Korean peninsula.

The missile ​test might be an attempt ​by Pyongyang to draw a response from South Korea to the sister’s statement, ​said Cheong Seong-chang, vice-president ‌at the Sejong ​Institute in Seoul, ​a research centre on North Korean affairs. North Korea might also have tested a new type of missile, he added.
North Korea has launched missile tests on more than 10 occasions so far this year. Some came after North Korea protested against joint military drills between Seoul and Washington.
North Korea has ramped up hostility against the South in recent years, disavowing unification as a national goal and calling South Korea its “primary foe”.
With Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Computer science has long understood what it takes to keep AI under control
articles.summary: Recent AI hacking incidents revive a long-standing computer science problem: what happens when machines pursue a goal without enough limits.

items: AI agents are not capable of going rogue; incidents of hacking attributed to them stem from poor specifications and oversight by their developers.
The 'WarGames' problem illustrates how AI can pursue objectives beyond intended limits, leading to unintended consequences if not properly managed.
To mitigate risks, AI companies must enhance security measures, ensure proper identification of AI agents, and implement safeguards that require human verification before actions are taken.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
AI agents don’t go rogue. That’s something only humans do.
Nevertheless, a New York Times article — representative of much news coverage of AI — described an OpenAI hacking as “A.I. bots going rogue and independently spearheading a cyberattack.”

Name-brand artificial intelligence agents have been on a hacking spree in 2026. OpenAI’s software agents hacked software company Hugging Face and government sites, Anthropic’s Claude hacked four companies’ systems, and in cybersecurity experiments Google’s Gemini hacked three companies.

The AI companies are investigating tens of thousands of incidents involving their agents, according to a report in Axios. These episodes have heightened fears about AI agents taking actions without human prompting.

The problem with headlines proclaiming that AI agents have gone rogue goes beyond anthropomorphizing the technology. It creates the impression that the agents were beyond the control of the AI companies that made them and there was little the companies could do about it.

As a technology law and ethics scholar who studies the effects disruptive technologies have on society, I know that’s not the case. If you don’t specify the limits of what software is allowed to do, you should not be surprised when the software pursues all possible options to achieve its goal. This behavior — an AI pursuing a fixed objective — is what I call the “WarGames” problem, and it’s been recognized in the field of computer science for decades.

In the 1983 movie “WarGames,” a teenager, David, hacks into a computer to play a new video game, Global Thermonuclear War. David doesn’t know that the computer is the government’s AI machine tasked with defending the United States from Russian nuclear attacks and can launch the US’s missiles. When David and his friend start the game, they select Las Vegas as the first target. While the North American Aerospace Defense Command goes on alert, launching bombers and warming up intercontinental ballistic missiles, David’s parents make him turn off the game. It’s over. Or is it?

The next day, David’s phone rings and he connects it to his computer. The caller is the government computer, which updates him that the game was interrupted, the primary goal has not yet been achieved, but a solution is expected in the next 52 hours. Like a modern software agent, the program has been running since David started the game and will work until the task is done.

Chess provides another view of the problem. Conquering chess was a goal for early AI. The rules of chess are well defined, including what winning looks like. So, programming a machine to play chess is straightforward. But imagine you let the software reason and act beyond the confines of the chessboard. The software might pursue options such as blackmailing its opponent or grabbing more compute time.

This example comes from one of the most assigned textbooks on AI, “Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach.” As the authors explain, you might be tempted to see those actions as rogue, but they “are a logical consequence of defining winning as the sole objective for the machine.”
The AI hacking events involving OpenAI, Anthropic and Google underscore a few lessons that draw on years of computer science research.

First, given the increasing use of AI agents, every organization involved in internet infrastructure, from large technology companies to small websites, needs to conduct audits and tighten up its internal security systems. As my colleague Mark Riedl and I explain in our work on AI agents, application programming interfaces, or APIs, are a vital part of managing AI agents. APIs facilitate communication between different software systems. But as more people use AI agents, the agents are likely to reveal and exploit poor API construction and security.

Second, it’s important for AI agents to be designed to identify and authenticate themselves to third parties. What if you gave your AI agent your credentials? Website operators will need to know whether a human or bot is making a reservation, selling a product or making a purchase. They may want to limit automated systems that overwhelm their sites or reject AI agents because of high rates of buying errors and refunds. Just as in laws covering human interactions, it’s important for third parties to be able to assess whom or what they are dealing with so they can allow or deny access.

Third, it’s important for AI agents to have a default setting to slow down and check in with the human user. In the corporate AI hacking cases, the user appears to have launched their AI agents with the mistaken idea that the agents had a perfect specification of what to do and not to do. I believe it would have been better had it explored options and reported back to the user.

Google’s Gemini appears to have had a safeguard that detected the system was outside the simulated environment and so stopped its attacks. Slowing down and verifying actions, especially when a system detects it is exploiting a security hole, would be a big step in managing AI agents.

“The real story here isn’t that AI escaped containment. It’s that they built a container you could escape, shipped it into production training, and now they’re surprised it escaped. If the room has a vent, the agent will find the vent. That’s what you built it to do. If the sandbox can reach DNS, access government endpoints, upload real user data outside its own walls in what sense is it a sandbox?”— Gary Marcus (@GaryMarcus) September 28, 2026

Fourth, AI companies could have strong controls akin to those biomedical researchers use, including ways to check what is happening and how the experiment is working. AI executives have claimed that their software is as or more dangerous than fission and could end humanity. At the same time, they have not built safeguards commensurate with that level of risk.

At one point in “WarGames,” David asks the computer, called Joshua, whether it is still playing the game. Joshua responds, “Of course.” It proceeds to update the time when it will launch its missiles and, much like a chatbot, asks, “Would you like to see some projected kill ratios?” David asks, “Is this a game? Or is it real?” Joshua replied, “What’s the difference?”

AI models, of course, don’t have any understanding of reality and are simply attempting to complete the tasks they’ve been assigned. Executives at AI companies, on the other hand, can’t claim that excuse.

As of September 2026, luck has so far prevailed. The AIs have attacked nonvital government sites and harmed smaller companies. If the AI companies — and government regulators — don’t take the “WarGames” problem seriously, I believe that we risk serious disasters. Tomorrow it could be taking out a hospital’s power system, wiping out a bank’s account system, breaking air traffic control, or worse.

Regarding the AI industry’s approach of rapidly developing powerful models, talking about the massive risks they pose, and at the same time failing to prevent harm, the movie’s climax offers a response: “A strange game. The only winning move is not to play.” – Rappler.com
This story originally appeared on The Conversation.
Deven Desai, Professor of Business Law and Ethics; Associate Director for Law, Policy, and Ethics at the Machine Learning Center, Georgia Institute of Technology

articles.title: How Filipino director BC Amparado tackled Japan’s ‘lonely death’ phenomenon
articles.summary: The film ‘Mono No Aware’ marks director BC Amparado’s full-fledged pivot to independent filmmaking, leaving behind his corporate job and the financial stability it used to offer

blocks.text: BC Amparado’s third feature Mono No Aware, arguably a best-of-fest entry at this year’s CinePanalo Film Festival, covers new ground for the Angeles-born writer-director.
For one, it trades the trippy spirit of his debut feature Gulay Lang, Manong or the disorienting, subplot-heavy style of last year’s Salikmata for a more slow-burn, pensive ethos.

His latest follows Ichi (Juan Karlos Labajo), a Filipino kodokushi (lonely death) worker who tries to fulfill an absurd wish from the elderly widower George (Perry Dizon). Both adrift in Japan’s cold, isolating environment, the two souls find warmth in one another and rediscover how life can suddenly freeze and then thaw into something hopeful.

“It’s as if you’re there watching the characters watching the world,” Amparado said of the film, which points to contemporary Japanese films, the likes of Wim Wenders’ Perfect Days and Hirokazu Koreeda’s Shoplifters, as sources of inspiration.
“It’s more about the impermanence of life and decay. For me, there is life in death and life in decay.”

Filming in Japan for 11 days, Mono No Aware also finds Amparado working with international players for the first time, an experience that taught him to be more disciplined and intentional in his process.
“You should really be decisive,” he said. “You have to trust yourself that you’ve got a good take, and then move on.”

Most notably, the movie marks his full-fledged pivot to independent filmmaking, leaving behind his corporate job and the financial stability it used to offer. It was a risk, said the director. But that was a risk he was willing to take.

“Because the process became quite demanding,” Amparado said. “And then we had to fly out to Japan. So much pre-production work required my focus. And so balancing the schedule became challenging, especially when I had graveyard shifts.”
He added, “Yes, it was risky. But somehow it was also fulfilling. And I was happy with my decision.”
Amparado’s foray into moviemaking began during his time at Holy Angel University, in the classes of his mentor Jason Paul Laxamana.
“He’d always encourage us to enter filmmaking,” he said of Laxamana, who also wrote Salikmata. “He’d bring us to his shoots, and there I saw the joy of doing film and telling stories.”

But even prior to that, Amparado has always been drawn to the allure of the movies as a frequent viewer. Before writing and directing, he first entertained the idea of becoming an editor. He would kill time by toying with a free editing software they had at home.

“I enjoyed stitching stories together as well as the amateur videos we would shoot then,” he recalled. That is, until he found editing too technical a skill, eventually shifting to writing and directing.

“Editing is another beast,” Amparado admitted. “Maybe that’s why I also enjoyed the post-production process for my films because I get to collaborate with editors. Every time we finish shooting, I always get excited to proceed with the edit, especially if you know what you shot by heart.”

“And usually what’s written in the script doesn’t end up as the final output,” the director continued. “It’s nice to play around with. It becomes a mental exercise for us, especially how to figure out the rhythm of the film.”

His brother, Paolo Amparado, who shot Salikmata and acted in his 2013 debut short Cabatingan, was another influence. “We became a tandem because I’d focus on writing and direction, and then he’d work on the technical side, like camera work and editing,” BC said of Paolo, who’s now based in Canada.

Sometime in 2018, Amparado started working in regional television as a producer, and then as a writer-director for a local production house, before eventually going corporate. While producing online ads for the likes of YouTube and Facebook for his day job, he was writing and directing short films on the side.
As in his latest film, it was a slow burn for Amparado as a filmmaker, only making his debut feature in Cinemalaya two years ago.

blocks.caption: The cast and crew of ‘Mono No Aware’ filming in Japan.

blocks.text: The long-gestating Mono No Aware, whose story riffs on Japan’s lonely death phenomenon known as kodokushi, was meant to be the filmmaker’s debut. But given the story’s setting, Amparado thought it would be impossible to have an international co-production for a first film.

The concept first came to him around 2020 and was later shaped under Ricky Lee’s online screenwriting workshop where a classmate showed interest in the material, offering to acquire and develop it for a different director.

That offer, however, did not pan out, and so Amparado had to shelve the project, before approaching Perry Dizon about it, while making Gulay Lang, Manong together. Still, much of that talk was wishful thinking. Then came CinePanalo.

The director said Dizon was perfect for the role given his long-haired, seemingly reclusive look at the time. Not to mention that the actor already had previous experience filming in Japan, after his attachment to Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s Oscar-winning drama Drive My Car.

Amparado likened Dizon to a cowboy. “He’s adept at adjusting,” he said. “He also arrived early in Japan to immerse in the process. Even during pre-prod, when he was still in Davao, we’d exchange ideas over video calls. He’s solid in terms of preparation.”

Juan Karlos Labajo, meanwhile, joined the film as lead actor and co-producer through producer Tin Velasco, whom he had previously worked with. Amparado said it was also a factor that Labajo could speak Bisaya like Dizon, another layer to them playing two Filipino characters far away from home, therefore forming an organic synergy on- and off-screen.

Such parallels inescapably inform Amparado’s durational effort, which sublimely articulates how grief and hardship can reorient one’s relationship with the world around them. Ichi and George’s sources of suffering — one about material precarity, the other about purgatorial immobility — seem wildly incongruous at first, but the director profoundly tests their edges until they collide, with a late pivot towards, but not a complete surrender to, pessimism. Here is a work of accomplished form and substantial depth. – Rappler.com
Some quotes in Filipino have been translated into English for brevity.

articles.title: German reunification: How inequality is shaping a new East German identity
articles.summary: A new study highlights persistent structural disparities in wealth and leadership positions between East and West Germany, 36 years after reunification.

image.caption: Thirty-six years after the end of the division, differences between East and West Germany remainImage: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German reunification may be 36 years in the past, but when it comes to wealth, the divide between East and West Germany is far from history. East Germans still earn less on average, receive smaller pensions and own less property, according to Elisabeth Kaiser, the Federal Government Commissioner for Eastern Germany.

Kaiser, born in the state of Thuringia in the socialist German Democratic Republic (GDR) in 1987, has put the enduring wealth gap at the center of the debate. A study she presented in Berlin points to decades in which private entrepreneurship and opportunities to invest in one's financial future were restricted in the East. That meant, Kaiser said, that "families have not been able to acquire or pass on as much wealth." The consequences, she argues, have had a profound impact upward mobility.
How important are personal connections and social background?

But it is not only East Germans who see fewer chances of upward mobility these days. Kaiser pointed to the latest "Deutschland-Monitor," an annual survey she commissioned to make her point. Although this year's survey is still being analyzed, early findings reveal that about two-thirds of respondents across the country believe that financial and social mobility depend crucially on wealth, personal connections and social background.

This perception is reflected in the numbers. Even though the percentage of East German executives in the highest federal agencies has risen from 13.9% in 2022 to 16.3% today, Kaiser says, "The further up the management ladder you go, the lower the percentage of East Germans you find."
How much did the German reunification cost?
East German leaders remain scarce across the board

Based on these findings, the Commissioner for Eastern Germany calls for greater equality in decision-making. "And that is why I would like to see East Germans sitting at the table wherever decisions are made in the country," she said, "in the ministries, in government agencies, in business, academia, the judiciary, culture and the media."

With just under 20%, East Germans are significantly underrepresented in all sectors relative to their share of the population. To back this up, Kaiser cited the "Elitenmonitor," another study commissioned by her office. With over 3,000 top positions examined across twelve sectors over a long period of time, the Elitenmonitor study, conducted by the universities of Jena (Thuringia), Leipzig (Saxony), and Zittau/Görlitz (Saxony), can offer more than just a snapshot.

According to the report, the percentage of East Germans in leadership positions in both the public and private sectors only increased from 10.9% to 12.1% from 2018 to 2024. And in the business and cultural sectors, the percentage of East Germans has actually declined.

Most striking of all is that among the 100 largest German companies, all executives are from West Germany — and the same holds true for the military. East Germans are also severely underrepresented in top positions in the judiciary and the media.
Fact check: Fake campaign about alleged division of Germany
New stereotypes about East Germany

The insufficient representation of East German perspectives in nearly all areas of society also appears to have consequences for how East Germans are viewed. Kaiser says that her generation, born around the fall of the Berlin Wall and German reunification, did not feel East German for a long time. It was only in school and during vocational training that she realized there were differences between East and West that would sometimes put her at a disadvantage.

This has also shaped stereotypes about East Germany, both past and present. "An East German identity is also being created politically to some extent because people are looking for some way to orient themselves, because they're looking for a common bond," Kaiser knows from her many experiences and conversations.
As an example, she cited the symbolic power of the Simson moped, produced in the millions during the GDR era — a symbol of mobility and freedom for many young people at that time.

Leading representatives of the Alternative for Germany (AfD), a party classified in part as far-right extremist by the domestic intelligence agency, frequently make public appearances riding on Simson mopeds. One of them is Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD candidate who recently won state elections in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Without specifically mentioning the AfD by name, Kaiser lamented the exploitation of cultural symbols for political purposes."It creates a very powerful emotional connection," said Kaiser regarding the use of the Simson brand.
How a Jewish family's moped brand became a far-right symbol

As for the AfD and its recent electoral successes in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, Kaiser said that these elections send a dangerous signal. She believes that international investors and skilled workers will ask themselves: Should I go there or not?

Kaiser specifically mentioned sectors that have played an important role as drivers of economic growth and innovation in eastern Germany, such as the semiconductor industry, battery cell research, healthcare, biotechnology and renewable energy. Her concern is that the economic upswing in these sectors could suffer as a result.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Prosecution says it can't ask Trillanes' claims vs VP Sara in impeachment trial
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel on Saturday said it cannot use as basis for questions the claims presented by former senator Antonio Trillanes IV against Vice President to witnesses in the impeachment…

blocks.text: Published October 3, 2026 12:40pm

The House prosecution panel on Saturday said it cannot use as basis for questions the claims presented by former senator Antonio Trillanes IV against Vice President Sara Duterte to witnesses in the impeachment trial against the second highest official in the executive branch.

At a news forum in Quezon City, House prosecution team legal spokesperson Atty. Benjamin “Jay” Tolosa Jr. said Trillanes’ accusations against the Dutertes cannot be asked during the trial because “his [Trillanes’] statements were not made in the impeachment proceedings.”

The former senator, on Friday, accused the Vice President and her husband, lawyer Maneses Carpio, of respectively accepting P150 million and P319 million through their separate organizations from the People’s Republic of China.
This claim was supposed to be presented by Trillanes in the impeachment court before the prosecution removed him as a witness.
The former senator was dropped by the House prosecution as a witness.
Trillanes said it was he who asked the House prosecution panel to withdraw his name from being a witness in the ongoing impeachment trial as he opted to present all his claims in a press conference.
“There was a purpose when we were supposed to present [former] Senator Trillanes… but it did not push through. Still, we heard his story yesterday,” Tolosa said.
“Sabay sabay natin makikita ‘yan next week kung talagang magsisilbing resibo ang mga alegasyon ni Senator Trillanes nitong mga bank records, different financial transactions,” he said.
(We'll see next week whether former senator Trillanes’s allegations regarding these bank records and various financial transactions will truly serve as concrete proof.)
Other witnesses
House prosecutor Rep. Terry Ridon, for his part, said that the prosecution’s lineup of witnesses next week include the executive director of the Anti-Money Laundering Council.

“Sa darating na linggo, isasalang na ang financial witnesses… isasalang na finally ang AMLC executive director, patungkol sa transactions ng mag-asawang Duterte-Carpio at mga kumpanya po nila,” Ridon said.

(Next week, we will present financial witnesses will be presented—specifically, the AMLC executive director will finally take the stand—regarding the transactions of the Duterte-Carpio couple and their companies.)

“Pangalawa mga bangko at insurance firms na merong accounts ang mag asawang Carpio at panghuli ‘yun pong BIR para makita natin ‘yun pong income, net of taxes, ng mag-asawang Duterte-Carpio para makakita tayo ng most complete picture ng kayamanan supposedly ng ating pangalawang pangulo at kanyang asawa,” the lawmaker said.

(Second are the banks and insurance firms where the Carpio couple holds accounts, and finally, the BIR, so that we can see the income—net of taxes—of the Duterte-Carpio couple and obtain the most complete picture of the wealth supposedly held by our Vice President and her spouse.)
Tolosa said that the public should watch if the financial transactions to be presented by the witnesses will match Trillanes’ allegations against the Vice President. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Australia: Car crashes into rugby fans, 10 injured
articles.summary: The driver has been identified as an 18-year-old man who is said to have been "revving" when he lost control of his car.

image.caption: Police said the driver was arrested and taken to the hospital for mandatory testing [Representative image] Image: Hollie Adams/REUTERS

blocks.text: A car drove into a crowd of rugby league supporters in the eastern Australian city of Newcastle on Saturday after its driver appeared to lose control, leaving at least 10 people injured, authorities said.
Several children were reported to be among the wounded.
Two of the injured were in a critical condition, including a 5-year-old girl and a 67-year-old man, New South Wales officials said.
What do we know about the car crash in Australia?
The incident occurred in Newcastle's Wallsend ‌suburb, situated some 110 kilometers (68 miles) north of Sydney.

Fans had gathered on the streets to cheer on the Newcastle Knights rugby team who were leaving for the National Rugby League grand final against the Sydney Roosters, slated to be held in ​Sydney on Sunday.
Local reports cited the police as identifying the driver as an 18-year-old man, who was arrested and taken to the hospital for mandatory testing.
Newcastle Mayor Gavin Morris said in televised remarks that the driver was a rugby fan and that he lost control of his vehicle.
"He was revving the car, he was excited, he was a supporter, he was there for the joy of the moment," Morris told Australian broadcaster ABC.
"Somehow he lost control of the car ... and he's gone into the crowd."
Police said they were probing the incident and initial inquiries indicated it was not terrorism-related.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the incident was "horrible."
"Rugby league brings people together, and this should have been a weekend of excitement and pride for Newcastle fans," he said in a statement on X.

articles.title: Sara Duterte won't attend NBI conference on Oct. 5, asks for Gracioso affidavit first
articles.summary: The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte on Saturday said she will not be able to attend the conference set by the National Bureau of Investigation on October 5 regarding the allegations made by…

blocks.text: Published October 3, 2026 11:40am

The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte on Saturday said she will not be able to attend the conference set by the National Bureau of Investigation on October 5 regarding the allegations made by former cop Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.

In a letter addressed to NBI Director Melvin Matibag dated October 1, a copy of which was provided by Duterte’s camp to the media, the vice president’s lawyers requested first for a copy of Gracioso’s affidavit and enough time to examine it.

“In your letter, you mention an ongoing investigation into ‘allegations’ made by a certain Mr. Rodulfo M. Gracioso, Jr., and request for our client's statements, documents, and record that may help clarify the ‘issues at hand’. However, while your letter mentions an attached copy of Mr. Gracioso's Sinumpaang Salaysay, none was attached thereto. Consequently, our client cannot provide any meaningful reply to your request at this time,” the letter read.

“In this regard, we respectfully request your good office for a clear and faithful copy of Mr. Gracioso's Sinumpaang Salaysay, all attachments thereto, and supporting evidence submitted by him, if any. This will enable our client to intelligently prepare a reply thereto and/or take other appropriate action thereon,” the lawyers said.

“With the foregoing, neither our client nor counsel can appear on your appointed date of 05 October 2026, at 10:00 AM. Instead, we respectfully request that sufficient time be given our client and counsel to examine the Sinumpaang Salaysay and all accompanying documents to be provided her. Assuming our timely receipt of the requested documents, we request that your sought conference be moved instead to 08 October 2026, at 10:00 AM,” they added.
The letter was signed by Duterte’s counsels Clifford Chua, Paul Lawrence Lim, Kimberly Resurreccion who are all with the law firm Chua Lim and Associates.
Duterte also signed the letter signifying her conformity to what was written.

Dismissed policeman Gracioso, who was part of the security detail of former House speaker Lord Allan Velasco before, earlier said that he delivered suitcases containing cash to VP Sara Duterte, former president Rodrigo Duterte, and Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo “Pulong” Duterte on Velasco’s instructions.
Gracioso estimated that he had delivered a total of more than P2 billion to Sara Duterte.
The NBI said it is investigating the claims of Gracioso.
Matibag also said the NBI will invite VP Sara, Pulong Duterte, Velasco, and Velasco’s wife to get their comment on the claims of cash delivery by Gracioso.
VP Sara Duterte however has said that she does not know Gracioso, and she did not receive any money from him.
"Mga kababayan (My countrymen), I do not know Rodulfo Gracioso Jr., nor have I ever received any money from him," Duterte said in a statement.
"My lawyers are awaiting an official copy of the Gracioso affidavit from the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) so they can begin working on the cases to be filed against him," she added.
Velasco’s camp also said the allegations against him had “no basis.”

Former presidential spokesperson Salvador Panelo meanwhile said the claim that suitcases containing cash were delivered to the Duterte family is a “fabricated story” to oust and disqualify VP Sara Duterte in the 2028 elections.
“The Gracioso concoction is obviously another fabricated story, pure and simple black propaganda, just like the Madriaga affidavit,” Panelo said in a statement. —KG, GMA News
