articles.title: 'Malicious fabrications': Sara Duterte camp slams Trillanes' claims
articles.summary: The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte rejected Saturday the accusations made by former senator Antonio Trillanes IV that she and her husband allegedly received hundreds of millions of pesos from…

blocks.text: Published October 3, 2026 10:54am

The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte rejected Saturday the accusations made by former senator Antonio Trillanes IV that she and her husband allegedly received hundreds of millions of pesos from China through their organizations.
Duterte's spokesperson Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr. said Trillanes has been repeatedly lying about the vice president and her family for years.

"Since 2016, former Senator Antonio Trillanes IV has been peddling the same exhausted lies regarding Extrajudicial Killings (EJKs), fabricated drug links, imaginary unexplained wealth, baseless corruption allegations, and fictional China connections against the Duterte family," Panelo said in a statement.
The statement comes a day after Trillanes claimed in a press conference that Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio, received P150 million and P319 million, respectively.
He claimed that the vice president received the money from the Chinese embassy through her foundation, while Carpio received his through a corporation.

Panelo used Peter Joemel Advincula or "Bikoy" as an example. Advincula accused former president Rodrigo Duterte and several members of his family of being part of an illicit drug trade, but later withdrew his claims, accusing Trillanes of being behind the plot.

The Duterte spokesperson also cited lawyer Jude Sabio, one of first personalities to bring former president Rodrigo Duterte's crimes against humanity case to the International Criminal Court (ICC) but later withdraw his case. The elder Duterte's trial before the ICC is scheduled to begin in November.

"(Trillanes') malicious fabrications have been exposed at every turn by the very pawns he used to rely on… Because of these repeated, unmasked deceptions, the Filipino people have rightfully and overwhelmingly rejected Trillanes in every subsequent attempt to get elected back into public office," Panelo said.
Panalo criticized the Marcos administration for giving a platform to Trillanes' claims.
He also slammed Trillanes for not stating these claims in the Senate impeachment court, where he could have been under oath. The vice president's defense team also was not able to question him.

"This sudden retreat is absolute proof that his claims cannot survive real legal scrutiny, and are nothing but black propaganda, which is par for the course for a professional character assassin," Panelo said.
Trillanes was withdrawn Thursday as a witness for the prosecution in the Senate impeachment trial of Duterte.
The former senator said he requested House prosecutors to withdraw him as he would conduct a press conference wherein he would reveal everything that he would have disclosed in the trial.
Trillanes also claimed that he was unwelcome in the impeachment trial, but the impeachment court spokesperson Regie Tongol dismissed this.

He likewise claimed that Duterte failed to declare millions in time deposits in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) from 2007 to 2010 when she was Davao City vice mayor. Further, Trillanes alleged that she also did not declare millions of dollars worth of life insurance in her 2010 SALN.

"The Vice President would gladly sue him for these endless fabrications, but we have already witnessed how those who actively peddle malicious lies against her and her family are openly protected and propped up by this administration," he added. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Why electric cars might be making some passengers feel sick
articles.summary: Motion sickness is caused by a mismatch in sensory cues and women and children are more susceptible, experts say.

blocks.text: EV drivers love their cars, but some passengers feel sick - this could be why
Image source, Getty Images/Halfpoint Images
Lola Baird has just asked her boyfriend to pull over. Forty minutes into a journey and she's feeling "overwhelmed" by nausea - and can't stop herself throwing up on the ground next to his car.

Lola, 24, from north London, had never experienced motion sickness until her boyfriend bought an electric vehicle (EV) two years ago. Ever since, she's been feeling "very nauseous" when he takes her on long car journeys.
It's become so severe she's even asked him to change his car.

Lola isn't alone. Other people told BBC News that they or their children notice feeling more car sick when sitting as a passenger in an electric vehicle. But at the same time, many EV drivers say it's not been a concern.
So what could explain these reports of motion sickness?

Dr Irene Di Giulio, senior lecturer in anatomy and biomechanics at King's College London whose research includes motion sickness, says research so far suggests some people experience more severe motion sickness in electric vehicles than in non-electric vehicles.

It's something Dr Nicholas Hac, a neurologist at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago who specialises in dizziness and vertigo, has also heard from some of his patients. "They just notice that they're much more likely or prone to be motion sick" in electric vehicles, he says.
"I've heard about it many, many, many times," he adds, saying about two patients a month specifically reference feeling motion sick in electric vehicles.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Lola Baird noticed that she felt sick in electric vehicle taxis as well as her boyfriend's car. "I started to put two and two together," she says

blocks.text: Image source, Lola Baird
Lola Baird noticed that she felt sick in electric vehicle taxis as well as her boyfriend's car. "I started to put two and two together," she says
But research into any possible link is still in its early stages, and some academics say there isn't sufficient evidence to say anything definitive.
Dr Bill Yates, who has researched motion sickness at the University of Pittsburgh, says the body of research is "pretty sketchy at this point".
"There's some anecdotal information, but not a lot of really serious, extensive studies done yet," he says.
'Wonderful to drive... but my daughter gets unwell'
When Mark Quigg was looking at options for a new car last year, an electric vehicle seemed like the best choice because of the lower running costs.
Mark, 45, from Lincolnshire, says his shiny new electric vehicle has been "wonderful" to drive - but he quickly noticed that his nine-year-old daughter's motion sickness got much worse in it.
She only used to get motion sick on their 600-mile drives to France during the school holidays, but now he says even the 30-minute trip to the nearest city makes his daughter feel unwell.
On one recent journey, he says his daughter even threw up, which had never happened before.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Mark Quigg says electric cars are a "lovely driving experience for me, personally, because they are a lot quieter"

blocks.text: Image source, Mark Quigg
Mark Quigg says electric cars are a "lovely driving experience for me, personally, because they are a lot quieter"

Motion sickness doesn't affect all EV passengers - many owners got in touch with BBC News to say they and their relatives don't get sick in electric vehicles. Others said they felt less sick in EVs compared with traditional combustion engine cars.
Vicky Edmonds, the CEO of EVA England, an association for electric vehicle drivers, says motion sickness isn't a concern among her members. "This has never come up as an issue," she says.

But Chinese electric vehicle maker XPeng, which has showrooms across the UK, has previously publicly addressed the issue, external, telling people who've noticed a link between electric vehicles and travel sickness that "it's a fair question, and it's not your imagination". It's caused by "side effects of how electric cars are engineered," it adds.
What could cause it?

Motion sickness is caused by "a mismatch in sensory cues," Hac says. Our bodies rely on three main sensory inputs to show that we're moving, which come from what we see, what our inner ear's balance system perceives, and what fibres in our body sense, he says. When one of these is in conflict with the others - like if you're looking at your phone so you don't see visual signs of movement out of the window - that can cause motion sickness.
Research suggests several reasons why it may be more severe in electric vehicles.

Humans have adapted to associate sound with movement in vehicles, experts explain. Because electric vehicles don't have the auditory cues and vibrations from the engine that we're used to, which indicate when the car is accelerating, this could trigger motion sickness, Di Giulio says.

Another reason is regenerative braking, the process whereby when drivers release the accelerator, the electric car starts to slow down and uses the energy to feed the battery. However, it is a process that needs to be done smoothly with the accelerator being released gently, or it can lead to harsh deceleration.
"It forces the person to perhaps feel like they're rocking back and forth for that brief moment when the speed of the car suddenly changes," says Hac.

This is something Carolyn Le, 24, from California, has noticed. She gets "horrendous" motion sickness when her friend drives her in his electric vehicle in busy cities, she says. The regenerative braking means it "constantly feels like the car is stopping all the time".

blocks.caption: Image caption, "It's actually horrendous," says Carolyn Le, who blames regenerative braking for her motion sickness

blocks.text: Image source, Carolyn Le
"It's actually horrendous," says Carolyn Le, who blames regenerative braking for her motion sickness
Electric vehicles can also accelerate and decelerate much more quickly than conventional combustion cars, which Di Giulio says can cause motion sickness.
Edmonds, of EVA England, says developments in electric vehicle design have made them better at moderating the acceleration so they don't gain speed as rapidly.
She adds that the association thinks motion sickness in an electric vehicle is caused by "other factors" like the motorist's driving style rather than the vehicle itself.
Some people are also just more prone to motion sickness, and genetics have the biggest influence on this, Hac says. Women and children are more susceptible, experts say.

Motion sickness typically peaks between the ages of eight and 10, after which it decreases through more exposure, says Prof John Golding, who has researched the subject at the University of Westminster, the Royal Navy and the RAF.
Hold your head still and open the window

As their popularity increases, avoiding electric vehicles can be a challenge - the number of new zero-emission cars registered in the UK rose by 40.5% in April to June 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, latest Department for Transport figures show. , external
At the end of June 2026, 5.8% of all licensed cars on UK roads were zero-emission vehicles, the data shows. The sale of new purely petrol or diesel cars is set to be banned from 2030.
Lucinda Harrison, 24, from London says she often books taxis that turn out to be electric vehicles, and has to endure the trip feeling nauseous, sweaty and clammy.
The thought of travelling in an EV fills her with dread, she says. Even just a five-minute lift from a colleague to a Tube station recently was enough to make her feel "horrific".
Academics say there are several steps passengers can take to reduce feelings of motion sickness.

items: Look out of the front window and don't look at your phone or read a book
Sit in the front passenger seat rather than in the back, if possible. If you do have to sit in the back, opt for the middle seat so you can still see out the front window
Keep your head still by holding it against the headrest
Recline your seat
Regulate your breathing
Open the window to let in fresh air
Take travel sickness tablets if needed, though these can cause drowsiness
Before a long journey, make sure you're hydrated, have slept well and have eaten non-greasy food

blocks.text: Experts also say we can become desensitised to motion sickness through prolonged exposure. The more journeys you take in electric vehicles, the less likely you are to become motion sick as your body adjusts, Golding says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Looking out the window can ease motion sickness, which children and women may be more prone to experiencing as passengers

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images/Cyndi Monaghan
Looking out the window can ease motion sickness, which children and women may be more prone to experiencing as passengers

There are also things carmakers can do to alleviate motion sickness in electric vehicles, says Prof Cyriel Diels, professor of mobility design at the Royal College of Art. These include having software that smooths out rapid acceleration, adding sound systems and subtle seat vibrations to signal to passengers that the car is moving, and offering adaptive regenerative braking that reduces sudden deceleration.

Matt Adams from BEAMA, which represents UK manufacturers of electric vehicle charge points, says he's confident that "if future research identifies the reason for car sickness that vehicle manufacturers can respond and improve accordingly".
But for Lola, she just wants her boyfriend to trade in his car. She says that day can't come soon enough.
Get in touch
Are you an EV driver or have been a passenger in an EV? Have you experienced nausea due to motion sickness? Tell us your story.

articles.title: US, Australia suspend consular services in Brazil
articles.summary: The US and Australia have announced a halt to their consular services in Brazil beginning Friday. The news comes two days before Brazilians head to the polls to vote in the high-stakes presidential…

image.caption: A US flag flies outside the US Embassy in Brasilia after the US suspended consular services ahead of elections in BrazilImage: Adriano Machado/REUTERS

blocks.text: The United States announced it was suspending consular services at its embassy and consulates in Brazil due to security concerns starting Friday.
The US did not specify the kind of security issues it was looking at and it did not link issues to the presidential elections in Brazil this Sunday.
The Australian Embassy in Brasilia also said it was closing on Friday, citing the US alert and advising Australians to avoid US diplomatic missions.
The US State Department said it was working closely with its Brazilian counterparts to address security concerns, the Associated Press reported.
The Day with Phil Gayle: Brazil's elections
What to know about Brazil's heated election
The news comes at a tense time in US-Brazil relations.
Brazilians are headed to the polls this Sunday for what will likely be the first round of the presidential elections that has effectively shaped up to be a rematch of the 2022 contest.

Surveys show the contest is a statistical tie between left-wing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who is seeking a fourth term, and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.

blocks.caption: The vote this Sunday is shaping up to be battle between incumbent President Lula da Silva and right-wing challenger Flavio BolsonaroImage: Sergio Lima/AFP

blocks.text: The elder Bolsonaro, who is a staunch ally of US President Donald Trump, was sentenced last year to 27 years in prison for attempting to overturn the results of the previous presidential election in Brazil.
Trump has not endorsed a candidate, but there are fears that he may be too deeply involved in the outcome of the election results.

US Democratic lawmakers, for example, in late September expressed "grave concern" in a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio over what they said was the administration's "coordinated effort to threaten our strategic alliance with Brazil and undermine the Western Hemisphere’s second-largest democracy ahead of its upcoming presidential election."
Who is Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro?
Lula and his allies have warned of foreign interference in the election, pointing to tariffs and an effort this summer by Washington to send US officials to Brazil to "discuss electoral integrity."
When asked at the White House whether he would support Bolsonaro in the election, Trump said: "Well, we're looking at that whole thing, and we're watching that election very closely."

Brazil is surrounded by neighbors who've swung to the right and the election outcome — which could be determined on October 25th when the country advances into runoff if no candidate secures a majority of the vote this Sunday — will determine the direction of the country's foreign policy.

articles.title: Bangkok at breaking point as floods turn streets into stagnant lakes
articles.summary:
With 40 dead and a disaster declared across all 50 city districts, experts warn extreme flooding will only worsen across south-east Asia

Bangkok is used to absorbing the sudden afternoon…

blocks.text: Bangkok is used to absorbing the sudden afternoon downpours that inundate the city during the rainy season. Even streets in many central high-rise districts can briefly turn into rivers, with rats and cockroaches racing out of sewers and taking temporary refuge on trees and buildings as the subterranean world is flushed out.

But every city has a breaking point, and this year rain fell so fast and so hard that whole neighbourhoods of the Thai capital have been transformed, not into rivers, but stagnant lakes. In parts of the city, roughly 300mm of rain – the equivalent of half a year of average rainfall in London – fell in about two days.

blocks.caption: A person wades through flood water in Lat Krabang district, Bangkok. Photograph: Rungroj Yongrit/EPA

blocks.text: About 40 people died in flood-related incidents, according to the government. A number of the deaths were from drowning and several from accidental electrocution. Thousands of people stayed in more than 230 shelters across the city, authorities said.

Suleemas Kurangkul, a 73-year-old resident of a block of flats whose ground floor stairs are still under water, said last weekend’s rain was not the usual evening storm but was constant, “like all day, all night”.

“The water just kept rising,” said Suleemas, whose flat is above the waterline on the second floor. By the time she and her neighbours received a mobile phone warning, it was too late, and the street-level water was waist-high.

The 1970s Khlong Chan flat compound in north-east Bangkok where Suleemas lives has become a symbol of the disaster. Photos have been shared across Thailand of the flats rising out of the brownish water, with the rooftops of parked cars barely peeking above the surface, although the authorities had managed to drain away the worst of it by Thursday.

Later in the week, during a brief respite in the rain, Suleemas said the water had receded somewhat. “People are so happy to see the sunshine,” she said. “Yet, the smell is getting stronger. So much debris and rubbish floating all over the place.”

Built on a vast floodplain of the Chao Phraya River, Bangkok, a megacity of millions, relies on a network of muddy canals to drain water, as well as pumps and dikes. But concrete construction has destroyed much of the canal network, and the city is unable to cope.

The government has declared a flood disaster across all 50 of the city’s districts. Some neighbourhoods have turned into dystopian scenes, with people using blow-up paddling pools or, in one case, a floating fridge, as boats to reach their homes. One man was arrested for riding a jetski along a main road.

blocks.caption: A resident uses a floating fridge as a boat. Photograph: Rungroj Yongrit/EPA

blocks.text: “It’s a lesson,” said Chaleerat Chamrasporn, 55, a resident. “The kids are into doomsday-themed content, so now they can see what the ‘end of the world’ is actually like, or rather, that this is just the beginning.”

Flooding has also disrupted Bangkok’s main Suvarnabhumi airport, with about half ⁠of Thai Airways’ workforce unable to report for work at one point this week, causing thousands of items of luggage ​to pile up and forcing flight ​cancellations. Many schools have closed, and with much of the capital in gridlock even people in less affected areas have been stuck at home.

Thailand’s prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, told reporters that Bangkok’s metropolitan area was still at risk from flood waters flowing in from ​the north, and said a war room had ‌been set up to monitor ‌the situation. Thailand’s weather ⁠agency has forecast more ​heavy rain for next week.

blocks.caption: People stand on benches on the flooded pavement in Ramkhamhaeng in Bangkok. Photograph: Lillian Suwanrumpha/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: It is part of a pattern that seems to be setting in this part of the world. South-east Asia has already seen a worsening of extreme floods, scientists say, a trend that is set to worsen as fossil fuel pollutants bake the planet further. Hot seas evaporate more water and warm air can hold more moisture, allowing downpours to crash down with far more force.

“In central Thailand, I can see from my maps, we have already seen a small but significant trend towards extreme rainfall,” said Nikolaos Skliris, an ocean scientist at the University of Southampton who has studied heavy rain in the region. “In the long-term, all models show this will be amplified – more rainfall, and more extreme rainfall.”

It is too early for scientists to attribute these particular rains to climate breakdown without doing a study. They were caused by a low-pressure system that moved from an unusually warm South China Sea over Cambodia and Vietnam before getting stuck above Bangkok, which was fairly cool, data from Copernicus Climate Pulse showed.

The picture is complicated by the emergence of an abnormally strong El Niño, a cyclical weather pattern that brings record heat and more violent extremes around the world. Its presence typically leads to drier summer conditions in south-east Asia but recent research suggests it still exacerbates days with extreme rainfall.

Naim Laeni, a consultant and part-time university lecturer who co-authored a study on Bangkok’s flood resilience, said authorities had underestimated the strength of the rains, which persisted for days. The city’s drainage canals can handle about 60mm of rain an hour, rising to 80mm in upgraded sections, but localised bursts exceeded this while leaving too little time between periods of stress.
“The government did not communicate the seriousness,” said Laeni. “Usually in Bangkok we receive heavy rain for a few hours, not for days.”

blocks.caption: People wade through a flooded area during heavy rain in Bangkok. Photograph: Patipat Janthong/Reuters

blocks.text: Neighbouring Myanmar has suffered from the same weather system, with flash floods and blocked roads complicating rescue efforts in the country.

Rescuers were pulling bodies from a landslide that devastated the village of Ka Det Nge Htein in Myanmar’s south at the weekend. That disaster had already claimed nine lives, and eight more people are missing under the mud in another village, local officials said.
Civil war across the country, and a junta that restricts the media, have made it hard to get information, and hampered aid organisations.
Back in Bangkok, pumping stations have been operating at full capacity, but it could be days before the waters fully drain.
At her apartment complex, Suleemas said she would stay where she was with her neighbours.

“It’s hard, yes, very hard,” she said. “But together we are fighting and biting through it. When we get together to help one another like this, our spirit can keep us on our feet; we can get through it all together.”
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

articles.title: ICC grants prosecution's request to include prior testimony of witness in Rodrigo Duterte case
articles.summary: The International Criminal Court Trial Chamber has granted the Prosecution"s request to admit into evidence the previously recorded testimony of a key witness in the crimes against humanity case…

blocks.text: Published October 3, 2026 9:53am

The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber has granted the Prosecution’s request to admit into evidence the previously recorded testimony of a key witness in the crimes against humanity case against former president Rodrigo Duterte.
In an order dated October 2, 2026, the ICC said it “GRANTS the Prosecution’s Request to introduce into evidence the written statement of P-1100 pursuant to Rule 68(3) of the Rules.”
In a document dated September 7, the Prosecution asked permission to introduce the prior recorded testimony of witness P-1100 under Rule 68(3) of the ICC Rules of Procedure and Evidence.
The prosecution also asked to conduct a focused supplementary examination of the witness once he appears in court.

“Granting the request will enhance the expeditiousness of the proceedings by reducing the length of the witness’s direct examination from seven hours to two hours, thus saving at least five hours of court time,” the Prosecution said.
Duterte’s Defense team had asked the Chamber to reject the prosecution's request to admit the previously recorded testimony of a witness.
In a filing dated September 22, Duterte's Defense team pointed out that the testimony of witness P-1100 is neither sufficiently relevant nor probative to the case.

“For the foregoing reasons, the Defence respectfully requests that the Trial Chamber REJECT the Prosecution’s Application on the basis that P-1100’s proposed evidence is not sufficiently relevant or probative of the matters in dispute in this case,” it said.
The Defense argued that P-1100, the prosecution’s intended fact witness, does not have sufficient personal knowledge of the matters being disputed in Duterte's case.

The Prosecution, however, in its request, said the testimony is relevant to its allegations involving a policy to “neutralise” alleged criminals in the Philippines through violent crimes, including murder.

The testimony also provides evidence on the alleged modus operandi of the Davao Death Squad (DDS), as well as Duterte's alleged individual criminal responsibility, including his knowledge and intent, according to the Prosecution.

The ICC Trial Chamber said, in its decision, that “Rule 68(1) of the Rules mandates that the introduction of a prior recorded testimony is not prejudicial to or inconsistent with the rights of the accused or the fairness of trial.”
The Chamber also admitted five reports from witness P-1100 — PHL-OTP-0025-0267, PHL-OTP-0005-0737, PHL-OTP-0003-2952, PHL-OTP-0000-1797, and PHL-OTP-0000-1798.

“The Chamber is further satisfied that the introduction of P-1100’s prior recorded testimony will advance the expeditiousness of the proceedings, reducing the time required for his questioning by the Prosecution,” the ICC said.

“However, the Chamber notes the Prosecution’s request for two hours to conduct a supplementary examination of P-1100.50. The Chamber finds the requested amount of time to be excessive given the nature and content of P-1100’s evidence and defeats the purpose of Rule 68(3) of the Rules. The Prosecution shall therefore streamline its questioning so as to the complete its examination of P-1100 within one hour,” it said.
The trial is scheduled to begin on November 30, 2026.

Last April, the ICC confirmed the charges of crimes against humanity against former Duterte in connection with the killings during his war on drugs when he was mayor of Davao City and when he was president. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Digger is poised to be one of the biggest box-office flops of the year
articles.summary: Despite a major star's return to dramatic acting, a two-time best director winner at the Oscars and enough publicity to rival the moon landing, Digger looks set to become one of the biggest…

image.caption: Digger is an R-rated black comedy about an oil tycoon tasked with saving the world from a catastrophe his drilling caused. Warner predicts the film will only earn $12-15 million US domestically this weekend. (Warner Bros. Pictures)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Despite a major star's return to dramatic acting, a two-time best director winner at the Oscars and enough publicity to rival the moon landing, Digger looks set to become one of the biggest box-office disasters of the year.
Tom Cruise-led Warner Bros. film is projected to rake in a disappointing opening weekend

According to Variety, the dark comedy from director Alejandro G. Iñárritu and starring Tom Cruise saw its costs balloon from an original budget of $125 million US to $160-180 million — putting a break-even return around $350 million US when including its marketing spend. (Warner Bros. pushed back on this, telling Variety their actual break-even point is around $300 million US).

It earned only $1.2 million US in previews. And according to the Hollywood Reporter, Warner predicts the film will only earn $12-15 million US domestically this weekend: a dismal opening for the studio in a year already littered with poor performers. Following their films The Bride!, Supergirl, The End of Oak Street and Practical Magic 2 all releasing to apparent losses, that string of failures will possibly be capped by one of Warner Bros.'s biggest flops of the decade.

A bizarre story about an oil tycoon tasked with saving the world from a catastrophe his drilling caused, Digger was always a risk. The R-rated black comedy opted to skip the festival circuit entirely — instead operating on the hopes that strong word of mouth and big-name buzz would convince audiences to get off the couch and head to theatres.

The strategy of avoiding early critical negativity and gunning straight for Cruise fans made a sort of sense: it represents the actor's first non-franchise film since 2017's Barry Seal biopic American Made.
Tom Cruise's performance in Digger is brilliant, says our reviewer. You might disagree

And it is directed by Iñárritu: the auteur whose Birdman won best picture and director at the Oscars, while the following year's The Revenant snagged Leonardo DiCaprio his long-awaited best actor award along with another director win for Iñárritu. But as its earliest critical responses started to release last month, a wave of negative press threatened to sink those chances.

It has been called "the worst movie of Tom Cruise's career" by the Boston Globe, "a metafictional morass" from RogerEbert.com and "a lumbering white elephant of a movie that it almost makes you sorry for everyone involved" by the New York Times. In response to the negative reviews, the film's producers released an ad positioning Cruise's character cursing out critics.
But largely, even critics who loved the film — such as this writer — widely predicted that Digger would be too experimental and odd to ever hope to recoup its budget.

That puts Warner Bros. in a potentially difficult position; after a strong, awards-leading 2025 (including hits like Sinners, Weapons and One Battle After Another) their 2026 slate only offers modest success. Wuthering Heights, Lee Cronin's The Mummy and Evil Dead Burn did pull off positive numbers, though not a single Warner movie has earned above $100 million US domestically this year.

At the most extreme estimates, Digger's failure could put it into the arena with 2026's other big flops: Melania, which earned roughly $16 million US off a reported $40 million budget, and the Anthony Mackie-led Desert Warrior, which made less than $1 million US off its reported $150 million US budget, is still the biggest failure of the year.

items: Tom Cruise is fantastic in Digger. You might hate it
Ridley Scott's The Dog Stars bombs at the box office. Here's what that tells us about what audiences want

blocks.text: Digger could still prove valuable for Warner Bros. Despite its dismal expected performance, there is still speculation on whether Cruise could be pushed to Academy Awards success in the end. And given Cruise films' strong brand recognition, it could prove to be popular on streaming.

But the failure comes as the last release before Warner Bros. is fully acquired by Paramount on Tuesday. Digger's failure also came the same weekend as the Hollywood Reporter suggested that Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy — Warner's famously director-friendly film chiefs — would not continue with the company after the merger.
Digger taking bold, thematic risks — and being rewarded with such poor box office returns — could bode poorly for the new conglomerate's artistic choices.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Cornell frat house rape accuser 'under siege' online, says lawyer
articles.summary: A lawyer for Jane Doe says she is "not doing well" amid attempts to uncover her identity.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images

The lawyer for the woman who alleges she was raped at a Cornell University fraternity house says she is "not doing well" as she finds herself "under siege" from online sleuths seeking to identity her.

Thomas Giuffra said the woman known in legal documents as Jane Doe was "incapable of consent" because she was "completely, grossly intoxicated" when she turned up at the home where she says the assault took place.
The woman alleges she was raped by seven men at the campus in Ithaca, New York, in 2024.
No charges were initially filed in the case. It has reopened since she filed a civil lawsuit that thrust the claims into the national spotlight, reigniting the possibility of criminal charges.
In an interview on Friday with CNN, Giuffra said: "She's under siege on social media where people are trying to identify her."
He said that postings have "incorrectly" identified other woman as Doe.
Watch: New York governor blasts handling of Cornell rape inquiry

In an interview with CBS, the BBC's US partner, Giuffra argued that his client, aged 20 at the time, was unable to provide consent because she was intoxicated when she arrived at the fraternity house.
Giuffra said she had been pressured into taking the drug ketamine before she was allegedly raped.
His comments came as New York Governor Kathy Hochul appointed the state's top prosecutor, Attorney General Letitia James, to take over the investigation.
At a news conference on Friday, Hochul said she had "lost faith" in the county prosecutor's ability to oversee the case.
"This young woman had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable, and then at every turn she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her," Hochul said.
She also vowed to close a "loophole" of state law that makes it difficult to press rape charges if an alleged victim voluntarily consumes alcohol or drugs.
Cornell students voice frustration at public hearing over rape case
Social media feeds are filled with women trying to shield the Cornell accuser's identity by posting videos of themselves under the title "I am Jane Doe".
As well as seeking to complicate internet searches for her name, the messages of solidarity included clips of women detailing their own experiences of sexual assault.

Efforts to rally round Jane Doe gathered pace after a political commentator vowed to unmask her, arguing it was unfair for her to remain anonymous while the men are publicly named despite not being charged with a crime.
Online sleuths have also tried to locate the addresses of the so-called Cornell Seven, leading to at least one case of mistaken identity.

An active-duty US Marine Corps sergeant who had the same name as one of the men was incorrectly served the woman's lawsuit, leading to a torrent of abuse and threats, according to the Free Press, external.

articles.title: Could El Niño mean there are no Atlantic hurricanes this year?
articles.summary: For the first time in three decades there has not been a single Atlantic hurricane in September, normally the most active month.

blocks.text: For the first time in more than 30 years, a hurricane has not formed in the Atlantic throughout September - normally the most active month for hurricane activity.
The eerily quiet season continues and with just two months left, there is an increasing possibility that no hurricanes will develop at all.
This would make the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season the only one in the satellite era without a hurricane.
The biggest reason for this is El Niño, which traditionally stifles activity in the Atlantic but brings a very active season in the eastern North Pacific.
The Atlantic hurricane season was predicted to be quieter than normal as a result of this.

With a very strong El Niño forecast, the US National Hurricane Center in May predicted a total of eight to 14 named storms. Of those, three to six were predicted to become hurricanes, with one to three becoming major hurricanes.
September is typically the most active month for tropical storm and hurricane activity.
But, this year marks the latest date on record since the start of the satellite era (1960s onward) where no hurricane has formed in the North Atlantic.
While El Niño is the natural warming of the tropical Pacific, it can disrupt weather patterns around the globe.
As wind patterns shift during an El Niño, upper winds over the Atlantic increase and this leads to more wind shear, where wind changes rapidly with height.
Increased wind shear rips apart thunderstorms, preventing them from growing into tropical storms or hurricanes.
Meanwhile, the Pacific typically becomes more active during El Niño because the sea surface temperatures here are much higher, combined with more favourable wind patterns.
The warmer waters give storms more energy to grow into tropical storms and hurricanes.

This year, temperature records have already been broken in a key region of the central-eastern Pacific, with daily sea surface temperatures now exceeding the previous record set during the very strong El Niño of 2015.
There have so far been 17 named storms in the basin including nine hurricanes, seven of which were major.
In terms of the amount of energy these storms have produced - known as the Accumulated Cyclone Energy - this season is around two and half times more active than normal at this point.
El Niño is predicted to continue to strengthen with forecasts suggesting it will reach its peak in November or December.

articles.title: Women given shorts at Oktoberfest to prevent upskirting
articles.summary: The step at the Munich festival comes after thousands of voyeuristic videos emerged on social media.

blocks.text: One woman made €9,000 (£7,650) from a single clip, according to BR, whose investigations found that a group of professional YouTubers from Ukraine and several people from Bavaria were behind the videos.
At least 32,000 videos of women on the Teufelsrad have been in circulation, according to Munich-based daily Süddeutsche Zeitung. Some have apparently been viewed millions of times.

The operator of the Teufelsrad, Elisabeth Polaczy, told the BBC that, for the past three years, she has been handing out free cycling shorts to women and girls wearing dresses, to protect them from people filming in the crowd.
This Oktoberfest she has handed out more than 100 pairs, she says: "I want to do everything I can to make people feel secure."
Polaczy, who is now 80, said donating cycling shorts wasn't cheap, but it was worth it for her own peace of mind.

The Teufelsrad tent is hung with signs and police posters in German and English warning against filming under people's skirts, but Polaczy says it is impossible to control everyone filming with smart phones.
Some waitresses at this year's beer festival say they have also started wearing cycling shorts under their dirndls.
A spokesman for the Bavarian police told the BBC that since 2025, it has run a poster campaign at the Oktoberfest, warning against upskirting.
This year, police arrested a 45-year-old Swiss man for using his phone to film under a German woman's dirndl. Last year there were 10 arrests for upskirting and seven in 2024.

However, Josephine Ballon, who heads German non-profit organisation Hate Aid, which aims to support victims of digital violence, told the BBC that the current law against upskirting does not provide enough protection.
Although she says there are plans for a new law, current legislation "applies only when you film under the skirt", and not when a skirt simply flies up and gets photographed.
The new camera glasses are also a threat, she believes.
Ballon wants anyone who has uploaded intimate pictures of women on the internet to be punished, along with the platforms that put them up.
Meanwhile, the city of Munich has sought to tighten up on influencers and content creators who earn money from their social media postings and who want to film at the Oktoberfest.
Munich has banned broadcasting live streams from the festival and requires anyone who wants to film there to hold a permit, which is issued by the city for a fee.
Hundreds of licences have been issued this year to influencers, who make money from product placement or sponsoring.

articles.title: Hudson Williams wore this cardigan. Then the Indigenous designer's business went viral
articles.summary: The Heated Rivalry star wore Indigenous designer Justin Jacob Louis's blue-and-black journey knit cardigan to an event in New York on Wednesday along with an orange ribbon on his chest marking…

image.caption: Hudson Williams wears Indigenous designer Justin Jacob Louis's blue-and-black journey knit cardigan to the Kate Spade New York Global Summit on Women's Mental Health on Wednesday. The cardigan, which costs $350, quickly sold out. (Jason Lowrie/BFA)

blocks.text: Entertainment

The Heated Rivalry star wore Indigenous designer Justin Jacob Louis's blue-and-black journey knit cardigan to an event in New York on Wednesday along with an orange ribbon on his chest marking National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.
Designer saw online sales spike and the $350 cardigan quickly sold out
When Canadian actor Hudson Williams stepped out wearing a piece by Canadian Indigenous designer Justin Jacob Louis on Wednesday, Louis didn't expect to go viral.
In fact, he nearly forgot it was happening.
The Samson Cree Nation-born designer was spending National Day for Truth and Reconciliation away from work. He was with his family, unplugged and out paddling on the lake.
And then he checked his phone.
"There was, like, a whole bunch of sales and the social media was lighting up and I was just like, 'What is going on? Did something happen?'" he said in an interview with CBC News.
"I realized that, like, every cardigan had sold out. At that time, there was like $12,000 in sales in a matter of an hour. And I was like, 'What the hell?'"
How Hudson Williams sold out an Indigenous-designed cardigan

The Heated Rivalry star wore Louis's blue-and-black journey knit cardigan to the Kate Spade New York Global Summit on Women's Mental Health, along with an orange ribbon on his chest marking National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.
For Louis, seeing his work worn that day by a prominent Canadian actor made the moment "pretty special."
"There was intention and genuine interest in supporting us behind it, so that made it more meaningful for me," Louis said.

items: Artist from northwestern Ontario creates huge YWG airport sign for National Day for Truth and Reconciliation

blocks.text: The cardigan, which costs $350, was designed by Louis, founder and creative director of Section 35 and the Justin Jacob Louis label. And it made its way to Williams as part of a last minute request.
How they connected
Louis said someone from Williams's team initially contacted him by email and over Instagram about the actor's interest in buying the piece — just last weekend.
Shipping it from his warehouse wasn't feasible within the timeframe, but he happened to have the right size at his studio in the Fraser Valley in Chilliwack, B.C.
Someone from Williams's team drove from Vancouver to Louis's studio that Sunday to pick it up.
Months of sales in two days
That choice had an immediate impact on Louis's small business.
The brand gained hundreds of new followers throughout the day. The cardigan sold out and other pieces began selling, too.
Louis estimates the shop did two to three months worth of sales in just two days.

items: Toronto fans go wild for Hudson Williams. And the cast of his new show goes wild for Canada

blocks.text: While the brand hadn't planned on restocking the cardigan, the huge surge in demand persuaded Louis to open up pre-orders.
"For an independent small business, it helps out so much," he said. "It's just been kind of a whirlwind."
Design based on a dream
Louis says the design came to him in a dream he had while feeling disconnected and homesick and living about 12 hours from the community where he grew up.
In the dream, he was back at his father's place, walking across the pasture in winter under the night sky, wondering where his ancestors were.
"The stars in the sky lit up and then they turned into eyeballs and looked right at me," Louis said.
"It was just kind of like this reminder that they're always with you wherever you are, no matter how far from home you are."
Louis says Williams messaged him directly to thank him for the cardigan. They've stayed in touch, and the designer says he'd love to work with Williams again.

items: 5 places to buy Indigenous-designed orange shirts in the London region

blocks.text: But for now, he's focused on continuing to design and build his labels.
Here's his advice to other designers and small businesses: stay intentional and true to your values and culture.

"That makes us who we are," he said. "Showcasing the beauty that exists within our communities. I think there's so much talent and the storytelling that comes from our people and our stories. It's what sets us apart. And I think staying true to that is so important."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Griffin Jaeger is a reporter and producer with CBC's entertainment unit. He also formerly hosted and produced content for The National’s digital platforms. You can reach him at griffin.jaeger@cbc.ca

articles.title: US road rage killer's sentence quashed because AI video of victim was shown in court
articles.summary: The Arizona appeals court ruled that airing an AI message from the dead victim "crossed that line".

blocks.text: An Arizona road rage killer will be resentenced after an appeals court ruled that an AI-generated video message from his dead victim was improperly aired in court.
Gabriel Paul Horcasitas was found guilty by a jury of shooting and killing Christopher Pelkey, 37, during a confrontation at a red light in 2021. He was sentenced to 10 years behind bars.
But his legal team appealed, arguing that the trial judge should not have allowed an AI video, created by Pelkey's family, to be shown in court ahead of last year's sentencing.
The Arizona Court of Appeals agreed, ruling that Horcasitas, 55, must be resentenced because the AI clip "crossed that line".

"Rather than document an event or recording a particular moment, the AI video presents a depiction of the victim and his thoughts created from the imaginings of the victim's sister," the court of appeals wrote on Wednesday.
Horcasitas' lawyer, Kristen Reller, who filed the appeal, declined to comment.
Jessica Gattuso, an attorney for victims in the case, did not respond to a request for comment.
Pelkey's sister, Stacey Wales, told the BBC last year the family had used voice recordings, videos and pictures to recreate him for the AI video.

"To Gabriel Horcasitas, the man who shot me, it is a shame we encountered each other that day in those circumstances," said the AI version of Pelkey in court in 2025. "In another life, we probably could have been friends."
"I believe in forgiveness, and a God who forgives. I always have and I still do," the AI version of Pelkey - wearing a grey baseball cap - continued.
At the time of the sentencing, the judge who oversaw the case, Todd Lang, seemed to appreciate the use of AI.
"I loved that AI, thank you for that. As angry as you are, as justifiably angry as the family is, I heard the forgiveness," Judge Lang said. "I feel that that was genuine."

articles.title: The vanishing world of India's street magicians
articles.summary: India's street performers are struggling to survive as audiences shrink and public spaces become harder to access.

blocks.text: Sitting in his cramped Delhi home, Ishamuddin Khan can still make a rope appear to rise into the air.
The 55-year-old magician spent decades performing a trick once dismissed as legend, and still keeps photographs and newspaper clippings from his years of international fame.
These days, he spends more time looking back at those memories than performing the trick.
"The times have changed," he says. "Street magic is dying a slow death. It is on a ventilator."
Khan's story reflects a wider change in India, where traditional street performers are finding it increasingly difficult to make a living from their craft.

Magicians, jugglers, puppeteers and acrobats once made a living from crowds in public spaces. Changing entertainment habits and tighter restrictions have made audiences harder to find, pushing many out of the profession.
Khan, one of India's best-known magicians, comes from the Madari community, which has a long tradition of performing in public spaces.
There are no official figures, but Khan says community records identify about 400 Madari families in Delhi, with hundreds more in Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Telangana.
Despite their small numbers today, the Madaris trace their roots back centuries.
Historian Ashok Mathur says Madari traditions have roots in Indian folklore, mythology and the long history of travelling performers.
"For generations, these skills were passed through families," he explains.
Khan followed the same path, learning magic from his father and uncles and performing from the age of 12. By his early 20s, he had mastered the rope trick that would later make him famous.

The trick – in which a rope appears to rise into the air before a boy climbs it – was long associated with the mythology of Indian street magic and widely considered impossible, until Khan performed it.

He says it took six years to master the trick, which he first performed publicly in 1995 outside Delhi's iconic Qutub Minar. Two years later, he performed it before 30,000 people on a beach in Karnataka.
His trick brought international attention, and that led to tours to the UK, France, Germany and Japan.
Khan hoped the fame would shine a light on India's traditional performers. For a while, it did. But the attention faded.
As audiences turned to new forms of entertainment and public performance opportunities dwindled, many magicians found it harder to make a living from skills passed down through generations.
One of them is 40-year-old Imam Khan.

Once a magician, Imam now makes a living collecting bottles and recyclables from Delhi's streets. He spends much of his time rag-picking near a western Delhi dump, earning about 200 rupees ($2; £1.57) a day.
Experts say the decline in street performance has multiple causes, chief among them the changing nature of public spaces.
Anurupa Roy, founder of Katkatha Puppet Arts Trust, says performers increasingly struggle to find audiences as public spaces shrink.
"Closed parks and residential societies that bar outsiders are limiting spaces for performance."
Researcher and performer Komita Dhanda says changing attitudes to public spaces are also driving the decline.
"With tighter security, especially in busy town and city centres, there is little space left for street performers," she says.
It is not just individual artists who struggle to get permission. Dhanda says her well-known street theatre group, Jana Natya Manch, often faces hurdles performing in public spaces.
For many artists, the challenge is not just finding a venue but navigating unclear rules over what is allowed.
Most street performers rely on voluntary payments, but experts say the line between performing for money and begging can blur.
Unlike the UK, India has no federal busking framework. Performers instead navigate state-level rules on public order, obstruction, noise and public land.
"This is why street performers often have to face municipal and police regulations governing public spaces, as well as state-specific anti-begging laws," says lawyer Kaushik Mitra.
For many artists, Covid made a bad situation worse.
When India imposed its 2020 lockdown, public performances stopped. Many magicians returned to their villages; some never came back.
"We saw a decline in public performances after this period," Dhanda says. "The brunt was especially harsh for street magicians and performers, many of whom did not return to cities."
For the artists who did return and continue the trade, the challenges only increased.
Shahim Khan, 42, still performs magic on Delhi's streets, sometimes with his 12-year-old daughter, Alia.
Much of his work is now confined to industrial areas, far from the busy public spaces where he once performed, hitting his earnings hard.
Before the pandemic, he could stage four or five shows a day, earning 1,000-1,200 rupees.
"Now I barely manage two shows and earn 200-400 rupees," he says.
The rise of short-form digital entertainment has added to the pressures on traditional performers, experts say. So have changing attitudes towards street arts.
"There was a lot of Western interest in things like the rope trick decades ago. But forms and tastes have changed, and so has what India chooses to showcase," Dhanda says.
For Khan, the loss is about more than money. He fears an art passed down generations could disappear if no-one learns it.
"A trick can survive only if someone learns it," he says.
His son, Altamash, began performing with him as a teenager but now works decorating parties with balloons. In his 30s, he has largely left performing behind.
Years without regular practice have dulled his skills. When he demonstrated his juggling for the BBC, he struggled to find the rhythm.
"I am slowly forgetting all the tricks," he said.
Khan had hoped his son would carry on the family tradition. Altamash had hoped to make a name for himself too, but it did not work out.
"I knew I may not achieve the fame my father has, but I did not think there would come a time when performing would not remain an option," he says.

articles.title: Christa Pike unconscious after failed execution — attorneys
articles.summary: Lawyers for Christa Pike said she's unconscious and on a ventilator after a botched execution attempt. Pike is believed to be the first person to have survived the administration of lethal drugs in…

image.caption: Christa Pike has been on death row ever since she was convicted and sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer. [File: 2007]Image: J. Miles Cary/Knoxville News Sentinel/USA TODAY NETWORK/REUTERS

blocks.text: Christa Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator in a Nashville hospital in the hours after her bungled execution attempt in Tennessee, her attorneys said in a court filing on Friday.
Pike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, was audibly snoring after she was injected with two doses of lethal injection on Wednesday.
The court filing is the first account of what Pike went through in the hours after the botched execution attempt.
Pike's attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the lethal drug, called pentobarbital, to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.

"Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike's body," they wrote in the court filing.
Instead of "remedying this failure," they prepared and administered a second dose of pentobarbital, her lawyers said.
Pike believed to be first person to survive administration of lethal drugs
There are now questions about what happens next and whether the state can attempt to execute Pike again given her medical state.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, a Republican, temporarily paused the state execution on Thursday, saying there would be a "comprehensive, third-party review" of the case.
Pike, who is 50 years old, was set to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years.
She is believed to be the first person to survive after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs in the modern era of the death penalty, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

articles.title: North Korea fires ballistic missile into sea, Seoul says
articles.summary: North Korea fired a ballistic missile toward the sea off its east coast, the South Korean military has said.

blocks.text: South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said North Korea fired a ballistic missile on Saturday.

"Our military detected a ballistic missile launched from the Wonsan area of North Korea toward the East Sea," the Joint Chiefs of Staff said, referring to the body of water also known as the Sea of Japan.

The test came amid heightened tensions between the countries.Land mine blasts injured three South Korean soldiers last month. South Korea and the US-led UN Command have said North Korean mines caused the blasts.

On Friday, ​Pyongyang's Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of ​leader Kim Jong Un, dismissed Seoul's demand for an apology over the blasts in the Demilitarised Zone, the heavily fortified 4-kilometer-wide (2.5-mile) area between the two Koreas.
Seoul called on Pyongyang to end efforts to fortify the border, including the use of mines and anti-tank barriers.
Kim Yo Jong called those demands "utterly pathetic," adding that the North intended to cut ties with the South.

The projectile launch on Saturday came after weeks of North Korean military displays, including tests of a purported hypersonic missile system, live-fire exercises and the commissioning of a new warship.
Kim Jong Un has also continued to flaunt his growing nuclear program despite US calls to revive diplomacy.

articles.title: Brazil’s Lula says only he can stop rise of fascism under Bolsonaro’s son
articles.summary:
President leads huge rally in Rio before election on Sunday seen as most important for decades

The Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has claimed he is the only thing standing…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: The Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has claimed he is the only thing standing in the way of far-right “fascists” reclaiming power, as he led a huge rally through the streets of Rio ahead of Sunday’s crunch election.

Speaking on the eve of the demonstration, the 80-year-old leftwinger said he had decided to seek a historic fourth term because he believed only he could prevent the family of his rightwing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, returning to government.

“If it weren’t for me standing up to these fascists they’d easily win another election. I’m the one standing in their way,” Lula told a popular podcast called Flow, before adding: “It’s either me, or it’s barbarism.”

blocks.caption: Lula led a campaign march through central Rio de Janeiro, travelling from Candelária toward Cinelândia. Photograph: Mariana Greif/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Hours later, Lula flew to Rio, staging what his team called a “victory march” between two highly symbolic downtown locations that played an important role in Brazil’s fight for democracy during the 1964-1985 military dictatorship.

“What’s at stake is not the victory of one man, it is the victory of an idea, it’s the victory of democracy,” Brazil’s president said after the parade set off from the Candelária church. The church is the location where more than a million people, including Lula, famously gathered in 1984 to demand direct presidential elections.
Lula, who was among those who spoke at that historic demo when he was an up-and-coming politician in his 30s, added: “Either we consolidate democracy, or we will lose it.”
From Candelária, a sea of red-clad Lula supporters marched a mile south towards Cinelândia, the scene of an equally well-known pro-democracy protest in 1968 called the March of the Hundred Thousand.

blocks.caption: Lula, who is seeking re-election, used the the march to mobilise supporters two days before voters head to the polls on 4 October 2026. Photograph: Mariana Greif/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “No gringo is going to lay a finger on Brazil’s things,” vowed Lula, in an indirect reference to claims Donald Trump’s administration is seeking to sway the vote in Bolsonaro’s favour with a campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure.
The decision to hold Friday’s rally between two such politically charged places spoke to how this year’s election has stirred up renewed fears over the future of Latin America’s biggest democracy.

Election-eve polls suggest Lula holds only a slender lead over his adversary, whose father, the ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a failed coup after Lula beat him in the 2022 election.

blocks.caption: Two Lula supporters.  Photograph: António Lacerda/EPA

blocks.text: Many Brazilian democrats fear that if 45-year-old Bolsonaro wins this year’s election, he will move quickly to free his father and his fellow coup-plotters from jail – and then set about dismantling and co-opting the country’s democratic institutions, such as the supreme court.

“This is the most important election of our lives – and we have to do everything we can to win,” said Marcelo Freixo, a politician from Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) who is running for a seat in congress.

Freixo warned: “We spent 21 years living under a really harsh dictatorship. We fought so hard to attain our democratic institutions. And a victory for the Bolsonaro family – a family that always … openly defended the dictatorship and tried to stage a coup … would spell the end for our democratic process and institutions.”

blocks.caption: Supporters of the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, at Rio’s largest leftwing protest in years. Photograph: Pilar Olivares/Reuters

blocks.text: Valmir Aleixo, a 55-year-old history teacher who was one of thousands of people who joined Friday’s pro-Lula demo, said: “This is [a choice] between democracy and the savagery of far-right fascism. This is perhaps the most important election since the return of democracy in the 80s.”
Noni Ostrower, 74, came to what was Rio’s largest leftwing protest in years carrying a homemade banner that read: “Democracy Is Valuable”.

“I’m the daughter of two refugees from nazism. They came to Brazil from Germany because of this,” Ostrower said. “I was born here in Brazil … and today I have grandchildren and I absolutely do not want to see fascism return to Brazil – it would be a tragedy for the country. That’s why I’m here today.”

During the campaign, Flávio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his 71-year-old father if elected, with some speculating Jair Bolsonaro could even become a minister. His brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, a radical former congressman with ties to Trump’s Maga movement, reputedly hopes to become foreign minister. Flávio Bolsonaro has announced plans to appoint five firmly conservative supreme court judges.
Luiz Eduardo Soares, a prominent anthropologist and writer, said he feared what might happen if the Bolsonaro clan managed to reclaim power.

“I think these elections could be the last ones in my life, for my generation … What was done over the course of 10 years in Hungary, [Bolsonaro] will do in two,” Soares predicted in reference to the European country’s transformation into an “electoral autocracy” under its former prime minister, Viktor Orbán.

Diogo Nogueira, a famous samba singer who came to the rally wearing his trademark panama hat, said: “We need to win in the first round so we don’t allow this type of people to get back into government. If they ​do get back in, it won’t just be a problem for four years, but for 10 or 20.”

Polls suggest the election is likely to go to a second round runoff between Lula and Bolsonaro on 25 October, with Lula expected to secure about 45% of votes on Sunday and Bolsonaro 40%, according to the Datafolha pollster. But at Friday’s rally Lula claimed he could pull off a shock first-round win by claiming more than 50% of the vote.

In an online broadcast, Bolsonaro insisted his campaign would prevail. “Brazil is a few hours from deciding its future … for the next 30, 40, 50 years. It’s the end of an era. It’s the end of the Worker’s party era,” he claimed, asking undecided voters to back him to achieve that aim, even if they didn’t like him.

articles.title: Hawaii's iconic 550-year-old Hōlei Sea Arch collapses
articles.summary: The lava rock formation protruding from the rocky cliffs of Volcanoes National Park crumbled some time last weekend.

blocks.text: Hawaii's famous Hōlei Sea Arch, a 90-foot-tall (27.4m) lava rock structure that formed about 550 years ago, has collapsed into the Pacific Ocean.

The collapse's exact time is not known. The arch was still projecting into the water from the coast of Volcanoes National Park on 23 September, but was gone by 27 September, the National Park Service (NPS) said.
"The coastline flanking the sea arch has shown signs of instability for years," NPS, which warned in 2021 that the arch would eventually crumble, said in a statement.
Located at the end of Chain of Craters Road on the island of Hawaii, also called "the big island", the formation was a popular - and heavily photographed - tourist destination.
The arch is believed to have fallen when the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo last weekend.
The park service said earthquakes during the 2018 Kīlauea volcano eruption and summit collapse had damaged the cliffs near the arch.
Its ultimate collapse marks "the latest transformation of the park's remote and rugged coastline".
In January 2020, new cracks and instability in the cliffs led the park to close the original arch viewing area, and a few months later, a new viewing area opened at a safer distance, NPS said.
Waves from a tropical storm later that year broke off a chunk of rock from the bottom of the arch.

"This formation is beautiful, but temporary, and has a limited life span," the park service said in 2021. "The sea arch will eventually crumble into the sea. However, others will replace it as the cliff slowly migrates inland."
Thousands of people have liked and commented on the NPS social media post about the arch's collapse, including sharing their memories of visiting the arch and posting photos of it.
"Nothing and no one is here forever," one Facebook user commented. "Millions of years from now the sun will die. Appreciate the good, the beauty, now."

blocks.text: A man has been charged with planning acts of terrorism, including against far-right politician and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, British police said.
"We have been running a hugely intensive and complex investigation for some time," Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said, saying the investigation resulted in "this very serious charge."
The suspect, Joshua Kerry, was also charged with the murder of former MP and Reform UK spokesperson Ann Widdecombe.
According to the prosecutor handling the case, Kerry allegedly hit Widdecombe on her head 21 times with a hammer while she had been eating lunch.
Widdecombe's murder triggered reactions from across British politics, including demands to improve lawmakers' security arrangements.
The new charges against Kerry include one count of preparing acts of terrorism for actions allegedly carried out between May 31, 2024 and July 8, 2026.
According to the police's statement, the 28-year-old suspect is due to appear in a London magistrates' court on October 7.

articles.title: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel after Trump export ban threat
articles.summary: The coordinated release is aimed at heading off further price spikes and avoiding a ban on US diesel exports.

blocks.text: The G7 has agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel in a bid to ease supply pressures that have caused prices to skyrocket.
The group of advanced economies, including the US, said the move would include a "substantial release" of diesel in the coming days.
President Donald Trump had threatened to ban diesel exports in a move which would have eased pressure on prices for US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections, but pushed up prices elsewhere.
In a joint statement, the G7 said member countries had now agreed to "refrain from export restrictions on energy and energy products" on one another.
The G7 includes the US, UK, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the EU also represented at its meetings.
Trump had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not agree to put more of their own stocks onto the market.
On Friday, he said on social media: "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately."
His Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had argued US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar.
Diesel is used heavily by the haulage industry and in agriculture, meaning rises in the cost of the fuel feed through into essentials such as food.

But, following a meeting of G7 leaders, French President Emmanuel Macron said the bloc had agreed to release reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" within four months under the coordination of the International Energy Agency (IEA).

The UK was represented at the meeting by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who said the measures would "stabilise energy supplies, build resilience in supply chains and shield households and businesses from price shocks".

Macron said the coordinated action would "bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel". Highlighting the agreement not to pursue export bans, Macron said "President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point".
Speaking at the White House, Trump later said an export ban on diesel was "never really on the table".

In the joint statement, G7 leaders said: "We will implement our commitments with a coordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels to begin immediately over four months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners."
It is not yet clear which partner countries will release stocks, nor how quickly.

The 100 million barrels will comprise a mix of diesel and crude oil. The price of global benchmark Brent crude oil briefly dropped below $100 a barrel, but rose back to around $102 by Friday evening. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73.
Matt Smith, director of commodities research at Kpler, said oil had risen again due to renewed strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.

"Oil prices were selling off strongly due to the announcement of strategic stock releases in Europe, but they reversed course on rumours of Saudi Arabia planning an offensive into Yemen as it looks to re-establish a safe path via Bab-Al Mandeb," he said.
European countries had pushed back against US threats to turn off American diesel, against a backdrop of the US-led war in the Middle East and reduced supplies from Russia and China.

The G7 leaders said they will also coordinate maintenance schedules to avoid multiple refineries being shut down at the same time, while encouraging countries with the capacity to do so to ramp up refining of diesel in particular.
Supplies of diesel internationally have been heavily constrained by the conflict in the Middle East, which has restricted the flow of both crude oil and refined diesel onto global markets.

Russia, which is also a major producer, has implemented its own export ban on diesel, following attacks on its refineries by Ukraine, further limiting supply. The G7 leaders stressed that they will maintain sanctions against Russia amid its ongoing war in Ukraine.
Diesel is harder to refine than petrol and, because of its use in the haulage industry and agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand.

articles.title: Magnitude 4.8 earthquake hits Victoria with tremors felt across Melbourne
articles.summary:
The epicentre was at Leongatha, 130km south-east of Melbourne, with residents reporting houses shaking just after 2am

  • Get our

blocks.text: A magnitude 4.8 earthquake struck Victoria in the early hours of Saturday morning, shaking Melbourne and waking people across the whole region.

Geoscience Australia said it detected an earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 4.8 at 2.01am near Leongatha, 130km south-east of Melbourne, with the tremors felt across the city’s eastern suburbs.
Geoscience Australia said it had received thousands of reports from people who said they had felt the earthquake.
Posting on Facebook, Brian Morley in Narre Warren said “felt it and woke me up”, while Theresa Stevens said: “Shook our house in Garfield.”
Other posts indicated the quake had been felt in Preston, Heidelberg Heights, Venus Bay and many other parts of Melbourne.
The quake was estimated to have struck at about 10km below the Earth’s surface.

Victoria’s State Emergency Service said the earthquake was a “timely reminder” to remember the drill to follow during an earthquake and that was drop to the ground, take cover under a sturdy piece of furniture and protect your head and neck, and hold on until the shaking stops.
The Bureau of Meteorology said there was no tsunami threat from the quake.
